speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to seek concurrence for the Main Estimates and the Supplementary Estimates (A) for the fiscal year 1991-1992.
The Main Estimates total $158 billion. Through these estimates, the government is seeking Parliament's approval for $47 billion in new spending authority. The remaining $111 billion represents the statutory payments that have been previously approved by Parliament. These main estimates reflect our continuing commitment to control the spending and contain the cost of government.
Since taking office in 1984, this government has given high priority to reducing the cost of government operations, while still providing Canadians with programs and services they need.
This indicates our commitment to good management and to the careful stewardship of the taxpayers' dollar. In this regard, much has been achieved over the past six years.
Annual growth in program spending has been reduced on average to 3.7 per cent between 1984-85 and 1990-91.
Annual growth in operating and capital spending, including public service salaries has dropped to an average of 3.3 per cent, which is well below the annual rate of inflation.
The public service has been reduced since 1984-85 to roughly the same size as it was in the mid-1970s. These achievements show the government's commitment to increased efficiency through the rigorous control of
Supply
expenditures as well as the implementation of innovative management practices.
Mr. Speaker, our record is one of success and we are confident that we are on the right track.
Growth in the Main Estimates is the outcome of a number of decisions affecting the budgets of all 142 programs delivered through 118 departments, agencies and Crown corporations appearing in the estimates. This growth can be divided into two broad categories: adjustment of statutory items, which amount to $7.2 billion and changes to the voted items, which amount to $2.7 billion. Therefore, only 27 per cent of the growth in the Main Estimates relates to voted items.
These estimates fully reflect the second-year impact of the expenditure control program announced by the Minister of Finance in his February, 1990 budget and the 1991-92 expenditure savings flowing from the expenditure reduction and management improvement measures announced by the former President of the Treasury Board in December, 1989.
Had it not been for these measures, the 1991-92 main estimates would be higher by some $2.7 billion. Again, these changes demonstrate the government's commitment to restraint and economic recovery.
In his budget speech of last February, our hon. colleague, the Minister of Finance, set forth a strategy for economic recovery. The strategy is designed to put the recession behind us and to move forward to continuing growth and renewed prosperity. Part of that strategy involves putting government finances firmly on the course towards a balanced budget. We are removing the build-up of the public debt as a source of inflationary concern.
In order to do this, the expenditure control plan announced in the 1990 budget is to be extended for three years, to 1994-95. The government is legislating mandatory program spending limits. This should provide Canadians with greater assurance that program spending will be managed within the fiscal framework.
We are establishing a debt servicing and reduction fund-and that was introduced yesterday in the House- solely dedicated to offsetting the costs of the public debt. By law, all revenues from the goods and services tax and from privatization will flow into the debt servicing and reduction fund.

June 13, 1991
Supply
In his budget, the Minister of Finance also announced a number of reforms intended to bring about both immediate savings and lasting efficiencies in government programs and services.
Apart from the measures I have just mentioned, the government is imposing tight controls on the cost of government operations, which are expected to produce a savings of nearly $870 million in the current fiscal year. Over the five-year planning period to 1995-96, cumulative savings will amount to over $5.2 billion.
The budget also contains measures that, beginning in the 1991-92 year, will restrain spending on programs and operations of federal departments and agencies.
First, over-all spending on operating and capital for existing programs will be effectively frozen to the 1990-91 level. This will be accomplished by a 3 per cent cut in the Main Estimates in the operating as well as the capital budgets of each department. We have frozen departmental salary budgets for 1991-92 and we have just recently advised the public service union leaders that we have lost the flexibility to negotiate any wage increase this year.
Second, the government will reduce the cost of grants and contributions by $75 million. The Hon. Harvie Andre, the government House leader, has met with his colleagues and discussed how these reductions can best be achieved.
Third, the government will streamline its operations by reducing the number of its executives by ten per cent. This reduction is being achieved through a governmentwide program aimed at decreasing to three the number of levels of executives below the deputy minister. This will streamline departmental operations, reduce costs, improve the speed of decision-making and generally increase the authority given to public service employees in the regions and at the point of service delivery.
These three measures alone will generate savings of $760 million. These savings enable us to ease the pressure on essential programs and services. The battle to bring down the deficit continues, however, as does our search for ways to deliver programs and services better and more efficiently.
So, Mr. Speaker, innovative management practices will remain a priority for this government. The government has been increasing its effort to extend user
charges within the principle of fairness and equity. Through these efforts, the burden of financing activities that provide benefits to specific users is being shifted more towards those users and away from taxpayers generally.
Revenues from external user fees now exceed $3 billion, which is more than double the 1984-85 levels. The government is continuing to seek out new areas where the application of user fees is appropriate. This program promotes greater management discipline and operational efficiencies, since market forces are brought to bear on both the demand for and the supply of services.
The government believes that many services and functions are best carried out by public service employees. However, to provide a full range of options for delivering services to the Canadian people, certain functions are better done through contracting out where this is in the public interest, either in terms of cost, efficiency or quality of service.
Special operating agencies continue to be a viable mechanism for improving the delivery of public services and providing good value for the taxpayer's dollar. Over the past year we have established five agencies, among them the passport office, which have had positive results. Six more agencies have been announced through these Main Estimates including the Canadian General Standards Board and the Canadian Conservation Institute. More candidates will be identified in the coming year with a strong emphasis on organizations that directly serve the public, where the potential for improvement is greater.
Privatization will remain a key priority. The government's program has already devolved more than 18 Crown corporations and other corporate holdings to the private sector and other levels of government. The government will privatize CN Exploration, an oil and gas company, and will wind up Petro-Canada International Assistance Corporation and the Canadian Oil and Gas Lands Administration. These measures reinforce the consistent action the government has taken since 1984 to control the cost of government operations. They are also expected to engender considerable changes in the way departments and agencies do business-that is, in the nature and type of resources used as inputs, in the technology applied and in the organization and methods of program delivery.
June 13, 1991

The Main Estimates you have before you are those of a government serious about restraint and serious about reform. We are determined to cut expenditures and to organize and operate government operations in a manner that suits the real needs of Canadians.
I note that one of the motions today, Mr. Speaker, is about the Senate. I don't know where the New Democratic Party stands on the Senate. I hope the hon. member for Kamloops will enlighten us, but it has always been my understanding that they have wanted to dispose of the Senate, to get rid of it.
Now we hear them saying- if I believe what I read in the newspapers-that maybe they do not want to get rid of the Senate; maybe they want the Senate to stay as one of the institutions of government in this country. If that is the case, I hope the hon. member will enlighten us and explain to us why they have had this change of heart. Since I have been here, and it has been a few years now, they have always believed that the objective of the New Democratic Party was to eliminate and abolish the Senate.
In that vein, I do not think any of them, or very many of them, have ever taken an appointment. We can speculate now that perhaps the New Democratic Party is hoping that somewhere down the line it will be able to take some of its senior and long serving members and appoint them to the Senate. I look forward to comments from the hon. member for Kamloops as to what the intentions of his party are.
Mr. Speaker, let me make the point very clearly to my hon. friend from Burlington-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Since there are no questions or comments, the hon. member for Kamloops.

I appreciate the co-operation of my hon. colleagues to permit me to get to an important committee meeting. Let me say right from the outset to my hon. friend from Burlington that I consider the existing Senate of Canada to be a parliamentary obscenity.
I believe that the present Senate is undemocratic and has no place in a modern democracy. We have been on record since day one. I must say we have never accepted one of those obscene appointments as members of the New Democratic Party. We will not accept becoming some appointed hack, a bagman, or some kind of political flack to the Senate. The New Democratic Party will not

accept an appointment to an obscene institution in our democratic parliamentary system. I think that makes our position relatively clear.
I want to say that my hon. friend from Burlington was pointing out ways that the government was hoping to save money. Let me give him an excellent way to save money. That is why I propose this motion that we save ourselves $30,645,000 by cutting out the operating funds for the Senate of Canada.
Some people might say: "Well, listen, those folks over there do a fair bit of work, don't they?" I am going to share with you some information which I think will make any decent Canadian sick. Is the Senate working? Are the senators working on our behalf, on behalf of the citizens of Canada now?
During the month of February the Senate sat for a total of nine hours and five minutes. All month long the House of Commons is sitting day after day after day. The committees are meeting day after day, and the Senate manages to sit for nine hours and five minutes.
On top of that, this is the same group of people who wanted to get themselves $153 a day bonus to show up to work in the Senate. They would not make much money considering how often the Senate even comes together.
I want to say that during January it was even worse. Some days it met for one hour. Another day it met for an hour and 40 minutes. That was a pretty major working day. Then in March the Senate sat for a total of 12 hours and 40 minutes. In April it sat for a total of 12 hours and 40 minutes again and in May it sat for a total of 15 hours and 50 minutes.
In other words, what most people would do in an average working week, the Senate took four months to accomplish. This is, as I say, a parliamentary obscenity. This is wrong. This is an abuse of the parliamentary system. This is undemocratic.
My hon. friend made some cynical comments about what he thought might be our position. This comment is from the member of a government that appointed eight more senators. It had too many senators, and the government said that in order to jam legislation through the Senate that the majority of Canadians oppose, it was going to have to do something never done before in parliamentary history. It was going to add eight new Tory appointments. It found some flacks out there who had been long-standing members of the Conservative Party and gave them, if you like-

favour of disbanding the Senate in its present form. That is what I am suggesting in this motion.
They would like to ban us too.

"They would like to ban us too, my hon. friend from Toronto says".

Mr. Speaker, to me as one of those 26 million Canadians, this is news that the NDP is now viewing the Senate with this incredible eye and with this incredible vision.

Therefore, I do not think it is fair to attack the Senate and attack the credibility of the Senate in terms of the quality of the people serving there. I think if we are to look at the issue, we should look at the system as a whole.
It has been echoed by the Leader of the Opposition. As well members of the NDP have been calling for an elected Senate for some time. I want to take this opportunity to say how disappointed I was when yesterday I read in the newspapers, of the past few weeks the major assault that was going on against our senior public servants.
I will close very shortly. If there is any reform, that is the area we should reform. Of course, with that concern for waste right now when everybody in the country is going through reorganization, there is no way we can exempt either House from that process of review.
I think he should also pass on these words of watching for waste or spending money that is not necessarily needed or that could be used more wisely. I think he should also pass on this concern to his friends and fellow NDP colleagues in the province of Ontario. We do not want a situation to creep into the province of Ontario. It can creep into anyone who has been around for a long time. Already, and we are not even talking a year, just this week it was announced that our premier, for whom intellectually I have a lot of respect, got a Question Period preparation team. They have calculated with this new budget he has acquired that it costs the taxpayers of Ontario close to $1,000 to prepare him for every question that we ask him.
Therefore, I think that yes, we have to eliminate waste in the Senate here. However, I think wherever we have friends in government right now we have to pass on that message I think Canadian taxpayers are equally concerned about all levels of government and the way we handle their money.

I appreciate the intervention by my hon. colleague. Yes, Canadians are concerned about how all levels of government are spending their tax dollars.
There is a reason for this motion today. If there is unanimity in the land on a single issue, it would be that the Senate as we know it today should be abolished. I have yet to run into a single person in my life who comes to me and says that he or she thinks the present Senate is doing a wonderful job and is worth $30 million a year in operating funds.
I have not found anybody who says the Senate is worth $2,425 a working minute. I have not found anybody. I have never in my life encountered a single person. That is why I say on this one issue that I think we can all agree the Senate as we know it today does not perform a valuable and useful function in a democratic society. As a matter of fact, it is an undemocratic society by definition.

I am talking about when the hon. member started; he was getting right into condemning the other place, and I thought I would just stop him at that point. I understand.

Mr. Speaker, I have searched very carefully through the list of prohibited expressions in Beauchesne's and I regret to inform the hon. member for Ontario that "two-faced" is not there. I want to explain what I meant by the expression in relation to statements by the hon. member for Kamloops. He has now said he wants to get rid of the Senate and he has introduced a resolution today which will stop the payment of any money to the Senate. If by chance that is carried the Senate cannot carry on its work.
I recall not many months ago when he was urging the Senate of Canada, the other place; to use its full authority under the Constitution to block the goods and services tax.
His party, the hon. member for Kamloops claims, is committed to abolishing the Senate. How you could be more two-faced than, on the one hand, saying we want the Senate abolished and, on the other hand, saying we want the Senate to block a major piece of government legislation and urging the senators on a daily basis to block the legislation, I do not know, Mr. Speaker. It is as two-faced as-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Oshawa on a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, on a second occasion in a brief period of time you have allowed one member to accuse another member of being two-faced. If that language is appropriate in this Chamber I have no problem. I have a complete vocabulary and can use that. But in my view, having been in a parliament for some time, it is not appropriate and the Chair will know that it is context not-

Mr. Speaker, if it is unparliamentary, of course. I have checked the authorities and am satisfied from my checking of Beauchesne's that it is not. If Your

Honour finds differently, of course I will respect Your Honour's view.
What I want to do is indicate the nature of that position that the New Democratic Party is putting forward. On the one hand, let us abolish the Senate; on the other hand, let us have the Senate block government bills. That is the-
And the trade unions asked them for it.
Of course the trade unions supported the Senate on that. Lots of Canadians supported the Senate on that. That is why the New Democratic Party decided it better jump on the bandwagon.
What do you call it?

It decided it had better abandon its policy of abolition and go for supporting the Senate. When it was politically convenient to support the Senate they were in there with the best of them, harping away on how great the Senate was and how it had better block this bill. As soon as the Senate did not block it because it got stacked by a number of Tory hacks, then we were stuck with the proposition where the New Democratic Party apparently changed its tune again-at least according to the hon. member for Kamloops.
But he has been wrong on this point before and I brought him to task on it before. I pointed out that his position on abolition, which he espoused so vociferously in this House about a year and a bit ago, was not in accordance with the party's position. I have some evidence here about that. I have a newspaper article from The Toronto Star. The hon. member for Ontario must be very familiar with The Toronto Star; it is published in his part of the province.
It talks about the position the New Democratic Party was finding itself in just last week before its convention. We had the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville who was supporting the idea of a Senate and changing it around. He wanted to make the Senate an elected body but he was quite anxious that half the Senate seats be reserved for women. He was apparently chairman of some constitutional committee in the New Democratic Party, so he is something of an expert in the party on this issue, I gather. I presume he speaks with some authority-I suspect more authority than the hon. member for Kamloops who has gone on a wing and a prayer in his speeches on this subject before in this House. He has gone off the party line, with respect.

June 13, 1991

This committee submitted a report and apparently the report was prepared prior to the big pow-wow in Halifax last weekend. It says in this particular Toronto Star article that: "The committee, whose report will be considered at a party convention in Halifax this weekend, does not say whether it will be better to reform the Senate or retain the long-standing NDP promise to abolish it". In other words, they are dithering again. They are waiting to see what the Canadian people think, because if the Senate becomes popular, you-know-who will want to support the Senate. However, if the Senate stays unpopular, you-know-who will want to abolish it.
It is "sit on the fence" time, the new NDP technique. They have learned this from their colleagues in Ontario. They got elected with all these rash promises to do this and do that, but they are sitting on the fence on almost every one of them now because they know that those policies are very unpopular.
What do you call it? The "old picket fence approach".

It is the "old picket fence approach", as my hon. colleague suggests.
Then he says-and this is continuing to quote from the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville: "But it is probably the first time that a group in the NDP has floated the possibility of an elected Senate with certain powers".
It might be, except that at a previous convention there was discussion about this and I was able to quote for the benefit of the hon. member for Kamloops about a year and a half ago how this matter was under study as a result of some convention. I do not know what the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville is talking about, but perhaps it is the first time he had considered it.
Then he goes on with this. He said: "Proposals for a Senate with equal representation from each province are "absurd", but the committee ducked the question of just how many seats each region should have". Well, I can understand them ducking that. If they weren't prepared to go with the equal concept, they had to come up with something else, and that would be a bit difficult. You know, when you abandon principles and you have no principle to go on, how can you possibly come up with an answer to any question? We all know that the principles here were abandoned lock, stock and barrel.
Let us hear more about this committee and what it isn't sure of. After all, this is the party that, according to its leader, the hon. member for Yukon, has become the White Knight of Canadian politics-dashing through, making decisions right, left and centre, slashing the other parties to bits. Well, we all know that is a lot of poppycock.
Here is what it says here: "There is no consensus in the party as to whether or not there should be one House of Parliament or two", the member for Yorkton- Melville told reporters. Boy, they haven't even decided on principles like that. Maybe there should be one House, maybe there should be two-maybe three. They don't seem to know. They haven't the faintest idea what to do with the Canadian Parliament. And this from a New Democratic Party that prides itself on principles. Where are the principles? What has happened to the principles?
The principle used to be that you could not have a Senate, it had to be abolished. Now, it seems to be in grave doubt. Boy, these principles are going down the tubes.
I was hoping that the hon. member for Kamloops would enlighten us on what happened at the convention itself. I thought that perhaps he could tell us what happened with this committee report. But I understand that because the public opinion polls have not gone one way or the other, this issue like so many others was swept under the carpet. I think it was sent back to the committee so they could look at the issue again and come back with more.
The hon. members who are here were at the convention in Halifax. Perhaps they could enlighten us later in the day. I would be interested to know just what happened.
It is the old fifty-fifty routine, as the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood says. They really don't know what they are going to do; they are waiting to see how the polls go. If the polls go one way, the NDP undoubtedly will go with them. They are quite anxious to please the public at every turn these days, because they feel if they can please the public perhaps they can follow the example set by their colleagues in the province of Ontario and win an election.


Frankly, I do not believe that is likely. I think the New Democratic Party did better in getting its 20 per cent of the vote when it stuck to its principles, but it appears that it is willing to abandon those in a desperate bid to steal votes from the Liberal Party. I notice now that instead of us adopting their policies, which they always used to accuse us of, they are adopting our policies holus-bolus.
1 am delighted to see some support for many of the positions we in this party have advocated. The abandonment of the policy of nationalization of the banks, I notice, transpired in Halifax. All those socialist dogmas that have plagued the NDP since the 1930s are being washed away.
They are becoming Liberals.
They are becoming Liberals. I am delighted to see this deathbed repentance.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I do not know whether this is going to be unparliamentary language or not. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry I stirred up such a hornets' nest on my left.
I want to turn to the party across the way because after all they are the ones who are causing the real problem today and that is why we are discussing their estimates.
I sat here yesterday afternoon and listened in rapt attention to a delightful speech delivered by the Leader of the Opposition on the subject of ministerial responsibility. In fact I think it could have been entitled, a speech on ministerial irresponsibility. I am sorry that the hon. member for Churchill was not here to hear the speech. He would have been entranced. It would have been an excellent lesson for him in constitutional law, which might have been helpful in this committee that I hope he is working on to try to solve the constitutional problems of the New Democratic Party.
The fact is the government got itself into a dilemma in recent weeks by its failure to deal properly with the persons working for the government and by its callous mistreatment of public servants. I think the opportunity that was presented yesterday to discuss this was a most
Supply
worthwhile one. I feel that what the government is seeking to do is rewrite the rules relating to ministerial responsibility.
I note this morning the government members voted against the words taken from the Public Service 2000 report which is, after all, their statement of what ministerial responsibility means. They abandoned the concept and voted against it. This government is opposed to the notion. It is abandoning the parameters, the principles of our Constitution. The members who are supporting it should be ashamed of their conduct in supporting such an outrageous attack-and a consistent one I may say- in a pattern over the years that has helped seriously to weaken our democratic institutions.
I want to review briefly for members the list of things that I think could, at least, top the list of abuses the government has proceeded with that in my view have damaged this institution, both the Senate and the House of Commons.
I could start the list with the excessive use of closure and time allocation. We have never had a Parliament before where so much use of those tools has been made. Closure has been used 15 times now in this Parliament. That is a record. It has been a record for quite some time. I think it became a record on the seventh occasion it was used.
I do not have my list here to tell me how many times time allocation has been used, but I think it is seven or eight.
In addition, we have had unilateral rule changes imposed by closure in this House. There was negotiation on some of the points. I concede that. But on many others, the government knows that it proceeded unilaterally and against the expressed wishes of both opposition parties. Those rules were imposed through the use of closure after a very limited debate. They have restricted the rights of members of the opposition to carry on their responsibilities in this House. They have been designed to protect the government from criticism because the government, at 14 per cent in the polls, knows that it has a problem. Anything it can do to silence its critics is a blessing. That is exactly what they look for, an opportunity to silence the critics. We see exactly the same thing proceeding in the other place.

June 13, 1991
Supply
Until December of last year we had a majority that was made up of members of this party. Nothing could have been more upsetting to the government opposite than to have to face the music in the other place when bills were sent down there that were no good. The veiy effective Liberal majority in the Senate, which the hon. member for Kamloops now talks of in such disparaging terms, was in fact a very effective, capable debating body which gave a very sober second look at the dreadful legislation this government forced through this House. It held the legislation up to public scrutiny. It allowed the public to see how bad it was. It went on cross-country tours and heard the views of Canadians when this government ignored those views for months and months and days and days of debate in this House.
There were no months of debate, just days, but month after month in Question Period the government ignored them. The hon. member knows that. He knows what I am saying is correct. If stacking the Senate was not enough-because what they did, as we all know now, was stuff the Senate with an additional eight Conservative members so that they could obtain a working majority in the other place-they are now proceeding to change the rules of the other place. The new majority has come up with a new set of rules that will limit debate in the other place so that it will become a rubber stamp for this government's rotten policies that have done so much damage in this country.
I think it is just another shocking example of the abuse of Parliament and its traditions and its forms that this government has indulged in. First of all you stack it, then you change the rules.
Sure, I have no trouble saying it with a straight face, and the hon. member I am sure agrees with me. I am surprised that he would have voted against the doctrine of ministerial responsibility in that vote this morning. Those are words that his government put forward as their statement and yet he was there with the best of them voting against it.
I want to turn to the appointment of the privacy commissioner as another example of the abuse of the processes of this House. The law provides that in the case of certain appointments, and the privacy commissioner is one, a resolution of the House of Commons and of the Senate is required for the appointment. The
Governor General in Council may appoint only after obtaining the approval of the two Houses.
What happened? The government introduced the motion to have the privacy commissioner appointed without any consultation with the opposition over the direct objection of the members of the opposition, and forced it through on a vote. In other words, there was no discussion. None of the usual parameters were followed.
The usual practice in all those appointments has been for consultation to occur between government and opposition and a consensus to be reached on the name of the nominee. Then, and only then, is the resolution normally introduced in this House, and it is normally passed then with a minimum of debate and by the unanimous agreement of all members.
No such discussions took place in this case. This was a case of a straight ram operation to jam this name through the House, a former employee of the Prime Minister rammed through the House. Favouritism and paying off debts, that is what this was. The opposition properly raised objections to this, and in the other place the matter was properly held up until once again the bully-boys from the government group forced the appointment through the Senate after the Senate had been appropriately stacked.
Then we could turn to the more recent attempts on the part of the government to change Question Period. They have decided that Question Period is the most damaging session of all for this government because there they have to stand and answer questions without notice, and they look so bad. It looked so bad just the last couple of weeks when questions have been asked on this Al-Mashat affair to see a minister of the Crown stand there and say: "I am not going to answer, Mr. Speaker. This matter is before a committee" and sit down. It is a complete abdication of their responsibility to this House.
Those ministers can answer in this House, and in case the public is in any way deceived ministers are entitled to give those answers whether or not the matter is before a committee. They have an obligation to do so, in my submission. They should have been here stating their answers in this House. They should be giving the facts to the House. Instead of that, they swept it off to a committee where they refused to allow the television cameras to go in order to ensure that the public could see how dreadfully badly these ministers have acted and how little they know about how to run their departments.
June 13, 1991

We could then also look at the fact that they introduced a motion to deem these bills to be adopted at many stages, at least in the early part of this Parliament, ones that had been discussed in the last session of this Parliament.
I spoke on that recently, about a week and a half ago, and I suggest to Your Honour that that is another case of contempt and abuse of the procedures of this House. They used a motion to reinstate five bills, and they used closure on the motion and thereby avoided the opportunity to speak and criticize the bill at each of the other stages.
Finally, there is their abdication of the doctrine of responsible government, their failure to defend the public servants who are working for them in the government where the Secretary of State for External Affairs has been trying her best to defend her former colleague who is now the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs. He clearly should have said that the responsibility for the admission of Mr. Al-Mashat was his responsibility.
He should never have pointed a finger at any person working either in his own office or in his department. All the ministers have a collective responsibility. They cannot say that it is not their responsibility because they did not know.
There are lots of things that happen in the Government of Canada about which a minister does not know. For a minister to stand in this House and say: "I am not responsible because I did not know so-and-so or so-and-so, that person is responsible," is a complete abdication of ministerial responsibility.
It is a shocking, disgraceful way to conduct oneself. The ministers involved in this case, who in every respect may have been able to defend their actions and put up with some criticism from the public, are paid to take that kind of criticism from the public.
Instead of taking criticism they stood around and said: "Who can we blame? Who will we shuffle this off to?" They got into a little meeting. It was a star chamber court where they sat about and decided that so-and-so is guilty and so-and-so is guilty. "We will blame them and say they apologized and that will be that".
That is exactly what was done in this case. It was disgraceful. It was disgusting. Because of their conduct, all three ministers should resign immediately.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say to the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands through you, sir, that when it comes to the conduct of members of Parliament, it may well be that some of what he was saying is worthy of our consideration and reflection. It is inappropriate in the extreme for the member to believe that this is a need for change that takes place in only one political party.
I want to set before you, sir, some observations that I have made after having been here for about 17 years.
What is still, as it was when I first arrived in Parliament, a part of parliamentary rules in Beauchesne's and Erskine May today would be some of the following: In Question Period a question is not to be argumentative.
If the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands from the Official Opposition reflects upon it, has he heard an argumentative question? I believe that he has.
Questions are not to have preambles. Anybody who does an objective measure of Question Period will know that there is more preamble than there is question. These are breaches of the rules, breaches made principally by the party of the member who has just spoken.
It is inappropriate, improper and wrong according to the rules of the Table to have innuendo. I cannot remember the last Question Period where there were no examples of innuendo. People are being accused and stand almost convicted for no other reason than an accusation was made.
For the member for Kingston and the Islands to come here and somehow hold himself up in the holy sepulchre of purity and to pretend for the moment that he can condemn all others because he thinks there is some breach of the rules, when he says that we on the government side somehow are trying to change Question Period, I tell him that if he were to put all the people in Canada who believe that Question Period is an appropriate mechanism today in Prince Edward Island and all of those who think that there is something wrong and needs to be changed on Vancouver Island, Prince Edward Island would be 3,000 feet above sea level because the weight distribution would be so changed.

June 13, 1991
Supply
Canadians do not believe that Question Period is serving their needs or their aspirations as to where a country should be.
I say to the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands through you, Mr. Speaker, that Erskine May says questions cannot be repetitive.
I came here when speakers used to say: "If the hon. member will check the records, he will see that that precise question was asked on Tuesday" and give some date two weeks ago. He would go on to another member. We now have Question Periods which repeat the whole question as many as five, six, seven times in a single Question Period.
The hon. member should know that any breach of rules is not a breach of rules that falls on one party, because he belongs to a party that is a principal partaker in the abrogation of the rules that have been so clearly and long established in this House. We cannot move when the mace is in motion, and yet members of Parliament here too frequently have disrespect for the mace. When the Speaker rises every member is supposed to be seated, yet often we see a Speaker rise and a member standing and the two are staring at one another. When The Speaker rises every member should be seated and there should be silence in the House of Commons.
I have spoken long enough, Mr. Speaker, and when you rise I will have to sit. But I say to the hon. member, could you answer me, in all clarity, is there not some reason for all of us to reflect on changing the rules of this House for more effective debate. It is a non-partisan issue, it is Parliament that is at stake and all of us, in the interest of our constituents in all parts of the country have a burden to make this place run better.

I, of course, agree with that part of the hon. member's statement, Mr. Speaker. The last question he put to me of course I agree with. We all have that responsibility and we all take it very seriously.
What I do object to, and I think he should know this, first of all concerns his suggestion that somehow Question Period today is radically different. I do not believe that it is. I think Question Period was the same in 1984, 1983, 1982 and in 1981 when the party that he represents
was in opposition. The New Democratic Party has been in opposition throughout that time and I do not believe its questions have materially altered in the course of the last decade or 20 years for that matter.
The hon. member thinks that maybe they have. If he looks at a recent article by Don McGillivray in, I think yesterday's, The Ottawa Citizen, he will see that on Mr. McGillivray's own checking over a 20 or 30 year period, I have forgotten how many years he went back-
Thirty years.

Thirty years. He pulled out the Question Period each decade on the day and looked at what had happened and found that the pattern was very similar to what it is today. Almost all the questions were asked by the opposition. In fact, my recollection is that on two of the days every single question was asked by the opposition. We are now allowing some government questions which I think is a change. In addition to that, the questions were argumentative, they had preambles, they had innuendoes, they were partisan. All of that is part of the mix. There has been no change in that.
What has changed is the standing in the polls of this government. It has gone down to 14 per cent. So the Conservatives feel that something must be wrong with Question Period for them to be so bad, that is the fear.
I think it is wrong. I think the Conservatives should regard that and look at it very carefully and say: "Are we trying to change this for the wrong reasons?" If members look in their heart of hearts I think they will see that is exactly what is going on. They do not really care how partisan it was because they enjoyed it themselves when they were in opposition and had the opportunity to ask. They are so bad in government that they just keep slumping in the polls and Question Period does not help them get out of the slump. That is why they want to get it changed. They want more softball questions from their own members and the backbench so that the ministers can look good once in awhile when they answer a question. They do not look good when they answer our questions because most of the time they do not answer them.
June 13, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I thought the member for Crowfoot would sit down when the Speaker recognized me.
What I should remind both members is that the issue before the House is the proposal by our party that the government can save on its expenditures by reducing the amount of money allocated to the Senate. It is interesting that every time we make this proposal the Liberals rush up to defend the Senate and then slam us for whatever particular reasons they can.
The reality is that a body that has worked so little over the last four months cannot be justified. The reality is, and the reason the Liberals get up and defend the Senate is, that not only has it been used for patronage, but it also provides Liberal election planning. The Liberal Party of Canada, at this time, cannot survive without the Senate because it would not have an election planning body.
If you take a look at various senators-I will not go through them name by name nor province by province- their reasons for being there are to raise funds, to organize campaigns in various provinces or to be campaign managers either at the provincial level or at the federal level.
I noticed that the Liberal member from Kingston and the Islands said that the NDP is always plagiarizing their ideas. He used the word "hypocrisy." I think perhaps he should look at himself. I remember reading the Liberal proposal to the Royal commission on the Elections Act. The Liberals took my private member's bill, added four words to it and pretended that it was their own legislation. He says they gave us credit. They said that we had dealt with a similar matter.
I have a proposal. I should give the member for Kingston and the Islands a chance to hear about it now so he can draft his own legislation. We are introducing changes to our definition of what election expense is, so when we do that I hope he will be ready to follow suit.
I think one of the suggestions we could make is that the cost of the Senate be divided. The Tories would allocate their senators as part of their election expenses and the Liberals would agree to count their senators

because they are involved, paid for by the public, and spend full time working on elections. I think it is only fair that since they like to steal our ideas with regards to election expenses, they would voluntarily include the cost of each and every one of those Liberal senators as part of their election expenses.

Mr. Speaker, the NDP as usual has put down what I think is an absolutely fascinating proposal. I want to say a few words about it and some other things in the few minutes I have at my disposal.
I want to say to my friend from Kingston and the Islands, who has great knowledge in this whole area of how Parliament functions, that I thought he overreacted. I say to him in generosity, I thought he had over-reacted this morning to the NDP shenanigans. Surely that is all they are. They are shenanigans.
Now he is being parliamentary.

The member for Oshawa talks about what is parliamentary. I thought he would have done well this morning to know the rules himself, to have realized that if he is going to get up and repeatedly interrupt what was a good speech by my friend from Kingston and the Islands, he ought to at least have a citation. He quoted no citation. The word "two-faced" is perfectly legitimate. It is also very accurate in the circumstance.
What more could you ask of a vocabulary than it be, first, legitimate, and second, suit the purpose, that it be appropriate. What could be more appropriate than two-faced when you talk about what the NDP is doing in this particular amendment.

June 13, 1991
Supply
Let us understand what they want to do. They want to wipe out the operational expenses that would be provided under the main estimates for the current year, as they relate to the Senate's operation. To do that, the member for Kamloops cites-he has done some arithmetic and we will assume his arithmetic is correct-that it is some $2,000 a minute. Of course, what he has done to arrive at that, I suppose, is to take the number of hours or minutes the Senate sits and then this operating amount that is in the estimates, and divided one with the other and come up with a couple of thousand bucks a minute.
An interesting question arises. He is telling us that it is his view that the only time the senators are at work is when they are in the Senate. That is what he has done in his bit of arithmetic; he has taken the number of hours they are in the Senate and divided it into the total expense of operating the Senate. And so he is extrapolating that the only time these senators are working is when they are in the Senate.
I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, and I put it to him, wherever he is now, the member for Kamloops, since he is not physically in the Chamber right now, is he not working either? Is that what he is telling us, that he should probably not be paid for that? I mean, how ridiculous.

A point of order, Mr. Speaker. I have two quick points. One, I think the hon. member knows the rule in the House about referring to the presence or non-presence of members in the House; second, the member for Kamloops is attending a very important meeting at this moment. He knows that very well and he should not abuse the rules of this House.

I thank the gentleman from Prince George-Bulkley Valley. He should not be telling us that the member for Kamloops is attending a meeting because in so doing he is drawing attention to his absence from this Chamber, and he is breaking the rules, you see.
However, let me thank the gentleman from Prince George-Bulkley Valley. Let me use him as an example. You see, he is in this Chamber. I am allowed to note the presence of somebody. He is in the Chamber. I see him. He is bodily in this Chamber.
The question is, and it is an entirely theoretical one, if the member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley were not in the Chamber-which he is, I point out-then by applying the arithmetic and the logic of his colleague from Kamloops, who I have to assume is in the Chamber except I was told just now that he might be at a meeting somewhere, who says that the only time you ought to
apportion cost is when they are in the Chamber, then I put it to you, sir, as a theoretical question understand, that if my friend from Prince George-Bulkley Valley were not in the Chamber then should he be paid?
Maybe he wandered off to attend a meeting somewhere, maybe to talk to a constituent on the phone, maybe as a member of a standing committee, maybe doing one or the other 114 things you do which are pursuant to your membership in this Chamber. Is that the thesis being espoused by the gentleman from Kamloops, that the only time you work in this place is when you are physically here yelling your head off, as I am doing now, or sitting in the Chamber? What utter nonsense. What utter hypocrisy. What utter two-facedness.
I should perhaps tell my friend from Oshawa the latest story making the rounds about his friend-and I see him there so well- from Kamloops. It was said about him recently that if somebody on the government side, with all the extra money they are making with the GST, if somebody decided that maybe what we needed on this Hill was a swimming pool-
Did you say swimming pool or cesspool?

Swimming pool. The member wants a cesspool, no problem. But let's stick with the swimming pool first.
Now it is suggested that if the government decided what we needed here was a swimming pool, the member for Kamloops would do two things immediately: He would jump up immediately and put down a motion condemning it, and then he would phone his secretary and say: "Would you go over and buy me a swim suit?"
Could we use Pierre's pool perhaps?

Mr. Speaker, that member will never get to use Pierre's pool.
However, I digress. I make the same mistake I had accused somebody else of making. Why do we get excited about a party whose slogan is "Having our cake and eating it, too". Why do we get excited about a party that has all kinds of principles, some of them are even compatible, but most of them are mutually exclusive. Of course, they are for the Senate and against the Senate. I say to my friend from Kingston and the Islands that he ought to know better. This crowd is for and against everything. They are against the Senate today in their motion, because it gives them a chance to get up and talk. But on Saturday in Halifax I read in the paper they were for the Senate.
June 13, 1991
That is what I heard, too.

They were for NATO and they are against NATO. I have resolutions from the Montreal convention of the NDP a couple of years ago and another one showing they are for NATO and they are against NATO. They are for a united Canada, unless you listen to the member for Chambly, who is for Quebec sovereignty.
I say to my friend from Kingston and the Islands; Do not get excited about the crowd whose slogan is: "Having your cake and eating it too". Do not get excited about the crowd that has all kinds of principles, most of them contradictory. Do not get excited about the NDP, a party that can come up with a new principle any day of the week, just by negativing the existing principle. No problem.
Get around to the banks. Get to the good stuff.

Mr. Speaker, I understand there is a nuance here. It is a new refinement in the way the NDP writes its policies. They are not just simplistic and for and against things any more. They want to keep the Senate today; they just do not want to fund it. They want a kind of charitable, voluntary Senate.
They tell us the Senate is not doing anything. That is right, the Senate is useless. I just heard the member for Kamloops tell us the Senate is serving no useful purposes. Listen to their comments three days ago in Halifax, when they wanted half of the Senators to be women. Is that their commitment to equality? They want to put them in a useless organization, do they?
Sometimes if they were not so treacherous in the venom and the deceit they spread they would be funny. The deceit that the member for Kamloops spread just now about the Senate spending $2,000 a minute skates deliberately misleading some essential elements of the Senate; one is that when the Senate is not physically
Supply
meeting as a Senate many other committees are meeting.
Secondly, many of those Senators have their constituents, whether organizations or individuals, who come to them, much as they come to members of Parliament. It is cowardly and dishonest for a member of any party to stand in this place and take the other place and the individuals in it apart in their absence. Particularly, when you tell deliberate, direct, falsehoods. That is one of the more cowardly things I have seen.
I have my views on the Senate and I can give them to you. In short, first of all, they ought to be elected. In terms of our present Senate, is it serving a useful function? Yes. Anybody who thinks it is not should go back and see what the Senate is there for in the first place. One of the reasons it was put there in the first place by Macdonald and the Fathers of Confederation, was to see that the regions were protected.
We from a smaller province like Newfoundland and Labrador look to the Senate, and have always looked to the Senate, for some of our regional protection. Is it doing its job as well as it could? No. But the same question could be asked about this Chamber too.
I come then to what my friend, the Conservative member for Crowfoot, was just saying because it relates to the point I want to make. He was talking about Question Period. He said that Canadians do not believe that Question Period is serving their aspirations. That is a fair statement. He said: Canadians do not believe that Question period is serving their aspirations. I would say that if he wanted to be completely accurate about it, he ought to be saying "some Canadians". Whether that "some" is 99 per cent or 15 per cent, "some" Canadians believe that.
I happen to run into many Canadians who want me to raise certain issues in Question Period, people like the columnist who said yesterday: "With all its warts, Question Period is a very good institution. Let us keep it".
That is an aside to what I really want to say to the member for Crowfoot.

Supply
He says that Canadians feel that Question Period is not serving their aspirations. He is right in that some Canadians feel that. Maybe more Canadians feel it than we would like to think.
I have a question for him, and it is a question that comes to the specific issue of the GST. Since when did he and his colleagues on that side give a hoot about what Canadians feel?
About 85 per cent of Canadians told him in a poll that they did not want the GST, but the government put it through anyway. I do not see what the rush is to get out and alter Question Period just because Canadians do not like it, if I were to follow his strategy to date.
If Question Period needs some change, I am sure it will get changed. Let's not do it for the wrong reasons. The way this place is being castrated by the government, Question Period is one of the few remaining opportunities for some accountability. Yes, it is a bit untidy at times but let's not use the argument to change and improve it as an excuse for making a eunuch of it.
When I hear a government member talk about change as it relates to Parliament, you can usually decode that to mean "muzzle". You can assume, can you not, that if everything is going well for the government, it would not be talking about change. Why would you want to change something that is working well for you?
The very fact that members talk about change day in and day out tells me that somehow they may not be enjoying the experience any more. Maybe all is not well over there. When I hear them pontificate to me in flowing terms about change, I decode that to mean muzzle the place. I am going to oppose them at every turn on that.
Let's remind ourselves that in addition to that mischievous little motion put down by my ever present member and friend from Kamloops, this debate is all about the main estimates and the billions of largess that this government would want to expend on all kinds of schemes: $157 billion.
The former Premier of Newfoundland, Joey Smallwood, had a way which I cannot really imitate at all, much as I would like to do so, of drawing attention to a large sum of money. In Newfoundland terms, $157 billion is an astoundingly large sum of money. Joey would do it by backing away from it and coming at it a
step at a time. He would say: "Do you realize that we are not talking here about $157 billion. We are not talking $10 billion, $20 billion, $30 billion, $50 billion or even $100 billion. We are talking $157 billion." Then he would proceed to translate that into thousands of millions of dollars and so on.
The point needs to be made to the people of Canada and to us in this Chamber that we are dealing with one awful large lump of money here: $157 billion.
One of the things I ought to ask on behalf of the 85,000 people who sent me here, fishermen, farmers, shipyard workers, railway workers- until the government got rid of the railway a couple of years ago-ferry dock workers, unemployed, students: Is the government spending this $157 billion in the best way?
Certain of these expenditures are statutory. Certain of them we could hardly change even if we wanted to, but the government does have some flexibility. The government will be the first to point out that a large percentage of that goes to servicing the debt that the debt has doubled. The government does not point out but some of it is in the area of having some flexibility.
I want to come quickly to two or three issues. One is the issue of the fishery. I realize from your signal, Mr. Speaker, that my time has all but elapsed and I wish I had a few more moments, but I do not, so very quickly let me say that I would want to have said more about the issue of the fishery and what is happening to it in these times of stock collapse. This is at a time when people need help to bridge the gap -fishermen, plant workers and communities-and a time when the government is not making the best use of its limited funds to assist that sector of the economy. I could talk about how students, and university students in particular, are left high and dry because the government, through a sleight of hand, has actually cut back the amount of transfer payments for post-secondary education. I could talk about the new anxieties that are created among senior citizens and others because the government has cut back medical care expenses to the provinces.
The list goes on. There are so many things that we will want to raise during the course of this day before we give our concurrence to the passage of any estimates. I recognize my time is up for now, but maybe we will have another go at it later in the day.
June 13, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Burin-St. George's, but I regret the fact that the issue of program spending, which he was in the middle of discussing when he was cut short by elapsed time, is an issue that is not only important for his riding, but is also important for all of our ridings right now. We are dealing with a government that has not only decreased program spending dramatically over the last five or six years, but, in the process of decreasing that program spending in light of the deficit that has been doubled, it has also increased the revenues that it receives by almost 50 per cent since it took office.
The government is not only taking less out of the economy in terms of stimulation, but it is also taking a lot more out of the economy in terms of its tax programs.
I would like the hon. member for Burin-St. George's to expand a little bit on the importance of this program funding and maybe the fact that there are some areas which are statutory and which the government cannot and should not touch. It has tried to grab some of the statutory payments to seniors, et cetera, and, of course, our established program financing. I think it is important for him to elaborate on the importance of where this money goes in terms of stimulating our small businesses and all sectors, whether it is the fisheries or tourism. Maybe he could elaborate a little bit on that.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my friend from Broadview-Greenwood. It is only in the last day or so that he and I were comparing notes on the severe downturn in the economies of our respective regions. He represents an urban riding in downtown Toronto and I have the pleasure to represent a very rural riding, 158 communities, the largest of which has a population of about 8,000 and the smallest a population of about 12 people.
So we are talking of two very different worlds, but it was interesting in our chat a day or so ago, to note that because the economy is in such devastation there are similarities emerging in what is happening and how people are coping.
He made the point to me, and I am sure he would not mind my mentioning this, that the small business sector is having some real difficulty. He said to me, in passing, that people in Toronto are now beginning to realize what rural Canada has been talking about. In rural Canada
there is often a cycle of activity; if the fishery is good then small business thrives and if the fishery is bad, either through market or the health of the fish stock and so on, then small businesses experience a very depressed situation.
To turn specifically to his question, we had to back off and say what is government all about? Government, I believe, is a free enterprise or ought not to be doing anything that free enterprise can do better.
I believe government was put in place primarely, and its continued reason for existence, is to do things that private business, small or large, cannot do for us. What better time to have a government that you can turn to than when the economy is at its worst and you need something to bridge the gap?
Specifically, I want to come not only to small business as it relates to my riding, but to the fishery. We have a situation in the fishery in Burin-St. George's and all over Atlantic Canada where 100,000 people, men and women, plant workers and fisher persons, including men and women, depend on the fishery. So it is a very big industry. One out of every four jobs in Newfoundland is in the fishery, for example.
When the economy is in a downturn is the time you most need a government. That is when private business cannot help and that is when government ought to be able to step in and help bridge the gap.
There is an argument the former Minister of Fisheries and now Minister of Employment has been espousing. To his credit, the new Minister of Fisheries, my pal from Newfoundland, from St. John's West has not been espousing this argument yet and I hope he has the good sense never to start it, because the government tells us that in four or five years the fish stocks are going to rebound.
If they are going to rebound and the fishery will be healthy in five years, why are we in such mad haste to dismantle the processing capacity? Why are we in such mad haste to retrain all those fishermen as labourers for southern Ontario or Alberta or wherever else they are shipping them off to? Why do we not find a way to bridge the gap over the next four or five years to keep those processing facilities up to scratch? We may have to mothball some of them, but let's not put the wrecking ball to them.

June 13, 1991
Supply
Why don't we find a way to keep at home those people who have a lifestyle in Gaultois and in Grand Bank and those other communities in my riding that are under the gun? Why don't we find a way to keep their skills and their lifestyle intact for the next three or four years? We may have to find something for them to do in the meantime. We may have to do some training. That is fair ball, but let's not ask them to walk away from their life skills and their whole value system and way of life.
That is where a government in tough times ought to be expending some of its money. When I see the kind of money that we are talking about here and the fact that an extra $400 million more was made than they thought they were going to make in the first four months, I ask how that is for pocket money, an extra hundred million a month more than you thought you had in your pocket.
Surely Lord, surely to goodness, having that hundred million dollars a month, they can find a few shekels to help those poor fishermen, those poor plant workers I am talking about, instead of saying: "You have got to pack your bags and say goodbye to your loved ones forever." I hope that answers your question.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to my hon. friend and I have a short question to put to him. He was going on at some length saying what a fan of the Senate he was. I think that is an interesting position for somebody to take. It must be very lonely, I would think, taking that position. I wonder if my hon. friend could comment whether he thinks it is getting good value for money when the Senate managed to sit for nine hours during the month of February, 28 calendar days, and they managed to sit for 12 hours during the months of March and April. Then in May they went all out and actually were in session for 15 hours for the entire month.
My question to my hon. friend is this: Based on this working of the Senate, the amount of time that senators have spent working on behalf of Canada, his being a believer of free enterprise and wanting to make sure we were getting good value for money, does he think paying
nearly $2,500 a minute for this kind of performance is worth it?

First of all I say to my friend for Kamloops that it is not at all lonely saying we need an elected Senate. Many thousands of Canadians are saying that we need an elected Senate. Almost every thinking Canadian who understands our process of government will tell you we need a second Chamber. People in his own party as recently as this weekend will tell you that we need it elected and that we need a second chamber.
I come to the real point of his question about the $2,000 per minute. He might have listened to my speech, but he missed that sentence because I addressed that very particular sentence. I said to him and to the Chamber that I thought he had been quite dishonest to suggest that the only time senators worked is when the Senate is physically sitting. I turn the question around on him. Is he suggesting that the only time he works is when he is sitting in this Chamber? I understood if he is doing his job as a member of Parliament because I happen to be a member of Parliament too and when I go out of here there are a few other things I do. Sometimes people call me. I actually spend some time on the phone. I actually sign a few letters once in a while. I actually go to a committee meeting, and I know a few senators who do the same thing. I actually saw a senator in a meeting once.
Once.

As a matter of fact I saw them several times. The point I make is that the gentleman from Kamloops knows he has lost this particular argument completely and so he gets up one more time and regurgitates his $2,000 a minute.
He is going to have to get more convincing or go off and buy those swim trunks I mentioned earlier.
