speechtext: The hon. member for Oshawa.

Mr. Speaker, I think what has transpired here this morning is perhaps what is
June 13, 1991

troubling the people of Canada. The member for Burlington stood in his place and introduced the government's motion in a very casual way and it did not seem to cause much of a ripple in the Chamber. He indicated some of the difficulties the Government of Canada was having at the moment dealing with its financial problems.
He said, almost as a throwaway line, that they have come to a position where they cannot offer people who work for the Government of Canada any wage increases this years.
I think that is a remarkable statement. It is a statement of some financial difficulty. It is certainly an insult to all of those men and women who work for the Government of Canada, all of those who are on the front line of providing government services, because those poor people are unlike members here; they do not have the luxury of reading in a public opinion poll that the people of Canada are unhappy; they do not have the advantage of being able to send out a staff person to write a letter to some disgruntled constituent. These are all the people on the front lines. They are the ones who stand at a wicket somewhere and take abuse from the people of Canada over a system they did not devise, over policies they may not agree with. I have often thought it would be a useful exercise to take the Minister of Finance and put that individual out in a parking garage collecting the GST as people drive their cars out of the garage and listen to the comments that people make face to face, not an opinion poll, not modified in the staff report, but listen to it. He should get right in their faces and hear what the people of Canada have to say about the policies of this government.
Yet those who do that will get no wage increase. That is an insult for the work that they have done. Of all the people you could think of in our society who could perhaps get themselves in a position where they do not need any increase, who did not have any cost of living problems this year, whose rent did not go up, whose food cost did not go up, to whom the GST did not get applied, last on that list would be the people who work for the Government of Canada. They are out there every day whether they like it or not, representing the Government of Canada because they have a little badge on their sleeve that says, "We work for the Government of Canada", or because they work in an office with a sign that says, "The Government of Canada operates something out of this office".
Supply
Every day they hear the frustrations about a million and one problems, about immigration, for example. They listen to all the tragedies right in front of them from the individuals and the families who face an immigration system that is extremely complicated and, by many standards, rather unfair. They take that abuse first-hand.
For them the government says there is no money in the kitty to give any increase at all this year.
The second thing I heard the member say, again almost casually, is that the government is very attracted to the notion of user fees. Having been around parliaments for a while, I have seen this debate in other chambers. It always sounds attractive for governments to institute user fees because it has that wonderful notion about it that you can charge people a second time for a service they have already paid for.
I know that the argument on the other side of the coin is that -while they may have built and paid for the hospital, now that they are actually using the facility we are going to get them again. If they have the audacity to use a hospital we will charge them another user fee. If they have the audacity to go fishing we will charge them another fishing licence. If they have the audacity to drive on one of the roads we built with their tax dollars, we will charge them again. It is another great source of income.
Well, we are turning the comer in Canadian politics when we enter into these concepts. One of the things that makes Canada different from many other nations in the world is the concept that we, collectively as a nation, pool our money and our income tax and we build different kinds of things for our people. We build roads and hospitals and we provide services. People have a reasonable right that, having paid for it once, they really should not have to pay for it again. A user fee is a polite little word that suggests one other method of taxation.
I,	like many Canadians, have begun to investigate the process of just how much taxation people can take. Just because you call it by another name, just because you call it a user fee, does not make it anything other than what it is. It is a tax. When Canadian consumers go into stores these days they are getting to the point where they are recognizing that when you charge a provincial sales tax and a goods and services tax and any other kind of tax, there is a dramatic impact on what you pay for goods or services you receive. It is getting to the point where people can see that clearly on their bill and they are starting to say: "Wait a minute. How stupid does the government really think I am? Just because it calls it by another name, does it think I will not recognize that it is a taxation process"?

June 13, 1991
Supply
Does it think they will not know the difference between shopping in Kingston, Ontario, and anywhere along the Thousand Islands, in Clayton or in Alexandria Bay? Does it think people will not see the difference in the taxation process between two countries? Well, of course they will. Does it think that by setting up some kind of border process which collects even more taxes that it will stop people from shopping in the United States when they have a chance? Well, it will not.
People should simply understand that the taxation levels in this country have gotten to a point where those who are left paying taxes, that broad band of people who have, perhaps, a weekly pay cheque or an hourly rate, sometimes known as the middle-class, are really beginning to feel the pinch of taxation at all levels. If one could simply define: "It is fair. We are going to do this on the income tax. If you make more money you will pay more money in income tax". People would not like that very much, but they would at least understand that there is a logic there, that those with an ability to pay, ought to pay. What they are objecting to is that every time they turn around they are getting hit with some other form of taxation and they know it.
They do not care whether the kid who pumps the gas into their car looks like a tax collector or not. They are beginning to understand that he is a tax collector. They do not care whether the woman who works in the little comer store looks like an agent for the Government of Canada. They are aware now that that person functions much of her day as a tax collector for the Government of Canada and they are mad about that and they ought to be.
Also they ought to be mad about this. They ought to be mad that services they have already paid for are being taken away from them or that they are being charged extra for those services. They ought to be angry about that and they ought to tell this government. This government ought to drop the opinion polls and drop all the people it hired to do public relations work, go back home and listen to them.
In the last few days I have heard Conservative members, a long way in the backbench, albeit, but Conservative members, stand in this Chamber and reflect some of
that frustration. Maybe it is true that it is not good enough to hear from the opposition side that your financial policies are unpopular. I am sure, having been around Parliament for a while, that they have heard this in their own private caucus meetings.
Now you are beginning to hear it here in the Parliament of Canada. The message is not getting through. There are some who would be callous enough to say- and I would be one of them-that what is happening here is that the government is not popular at the moment, that it is gathering up a war chest, a kitty for the next general election, and that between now and election day there will hardly be a Canadian left standing who will not get a cheque from the Government of Canada for something, some rebate, some grant, some award, some giving back of their own cash.
I would say to the Canadian people, think about this. If somebody robs you on the street today, holds your money for two years and gives you back a portion of it two years from now, should you be happy about it? I do not think you should, and I would bet that by the time the next general election rolls around, the people in this country are going to understand that basic, unalterable fact that you have taken money out of their pocket now and it really does not matter whether you give them back a portion of that before the next election or not. They ought to remember what you did now, and what was the end result of your financial policies.
In a very casual way, the member suggested that the government has to look at some alternatives, some contracting out. When I was first a provincial member and saw this little exercise being tried, it looked to me like something that maybe we should think about. Then I discovered some odd things happening. When governments talk about contracting out, what they mean is that they are going to take people from permanent, paid position here, they are going to leave them right there, right at that desk, but they are going to call them by a different name, and they are going to call it contracting out. The next week that person will do exactly the same job in exactly the same place, and what they have lost is their status as an employee.
June 13, 1991

Governments like to pretend that they can then write up huge reports at the end of the fiscal year and say, look at how much we have cut the civil service. I do not know what the parliamentary word for that is, but I do know that the same people work in the same buildings, do the same jobs, and someone has found a device for calculating that they are really not there, that somehow they have disappeared. Oddly enough, it always turns out to be friends of the government who run the companies that get all of these contracts. It always turns out that it costs more money and not less.
So what governments try to do is focus your attention on the notion that there are less people working for the Government of Canada. You have to read the fine print and find out that no, there really are not, and it does not really cost less money. They are just called by a different name.
It is the same process that they are using now in taxation, that somehow if you call a tax by a different name it is no longer a tax. The people who are paying out the change every day are beginning to smarten up. They are beginning to understand that it does not really matter whether you call it by a different name, it is a tax. It does not really matter whether you pass a law saying: We are going to put all of this money into a special fund, not the Consolidated Revenue Fund anymore, and we are going to pay down the deficit. It does not take very much reading of the fine print of that law to discover what is happening is that it is business as usual. All the money goes into the Consolidated Revenue Fund, and then they are going to set up a new accounting process which puts it into another account. Before the end of the fiscal year, they are going to take that money and pay down some part of the deficit. They make a promise in that bill that will crank up the same kind of idea next year.
People understand it does not matter whether you have one piggy bank on the kitchen table or two, it is the amount of money you put into piggy banks. What happens is that it costs you more money to buy the second piggy bank. That is the kind of shell game that this government has embarked upon.
Supply
One of the things that I hear constantly where I work, in my own constituency when I walk around, is that people challenge the role of all the institutions we have. If they have watched this debate this morning, they have a good reason to challenge that. They have a good reason to say: Did we actually pay somebody to go to Ottawa and stand up and play those kinds of silly games, that you can call people two-faced, but you cannot say they are hypocrites? Does that make any difference anywhere in the world? No, it does not, and they know that.
You can quote Beauchesne and Erskine May until you are blue in the face. It works in here. Try it in a pool room. Go into a local bingo and tell them: Listen, the words you just used are not on the list. Beauchesne does not approve of those words, so you cannot use them. See if that changes the course of the argument. Well, it will not. The shame of it is that there are people in this Chamber who believe that somehow if you learn how to play the word games, it changes the nature of it all. It does not. You can delude yourself into thinking that a Parliament is about reading Beauchesne's, about finding a list in Erskine May or that it is some kind of game about whether everybody is an honourable member. It is not.
People watch every day and see the kinds of words that come out of this Chamber. They say: "What a bunch of foolish people. Don't they know there are serious problems in this country? Don't they know that we have to stop and look at all of our institutions?"
Do you not really know that people all across Canada are asking the interesting question: "Why are people in the Senate playing kazoos?" Is that what it is about? Is the Senate such a valuable institution? How is it that the government can simply decide one fine day that the Senate is not doing what it is supposed to do, and therefore we ought to put some more people into the Senate?
Do you think people do not understand the game called stacking the deck? Sure they do. They have seen it a million times where they work, whenever they have had an argument, whenever a debate was going one way and all of a sudden somebody decides that the debate is not going that way because they are bringing in more troops.

June 13, 1991
Supply
They have probably seen a write-up of a Liberal nomination meeting. They know what stacking the deck is. They have been in a debate like that. They understand all of that.
There is something missing in this Chamber, at least I have not heard it because we do use parliamentary language. Maybe the country would be better if we set aside Beauchesne's for a day and said: "Let's just get together and report to the people of Canada what we have heard on the streets in our constituencies last week."
Hear, hear.

It would be an interesting debate, I must say. I am sure there would be many across the country offended by the language that would be used, but there is a certain tenor to all of that that you really have to hear. Maybe it cannot be expressed in parliamentary language.
Maybe those who are big fans of the Senate would care to go out on the street in your community and express the fine words about the sober second thought and all of that.
What we are trying to do as a political entity is what I am sure every political entity in the country is trying to do. I do not understand why people really believe that electing a Senate in its current form is going to solve its problems.
This much I do know. There are people in this country who fervently believe that regional differences which have not been addressed by the Government of Canada over a long period of time can only be solved by somehow redesigning the second Chamber. I am not that dumb. I am at least prepared to listen to what they have to say. I am at least prepared to hear their arguments. If someone would figure out a way that we can elect a Senate, fine. If someone can figure out what they are going to do after we elect them, I think that is pretty important. If someone can suggest some changes in the relationship between the Senate of Canada and the House of Commons that would work, I am prepared to hear that argument and to accept it. Everybody else in this Chamber had better be prepared to hear it and accept it as well.
Governments at all levels in this country are being challenged and not in polite academic ways. They are being challenged on the streets, in the factories, in the playgrounds, in the arenas every day all across Canada,
and it seems that governments cannot hear it. That is a tragedy.
I have followed for some time the government's frustration with the Question Period. I have seen it here and in the other Chamber. I am amazed that somehow anybody in his or her right mind feels that if we limit it to 30 seconds, that will solve the problem. That is not the problem.
I have heard really good questions in other chambers go on much longer than 30 seconds. If people know what they are talking about, are reasonably secure in their facts and are putting forward good arguments, it is not a question of whether it is 29 seconds long or four minutes long. It is a question of relevance.
As I listen to my constituents talk about this Chamber, that is the question they have on their minds: "What the hell is going on down there?" I have to admit I am hard pressed to explain what is going on down there. I do not know. I am listening to it. I am there every day. I am watching it all unfold. It makes no sense to me.
I saw a headline the other day. I think it was Preston Manning who accused this Parliament of being a "disgrace". I admit he has got me. It is a disgrace that this is the national Government of Canada, the biggest Parliament we have, and it cannot get its act together. Why not? I do not know, I just got here.
Is it because people are so mesmerised with their own wonderfulness? I have been in politics for awhile. There is nothing wrong with a big ego in politics. If you do not have one you will not survive. But is that all there is to it? Is it just word games? If it is, let us do it on the cheap. Let us take all of these wonderful wordsmiths and find them a nice place to go for the summer. It will cost them $1.95. Give them a free lunch and let them get out there, and we will call it our constituent assembly.
I can find you all kinds of people who will serve in that constituent assembly for nothing. We do not have to call it the Senate, we do not have to pretend that it is a Parliament. It is a bunch of people yakking in a field.
For those who think that parliaments are distinguished places, I want to remind you that the very first Parliament was exactly that, a bunch of people yakking in a field, and the field was called Runnymede. They had a great argument that there was no one in their jurisdiction who could address the needs of the common people, and so they called it a House of Commons.

They then wrote books about it. Perhaps that was the downfall. Perhaps it was the downfall of the parliamentary system that someone wrote a book called Beauchesne and another guy wrote a book called Erskine May. Somehow these have become almost biblical in stature, rule books for a Parliament, and Parliament does not have to be relevant, it just has to follow those rules.
I would bet if you took any person from across this country and brought him or her to this door over here and said: "Okay, you have a couple of minutes. Tell these people what you think of them." I think I know what would be said. It probably would not be parliamentary, probably a great deal of frustration and disgrace that this is their country, that they have a say, that they thought you were a decent human being, that you had a contribution to make, and they cannot see you making it.
I am an advocate and always have been of the parliamentary process. I think it is much better than the congressional process, but it has its warts. There is something about a parliamentary process that means once you get elected your brain is removed and that somehow, when you leave your caucus room where you have had your great arguments about the issue of the day, you are no longer allowed to speak to that.
In part, our little motion says: "Let us begin to investigate the institutions of Canada. Let us see if we can find a better way to construct a role for a Senate, if that is what you want. Let us see if we can at least make it democratic. Let us see if we can find a function for that."
But I have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, number two on my list is this place; this place is a disgrace and it ought not to be.

Mr. Speaker, I have only been in this Chamber for just under three years, but I want to say that the hon. member for Oshawa, who is a member of the New Democratic Party, has made one of the finest speeches that I have heard in this place. I want him to know that everything that he has just said is exactly what I hear in my riding. I would not argue a comma with this member.
But I do want to ask him a specific question. In the beginning part of his speech, he talked about the frustration that people are having with the tax system, and he specifically referred to the middle class. Again I
Supply
agree with him totally. In the last two and half weeks, when I have not been in the Chamber but in my riding, I can tell you that everyone, whether they are in small businesses, medium sized businesses, large businesses, everyone is so frustrated with what is happening.
In relation to the complexity of the tax system, we have just come through a period where people have just finished doing their tax returns, so naturally that frustration is intense. It is even more intense when you think that a lot of these people right now have either lost their jobs or they are afraid of losing their jobs. There is a lot of tension in the community and morale is at an all-time low. Part of our responsibility as leaders of our communities is to deal in hope. We seem to be having a difficult time, as the hon. member has said, in putting it together. I would like to ask him a very specific question: Because he has had experience in both chambers, provincially and nationally, does he have any specific ideas on how we might be able to reform the tax system so that the concept of fairness, the concept of efficiency, and all those things that might put some hope and motivation back into a community can exist? Does he have any ideas on that?

Mr. Speaker, I have had a chance to observe legislatures and parliaments around the world now for a fair bit of time. They are all different. They have their own little customs. They all develop their own taxation processes. The test the public puts them to asks: Is this fair?
At the moment I believe it is accurate to say that the taxation process in Canada is unfair every time you turn around. What angers people, as well, is that it is all-pervasive.
What should we do?

For example, when the major thrust of your taxation process is something like a goods and services tax, which is collected at the comer store, people object to it. People go to the comer store to buy goods and services, not to pay taxes. When there is a developing thrust in your taxation process which does not include sitting down at the end of the year to decide what is fair, that everybody is paying their fair share, then that concept of fairness is totally lacking in the taxation process in Canada.

Supply
I have heard some people talk about a minimal tax or a flat tax for everybody. That is perhaps a little simplistic for the world. But there is merit in that, and it is simply this: when people look around and see others making far more money than they are and paying absolutely no income tax, they think there is something wrong with the system and they are right. There has to be a base level of taxation based on income, I believe.
Second, I am constantly lost by governments at all levels with their little schemes about avoiding taxes. I think that message has got out to the Canadian public as well. Canadians do not understand, nor do I, how it is that the wealthiest people, the wealthiest corporations in our society, can wind up paying no taxes at all when they pay taxes every time they turn around?
I think the first principle that has to get injected into this system is some sense of fair play. Because, to be blunt, people think they are being screwed, and the truth is they are and they know it. They also know that collecting taxes at the comer store is wrong. They have to be declined dramatically.
I do not suggest for a moment that this is a simple thing, but I think that if you do not get back to a fairness principle, you will never have a taxation process that will be accepted by the population at large, because it should not be.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the hon. gentleman a question concerning his comments regarding this Chamber, Parliament and legislatures in Canada. If you go back over debates in this Chamber, and debates I suppose in practically every other provincial legislature, you will find that the same criticisms were made of the Canadian system as the Canadian system has evolved.
Since the hon. member has visited other legislatures and passed an opinion a few moment ago on the congressional system, I wonder if he has come to any conclusion as to what procedure should be followed to change, as he puts it, the procedures in the House of Commons to make it, as he also wishes, more relevant to the year 1991. What should some of these major changes be, and why does not he like the congressional system?
As he pointed out a moment ago, he said our system was better than the congressional system.
Does he think perhaps one of the major problems is the fact that individual members of Parliament do not have the ability under the present rules to investigate the administration or to change legislation in their legislative role?

Mr. Speaker, those of us who have been in legislatures and parliaments in Canada literally drool when we go and see an American congressional system that concentrates a lot of power on the individual member. You look at the kind of facts and figures that they get out of their governments and say: "Boy, would it ever be great if we had a finance committee that actually started off the budget year with every scrap of financial information that the government had, and then made recommendations about what we should do." If only that were our starting point. The big flaw in the congressional system, of course, is very simply that everybody is an individual player. If you go into a legislative chamber in the States where there are 100 members, there are 100 political parties at work and they are all free agents.
The big advantage of a parliamentary system is the cohesion. When you go to Westminster and watch the British system at work you say: "You belong to a party system as I do, in a parliamentary system as I do, how dare your Conservative members get up and challenge your government?" Why is it that when you watch Westminster at work there is as much laying of the lash from the Conservative side of the House as there is from the opposition side. Somehow we got diverted from the parliamentary system in Canada and we are more devoted to our parties than we ought to be. It is our curse.
I know it is a shocking thing to say, but it would be delightful if in this Chamber members on all sides rediscovered their brains and used them and used their human skills. It would be delightful in this parliamentary system if the government of the day had first to convince ordinary members on its own side, its friends, that the directions and the policies of the government, that the laws they wanted to propose were the right ones and if they could not get it through their own caucus they did not bring it in here.
June 13, 1991

I have been around long enough to know that that is the theory. That is the way the books write it up, but in practice what happens is the minister walks in and says: "This is the way we are going, folks" and everybody goes out over the cliff. If somebody just had the common sense to say: "Wait a minute, that is a cliff there; I don't want to jump off that cliff. Convince me. Don't tell me what I have to do. Convince me." Then the parliamentary system would work as it was originally designed.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative chair of the Senate Standing Committee on Transport and Communications has condemned this government's decision to gut Canada's international radio broadcast service.
Senator Finlay MacDonald says Canada's voice to the world has been silenced. Radio Canada International has now eliminated seven foreign language services and three-quarters of its foreign programming. These drastic cuts to a service with a world-wide reputation have sparked national and international outrage.
It was front-page news in Japan, where the Prime Minister recently opened a new embassy.

June 13, 1991
It is ironic that a government which is obsessed with broadening international trade fails to see that RCI is the best way Canada has of promoting itself to the rest of the world.
I urge the Prime Minister to listen to his colleague's warning. RCI is Canada's link to the world. Our policies and our industries were effectively explained on a world stage. Let us not cut an invaluable service which gives Canada an international identity.

Mr. Speaker, middle income Canadians feel that they are overtaxed. They feel that the tax system is unfair and much too complicated. They know they bear a heavy burden because of the excessive spending of the previous government, but there is no excuse for unfairness and complexity.
We have family allowance, the child tax credit, the dependent child tax credit, the equivalent to married credit, the child care deduction, the GST credit, the spousal deduction, and a plethora of shared cost programs. This is only the tip of the iceberg.
Middle income Canadians also know that the system is unfair. A married two-earner couple, with a combined income of $60,000 and three children, pays up to $5,500 more in taxes than an unmarried couple in exactly the same circumstances. More extreme differences exist when comparisons are made of other family structures and tax inconsistencies.
I urge the government to act quickly to simplify the tax system and make it fair for everyone, regardless of the lifestyle they choose.

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow, Mr. D'Iberville Fortier, the Commissioner of Official Languages, reaches the end of the mandate he was given by this Parliament in 1984. A new
Official Languages Act, the delay in producing regulations, the Conservative goverment's failure to act decisively, court challenges, language conflicts-these are some of the major obstacles and challenges that marked Mr. Fortier's term. His position has certainly not been an enviable one.
As the Liberal critic for Official Languages, I can testify to the tremendous effort and legal battles it took to defend minority rights. The courage shown by Mr. Fortier during the past seven years, against all criticism and despite emerging radical groups, has been remarkable, Mr. Speaker, and we are truly indebted to him.
The new commissioner will have to act with as much energy and vigour and have the same dynamic approach as Mr. Fortier. Only with people like him, who truly respect Canada's legislation on linguistic minorities, will we be able to ensure some day that both official languages in this country are treated equally. Thank you, Mr. Fortier, and the best of luck with your future plans.

Mr. Speaker, today the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs tabled a new bill on bankruptcy and insolvency.
On November 29, 1985, under No. 245, I presented a notice of motion, and on May 20, 1988, I tabled in the House of Commons a motion, which was adopted, asking the government to consider establishing a special wage insurance fund that would be responsible for paying workers any wages pending when a Canadian employer goes bankrupt.
Mr. Speaker, I must say I was veiy pleased with this bill which contains measures dealing with business restructuring, winding-up arrangements and personal bankruptcies; creates a wage claim recovery program; legislates the rights of unpaid suppliers; and finally, includes various technical changes designed to make it easier and less costly to administer this legislation. This is the kind of initiative designed to help all businesses and all Canadians through a difficult period.
June 13, 1991

Mr. Speaker, today the headlines in the local newspapers of Northumberland give no assurances to students looking for work this summer.
Over two-thirds of students registered at a student employment centre are unable to find summer jobs. Meanwhile, there has been no increase in the Summer Employment Experience Development Program, otherwise known as SEED.
The fact is that unemployment levels in my riding are higher than the averages used to calculate the SEED allotments.
In addition, there was an unexplained dramatic decline in allotment between 1989 and this year. This has meant many important programs in my riding have had to suspend summer programs which not only employed many students but benefited communities in important, economic and social ways.
The minister has made the commitment to redistribute funds to areas with the greatest change in unemployment above the provincial average, and therefore I strongly urge him to review the figures in Northumberland and increase SEED funding to more adequately reflect the desperate situation facing many young people in Northumberland.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Captain Rosella Bjomson was the first female in Canada hired to fly a commercial jet. She was recently honoured during National Transportation Week when she received the National Award of Achievement in Halifax on May 30. In Winnipeg, she received the Manitoba Award of Achievement on June 6 of this year in recognition of her exceptional leadership and success in opening the aviation door to women.
Captain Bjomson was bom and raised in Alberta. She was first hired in 1973 by Transair, now Canadian Airlines. Today, 18 years later, she is the only female jet captain employed by a scheduled airline in Canada.
Well done, Captain Bjomson. Well done, Canada.

Mr. Speaker, June 12 is an historic day for Filipino Canadians. Although we are now Canadian citizens, we carry in our hearts the memory of that day, 93 years ago, when our great-grandparents freed themselves from Spanish rale.
At that time, the Filipino people came to understand independence did not mean being alone, working in the interest of yourself; it meant standing together to attain greater goals.
Today, though we stand on Canadian soil, we carry from our motherland that spirit of independence.
Indeed, we believe the meaning of independence is unity, working together for the greater whole. This is one of the values we bring to Canada, along with goodwill and and understanding toward others. Happily they are values shared by all Canadians.
I hope the Filipino people in Canada and all Canadians will join us in celebrating Philippine Independence Day as we join together in our common search for national Canadian unity.

Mr. Speaker, on December 5,1990, the CBC closed its three television stations in Eastern Quebec, depriving the people of the Lower St. Lawrence, the Gaspe and the Magdalen Islands of a vital communications medium.
This situation has led to a dangerous level of underbudgeting for the CBC's radio stations, because initially, managers of television and radio stations had restructured their operations so that radio operating costs would be largely absorbed by the television budget.
Mr. Speaker, my constituents are worried, and they are afraid that what happened to television will happen to radio as well.
Mr. Speaker, I share their concern, and I want to ask the minister responsible for the CBC to do something about this right away.

Mr. Speaker, my what an interesting course has been followed in the privatization of de Havilland.
First the government sells it to Boeing, or should we say pays Boeing to take it of its hands. Investment Canada thinks it is great-it always does-but Boeing decides its hands are full and sells it to the ATR consortium. Hence, privatization leads to government ownership, only not our government.
The opposition identified trouble ahead from the very beginning in lost jobs, lost research and development and lost production of the Canadian Dash-8 series. After all, ATR's commuter plane competes directly with the Dash-8.
Our government saw no problem because privatization is good. Investment Canada saw no problem because foreign ownership is good.
The European community is as concerned as our government is not about the reduction in competition in commuter aircraft and will examine it.
The sale delayed, de Havilland's survival is now endangered by the loss of orders caused by uncertainty and doubt and the stupidity of this government.
What will the government do to make it right? Buy de Havilland?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the leader of the Reform Party gave a speech on Tuesday night right here in Ottawa. He spoke at length but never once mentioned that he was in favour of controlling government expenditures by cutting thick layers of middle management in federal administration. That is his policy and it affects the residents of this city of Ottawa.
He also never mentioned his policy of a 15 per cent cut to federal program spending across the board in every area. This 15 per cent cut means seniors receiving the OAS and GIS would have their incomes reduced by $120 per month or $1,427 per year. It seems to me the Reform
man has one message for Calgary and another message for Ottawa.
Why is he not consistent across Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I rise on an issue which is of great importance to my constituents, many of whom belong to co-operatives.
The co-operative is very important to Atlantic Canada. People in local communities, farmers, fishermen and consumers studied the problems that faced them and decided to solve those problems through the use of co-operatives. They have had great success. Today more than 174,000 families own 174 co-operatives.
With the GST, this government has created an unfair and unacceptable tax system which tilts the playing field against co-operatives. Today, if someone in Shediac or Buctouche wants to buy a share in a co-operative, they must pay GST.
On the other hand, someone wishing to invest in a large multinational corporation can buy the shares without paying the GST.

Furthermore, the GST is applied to certain foods purchased directly from a co-op, but it does not apply to the same foods purchased from a multinational chain. Because of this double standard, co-ops in the Atlantic provinces stand to lose over $1 million. This region needs a strong co-operative movement.
I feel the government should review this problem and give co-ops throughout the country a fair deal.

Mr. Speaker, today, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Conservative member for Bellechasse, the Hon. Pierre Blais, tabled new legislation on bankruptcy and insolvency.
It introduces provisions to protect workers affected by bankruptcy who lose their jobs and, in many cases, the wages they are owed.

From now on, these workers will be able to seek reimbursement for their unpaid wages up to a maximum $2,000, plus $1,000 for expenses in the case of travelling salesmen. They will receive this reimbursement within four to six weeks.
Mr. Speaker, this is a measure designed to help all Canadian workers.
I say: congratulations to the Tory government!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last edition of the cross-border report outlined the critical role of the Canada Customs in addressing the cross-border shopping issue.
In Sarnia-Lambton, cross-border shopping is visible through the line-ups at the Blue Water Bridge and the worrisome impact on local businesses.
The problem is serious, with no quick fixes. It will require effective, collaborative action by a number of players. This, however, does not preclude the federal government from seriously looking at our policies as they contribute to cross-border travel. This includes Canada Customs.
Locally this may include the trial of a PACE amended type program, the trial of tourist lanes or the use of new technology. Some or all may help improve service at the border, especially for our commuters and American travellers to and from the many tourist attractions in our area.
At the Blue Water Bridge, more personnel will help us address the line-ups. I have written directly to the Minister of National Revenue requesting more Customs personnel at the Blue Water Bridge.
With more personnel and other initiatives, the objective must be the collection of all applicable duties and taxes. We want no more wave-throughs and the absence of excessive line-ups at the Blue Water Bridge.

Mr. Speaker, for many years the native and white villages of Bella Coola shared the same water supply.
However, when the federal government put in a new system on the reserve, the white village was left with an inadequate, badly contaminated water supply. Now the native supply has also been found to be contaminated, requiring much more work.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is now working with both parties to resolve the problems. It makes good sense for both villages to co-operate to establish one good, safe system rather than duplicate costly installations.
I call on all parties to work together to provide a safe and secure water supply for all, not just for part of the populations. We need more examples of native-white co-operation, not confrontation.

Mr. Speaker, despite the removal of the Meme breast implant from the market, thousands of Canadian women remain deeply troubled by the lack of information available on the safety of breast implants.
It is now apparent that research into the Meme is being guided not by the desire to provide impartial and factual information, but by political considerations.
A woman in Montreal has been told by a surgeon that he will remove her Meme implant only if she agrees to donate that implant to a research project at McGill University, headed by Dr. Carolyn Kerrigan, who is doing research funded by the manufacturer of the Meme and is the same doctor whose report on the Meme for the Department of National Health and Welfare claimed there was no health risk with the Meme.
Are members of the medical profession now more concerned with manipulating research than finding the truth and allaying the fears of Canadian women with the Meme implant? Are they being aided by this government which has demonstrated over the last several years that it has neither the resources nor the intent to give us the answers regarding the Meme implant?

June 13, 1991
Oral Questions

Yesterday it was announced that Mr. Gordon Smith, Secretary to the Cabinet for Federal-Provincial Relations, was being reassigned overseas. Can the minister tell the House why Mr. Smith was let go? Why is the senior constitutional adviser to the government being sent overseas less than 60 days before the government tables its position before the country?

This is the number one priority file of the Government of Canada. Mr. Speaker, the appointment of the Prime Minister's right-hand man, Mr. Tellier, as Secretary to the Cabinet on Federal-Provincial Relations, means that the Prime Minister has retaken control of the constitutional file.

I used to be in that job. I have been there before, and I want to ask a very serious question of the minister of constitutional affairs. How can he stay on as minister when the Prime Minister has so little confidence in him, when the Prime Minister made him his dignified parliamentary secretary?
June 13, 1991

Hear, hear.

Before the minister assumed his new responsibilities, the newspapers reported that he insisted on working at arm's length from the Prime Minister. How can he claim today that he is still working at arm's length, when his deputy minister no longer reports to him but directly to the Prime Minister?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade.
Following yesterday's meeting on the Canada-U.S.-Mexico trade talks I understand there were six committees created which defined the priority areas for the talks, but nowhere on this priority list were environmental issues, workers' standards or indeed social standards.
Will the minister give this House some assurance that he will work for an agreement on workers' rights, on environmental standards and on social standards, or will he say there will be no trade deal until we have those for the people of Canada and for the people in Mexico and the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the discussions that we had yesterday were related to the trade negotiations themselves. They were not related to the parallel work that we will be carrying out with the Mexicans and the Americans on questions that she has just raised on labour standards and environmental standards.
As I am sure my hon. friend is aware, we have a memorandum of understanding with the Mexicans where we are discussing-and we have had it in place for a little over a year now-environmental issues. That work will be going on.

June 13, 1991
Oral Questions
I had a discussion with my colleague, Mr. Serra, and told him that we would like to have a group come down to Mexico City and discuss the work of that group in relation to the process of the trade talks.

Mr. Speaker, continually during the Canada-U.S. trade deal the minister said that it was just a commercial agreement and that it did not affect these other areas. However, if we talk to the 313,000 unemployed right now who have lost their jobs since the trade deal or the 1.5 million unemployed in Canada, if we talk to those people who had manufacturing jobs-and since 1989 one in six of those jobs has gone-clearly this government has to take seriously the concerns of working people and their futures and the futures of their families.
Many of the jobs, and the minister knows this, have already gone to Mexico. I could give a long list, but there are jobs from Burlington, Cambridge, Waterloo, Pene-tanguishene, and across Canada. We have seen companies moving out of this country. As one company official recently said: "These are jobs that will never come back to Canada".

I think there are precedents involved where contempt has been found involving the placing or the publishing of posters. I do not want to take the time of the House today to outline them all, but they are mentioned in, among other places, Griffiths, Parliament; Functions, Practice and Procedures.
There are two points here I would like to make. First of all, I think this could be resolved in a number of ways. If the persons responsible are prepared to pay for any damages, then that could be satisfactory. If it was thought appropriate, it could be taken up by the Board of Internal Economy and/or the Management Committee of the House. I think there is a responsibility to do that.
Madam Speaker, beyond that, if it is found by you to be a case, I would naturally be prepared to move the appropriate motion. However, as I said, there may be other ways to resolve this matter.
It is important to deal with it, however, because we in this House know what happens with precedents, even when we transgress a line and it is not that substantial a transgression. The fact is we must deal with this matter because we realize the kind of escalation this could lead to. I ask that you consider this matter and the references to Beauchesne's on this and on the fact that in the past there have been instances of contempt found relating to this sort of thing.

Madam Speaker, unfortunately, as is often the case in such matters, I fear the dispelling of the charges made will take slightly longer than the making of the charges. I would like to say at the outset, for myself and for all members of my staff to the best of my knowledge, I neither advocate, support, nor condone vandalism, the wilful destruction of property, public or private.
Having said that, I would like to deal with the question of the vandalism committed against the hon. member's office, who did it and how it was arrived at. I had hoped that in his presentation to the House today, the member would offer research evidence on the matter somewhat greater than simply reading an article from the June 7,
Privilege
issue of The Edmonton Journal. Unfortunately, no such evidence was forthcoming. Let me put him straight on a couple of counts.
The first deals with the meeting identified in the article. I shall read the sentence. I quote: "Curran", that is my constituency assistant, "who is a member of the network", which is to say the Action Canada Network, which does not, properly speaking, have members, but we will let that pass, "said she attended the meeting which planned the poster campaign as a private citizen".
In speaking to my constituency assistant, I found out that the meeting referred to and, in fact originally raised by the reporter and not by her, was the annual general meeting of the Action Canada Network in Alberta held several weekends ago over the course of a Friday, Saturday and Sunday. I attended the same meeting. All kinds of things were discussed at that meeting and absolutely no particular actions were decided upon at that time.
As well, I have through conversations with others determined that members of the interim steering committee of the Action Canada Network, of which Ms. Curran is not a member, were the ones who decided that the printing and circulation of a poster to Action Canada Network sympathizers would be undertaken. What those sympathizers then did with that poster was left up to them. Again, Ms. Curran had absolutely nothing to do with that.
Finally, I would note that Ms. Curran is not alleged by anyone to have actually taken part in the postering that has so distressed the hon. member. That is good, because I can assure that she did not.
For the hon. member to say, and I quote exactly his submission in this House, that Ms. Curran was involved in the planning of this is utterly incorrect.
She said it herself.

No, I am sorry. What she said was, and it is not a quote, it is a paraphrase. Ms. Curran "said she attended the meeting which planned the poster campaign as a private citizen". What was meant by what my assistant said to the reporter at the time was that she was present at the Action Canada Network annual general meeting in which all sorts of things were discussed. And had the hon. member taken the time to talk to either the reporter or the constituency association or, I would hazard, anyone involved with the Action Canada Network at the leadership level, he would have been able to discover that for himself. However, failing that, we are burning the time of the House in this pursuit.

June 13, 1991
Supply
In any event, I would conclude by noting that there is no hint anywhere here that can be sustained that my constituency assistant was in any way involved in any improper activity and I greatly resent the implication that she was.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE

speakeroldname: Hon. Pauline Browes (for the President of the Treasury Board) moved:
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That Vote 1, in the amount of $56,606,000, under FINANCE-
Financial and Economics Policy Program-Program Expenditures in
the Main Estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31,1992 (less the
amount voted in interim supply) be concurred in.
Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State
(Finance)): Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak today on Motion No. 2 in today's order of proceedings before the House.
The motion suggests that the government should abandon its financial and economic policies. On the contrary, it is vital that we continue to implement these policies for the very good reason that our financial and economic program is working directly at getting Canada out of the current recession and back to growth and job creation.
The government's plan for economic recovery, introduced in the February budget, emphasizes controlling expenditures and reducing inflation. This is the key to the lower interest rates that will boost consumer spending and business investment to fuel growth and new jobs.
This approach has its critics and of course that is no surprise. After all, for nearly 20 years through the early 1980s, Canadians were accustomed to a federal government with fiscal philosophies that could be summed up in two words: charge it. In fact, in 1984 the government was handing out $1.33 in programs and services for every dollar it collected in taxes. That philosophy has had harsh consequences.
June 13, 1991

We are now paying the price over and over again for too many years of consuming more government services than we are willing to pay for. This is the reason our national debt will reach $400 billion by mid-year; about $15,000 for every man, woman and child in Canada. That does not include another $100 billion in debt by other levels of government.
The interest costs alone on the federal debt lead up over $43 billion next year. That is equal to 36 cents of every tax dollar Canadians pay. It is more than the government spends on Old Age Security, unemployment insurance, veterans' pensions and family allowances combined. That is why the federal budget refuses to buy short-term recovery at the cost of a return to surging deficits and runaway debt. The lessons of the last 20 years make that point bluntly. This spendthrift approach only creates a vicious circle of higher inflation and interest rates, leading us back to the inevitability of economic decline, lost jobs and lower government revenues.
We have instead taken a different path based on a continuing commitment to deficit and debt control. The February budget severely restrains the cost of government, including wages and salaries for the Prime Minister, the cabinet, for members of Parliament and for the federal Public Service. It extends the two-year expenditure control program introduced in 1990, including limits on the growth of transfers to provinces, so that it will now continue through 1994-95 and the saving achieved will total more than $15 billion.
What makes this a watershed budget is that it also takes dramatic measures to achieve nothing less than a fundamental change in the political culture of government spending. These interlocking measures will transform good financial management by government from the realm of promise and political will into a matter of law. By so doing, they can play an important role in changing the expectations of Canadians regarding government spending, municipal and provincial as well as federal.
As part of this fundamental change, we will introduce legislation to impose mandatory limits on the annual program spending for the next five years. Flexibility will be confined to a very limited set of contingencies. It will not preclude new programs to meet new needs, but these must be funded from within the total legislated spending ceiling. In short, it will soon be against the law for the federal government to overspend.
Supply
The second leg of our commitment to guarantee spending control lies in the proposed debt servicing reduction fund introduced in the House yesterday. This fund ensures that all revenues from GST will be used to service debt and reduce the debt, and not to fund new program spending.
The third thrust of our strategy was to announce specific inflation targets to bring inflation down to 2 per cent by the end of 1995.
By working to meet these targets, we can establish the conditions that will make possible a sustained and lasting decline in interest rates. This will help control the interest charges on the national debt.
This interlocking strategy will deliver concrete and decisive results. The deficits for 1990-91 and the coming year will be held to $30.5 billion despite the difficulties caused by the recession. That is down from the $35 billion we were looking at when we started the budget planning process.
Then, for 1992-93, with economic recovery, lower interest rates and restrained government spending, the deficit will fall sharply to $24 billion. Three years after that, by 1995-96, it will have dropped to just $6.5 billion, the lowest deficit in nearly 20 years.
As well, the need for new government borrowing on financial markets will be eliminated even sooner, by 1994-95. This will meet the goal we first set out in the 1989 budget and will represent for the first time in 25 years that no such borrowing is needed.
Last, we will no longer be borrowing money to pay the interest on the money that we have already borrowed.
Underlying these results will be the truly revolutionary change in the politics of budget making that the plan launches. I want to be clear about what it means. It means any federal government that wants to exceed the specific limits or to use the GST revenues for a purpose other than debt reduction, will have to go to Parliament to change the law.
It will have to explain to the taxpayers of Canada why it plans to spend more of their money, and the government will have to justify publicly the consequences that this will have for the deficit and the debt, for taxes and for its own credibility.

June 13, 1991
Supply
I have said that these spending controls make this a watershed budget. At the same time, they build on the commitment of good financial management that has been the basis of this government's program since 1984.
Some people do not share that view. It is easy to use hindsight to say we should have taken even tougher steps than we did, but it is important to recognize how far we have come, the real progress made in dealing with financial problems the government inherited nearly seven years ago.
The fact is that the federal government's spending programs and service have been under tight control since 1984-85. This has required tough and often unpopular measures.
Payments to VIA Rail and CBC have been scaled back. We have eliminated programs on home insulation and oil substitution. Military bases have been closed. The structure of the Old Age Security and family allowance programs were changed to recover these transfers from high income Canadians who did not need them. We reduced the size of the Public Service substantially to the level of the early 1970s.
Thanks to these measures, we were able to hold increases in spending to an annual rate of just 3.7 per cent. That is well below the rate of inflation and the growth in our economy, and is well behind the growth in the over-all provincial spending.
By contrast, in the 15 years prior to 1984-85, the federal government program spending increased on an average yearly rate of 13.8 per cent. We have achieved a really remarkable change.
The results of our spending restraint have been substantial. As a share of Canada's economy, spending on programs has fallen from 19.6 per cent in 1984-85 to 16 per cent this year, the lowest level since the 1960s.
Without this restraint, federal program spending this year would have been $30 billion higher and our deficit would have more than doubled from what it is to nearly $70 billion.
This spending restraint has also substantially slowed the growth of the national debt. In 1984-85, the debt was growing at an annual rate of about 25 per cent. Today this is down to less than 10 per cent, but this is still not
acceptable. With our budget measures, we will eliminate completely the need to borrow money within four years.
When they hear these figures, many Canadians then ask: "Why is the deficit so high and the debt still growing?" The answer lies directly in the impact of compound interest on the $206 billion debt we inherited. The fact is that the interest payments on the 1984 debt are the only reason for our deficit position today and the direct cause for the debt having nearly doubled.
The next question people often raise is: "Why are you not making absolute cuts in total program spending rather than just restraining its growth in order to bring the deficit down even faster?" The answer lies in what the spending involves and the important public needs it serves.
More than half of all the program spending consists of major transfers to persons and to other levels of government. The transfer to individuals includes monthly Old Age Security benefits, family allowances, veterans' pensions and unemployment insurance.
Since half of these transfers are directly to the elderly, it is a combination of an aging population and full indexation of benefits to inflation that have made this the fastest growing area of government spending.
The other largest target area of program spending is, of course, provincial transfers. This is designed to support health care, education, welfare and other services of direct benefit to Canadians. Growth in this area over the past six years has averaged 6 per cent, just behind the growth in the transfer to individuals.
The rest of the program spending covers every other aspect of government activity including national defence, the internal operation of the government, foreign aid and programs for science and regional assistance. In many of these areas we have imposed dramatic disciplines. For example, transfers to business which cover regional development and science and technology spending has been cut from $4.7 billion in 1984-1985 to just $3.6 billion this year. Over the same period, spending on the operations of government has grown an average of only 1.2 per cent a year. Taking inflation into account, this means that the real cost of government today is actually 25 per cent less than six years ago.
June 13, 1991

These figures should drive home just how little room is available to make further cuts. An absolute reduction in total program spending simply could not be sustained without a serious impact on programs to help Canadians in need and on other essential services.
This does not mean that the deficit battle cannot be won. Rigorous spending restraint combined with the impact of lower interest rates and the higher revenues made possible by economic recovery will do the job. It is to make sure the job is done that we are instituting the legislated spending limits proposed in this budget.
Again I want to emphasize that there is no misplaced optimism or mathematical mumbo-jumbo at work when I say that the deficit will come down to $24 billion by 1992-1993. We will no longer be faced with the transitional costs of the GST, representing a $2 billion saving. The gulf war spending is behind us. The expenditure control plan will deliver savings of another $2.3 billion. Lower interest rates will ease the burden of servicing the debt, and economic recovery will reduce unemployment insurance costs and strengthen government revenues.
In turn, this sharp drop in the deficit combined with national recovery will see the debt begin to shrink as a portion of our economy. This threshold step will mean that government revenues, combined with the continuing benefits of lower interest rates and government spending caps, will be sufficient to eliminate the need for new borrowing in 1994-1995 as the budget states.
The legislated spending limits and the inflation targets we have set out should encourage all Canadians to recognize that we can no longer afford to buy government services on credit. They are also powerful tools that the budget provides Canadians to continue challenging their politicians about spending.
Our program of financial and economic policies is already proving its worth. While there is still real weakness in our economy, we continue to be confident that growth will resume in the second half of this year and rebound strongly in 1992.
This is not just a government perspective. The World Economic Outlook published by the International Monetary Fund this spring shares that view, projecting 1992 growth for the Canadian economy of 3.5 per cent, a
Supply
growth rate that, according to the IMF forecast, would lead all G-7 nations except Japan.
Looking further ahead, the continued easing in inflationary pressures expected over the near term will set the stage for strong growth over the medium term. We expect the real GNP growth to average at a rate of 4 per cent over the 1993-1996 period.
As I said, there is real evidence that we are indeed on track for that return to growth in the next six months.
Short-term interest rates have fallen over 5 per cent since their peak in May of last year. The real rate for 90-day commercial paper has declined from 9.6 per cent a year ago to 3.2 per cent this April. The Canada-U.S. interest rate differential has narrowed from the peak of over 500 basis points to under 300 basis points.
Reduced interest rates have helped generate a welcome upturn in the Canadian housing industry, a leading indicator of recovery. In April, housing starts were up more than 30 per cent over March. They increased another 16.4 per cent in May to an annual rate of 149,000 units. In fact, the total number of housing starts this April and May were 42,500 units higher, a more than 44 per cent increase over the same period last year. Employment has continued to increase for three consecutive months to 34,000 jobs in May, virtually all of them full time. And, while the unemployment rate edged up slightly last month after falling to 10.2 per cent in April from 10.5 per cent in March, it was the result of an increase in the labour force itself and not because of job losses.
There are other positive sides. The manufacturers' shipments of automotive products, another important indicator, increased sharply in March. The Conference Board of Canada index Business Confidences increased 29 per cent in the first quarter, with more executives expecting economic improvement than at any time since 1984.
The negotiated wage settlements, an important source of the inflationary pressure that pushes up interest rates, increased only by 3.4 per cent in April, down substantially from 6.2 per cent average increase in the settlement during the first quarter.

June 13, 1991
Supply
Let me say that we are not out of the woods yet. We could still lose the path to recovery if we abandon our commitment to restrain spending and bring inflation down. We must not let that happen. This government will not let that happen, because it would mean abandoning our commitment to the economic future of all our citizens, including those still facing hardships.
There is ample evidence to suggest that our financial and economic policies are working to put Canada back on the path to sustained growth and productive economic activity in the years ahead. I would ask the hon. members to bear this evidence in mind when the motion is put before this House.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE

Madam Speaker, I wonder if the hon. parliamentaiy secretary could comment on the subject of government finances and cutbacks that members of Parliament are being lobbied about at this very moment by the Canadian Nurses Association. The report by the Canadian Council of Welfare just a few days ago predicts that very shortly transfers to the provinces for health care will be reduced to zero at various times for each province.
