I would like the hon. gentleman to comment on that concern about medicare. With his many years here in this Chamber, I wonder if he could comment on the question generally and on what the government's position is.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, generally speaking our major concern-and while I know there are specific instances of nurses and other groups who may feel that they are being disadvantaged by not having a rise in their wages- is the long-term effect that continued growth in the public debt and continued growth in the deficit is going to have on this country in the long term.
We are moving into a new world, a global economy, and we are seeing massive changes in manufacturing styles in the world. We are seeing new productive facilities coming into place that require massive capital expenditures by people in business, and we are seeing an ever increasing debt load of services that the general public is demanding.
We have to tiy and find a balance between these things, and we are doing that to the very best of our ability. It may mean that there are some people who may
feel that they are disadvantaged by the course that we are taking. But our objective is to get more people working, to see that our industries are re-equipped in the proper way so they can compete in the global market, to see that we can knock down the barriers between our provinces and get trade moving fluidly across the country. That is what our objective is. We are not taking a swing at public servants or nurses or anybody in particular. We think the matter is so serious that it has to be shared around the country. I know that when you ask someone who feels they are on the edge, that they have nothing to share, then we feel for them and we do what we can through whatever programs we have available to assist them.
On the other side, if you look at the revenue we have had coming into the government over the years and the fact that for a number of years we have had to go offshore and borrow $30 billion, it is almost a locked-in position.
You bring out a budget and what happens? Your revenue is $30 billion under what you take in, so you just continue to allow that to grow until you have a massive public debt on which compound interest works miracles and makes it double and quadruple in a short period of time. The first thing you know, it affects your ability to operate outside the countiy. It affects the rate of inflation and the interest rates in the country. It has just gone far enough and we have to do something about it. That is why we have put these various programs in place to try and rectify what has happened in the past.
I do not want to comment on why it happened, how it happened, or the political climate of the time or the social climate of the time. I lived through it and the hon. member lived through it, so we both know it very well. I think we are doing the right thing. I guess time will tell.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all, before I go into another matter, in the member's last response, he referred to borrowing money offshore. The implication I got from that response was that we were borrowing approximately $30 billion offshore each year. That concerns me somewhat. I wanted to give the member an opportunity to correct that, if in fact, that was not what he said. I think he probably would want to correct that. My understanding is that somewhere between 18 and 25 per cent of the deficit is borrowed offshore now, as opposed to the rest being borrowed domestically.
June 13, 1991

I throw that over to the member for his opportunity to clarify for me what he meant by that.
Second, he has talked in his speech today about getting the deficit down to a more manageable position. I specifically wanted to have him talk for a minute to this House and to the people of Canada about the legislation that has been proposed both in the throne speech and the budget, the debt servicing and reduction fund. There have been various interpretations of this.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is on the right track, is it not?

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The member for Fraser Valley East said they are on the right track. I think if they did get the deficit under control, they would be on the right track. What I want from the member for Burlington is some indication that this is not simply a shell game. It seems to me that in the budget they have talked about various moneys going in to be used to service the national debt.
Quite frankly, right now we are servicing the national debt. That is the interest charges we pay; 35 cents on each dollar we take in is paid in servicing our national debt. Is this debt servicing and reduction fund simply a public relations thing to show the people that money is going somewhere where it is already being paid?
I am a little confused and I think the people I have talked to around Canada are a little confused. Is the government trying to pull the wool over the peoples' eyes? I would like the member to respond to this.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When I made reference to borrowing $30 billion offshore, I was speaking in very broad terms. I know that the percentage we borrow offshore will vary from year to year according to domestic conditions and markets offshore.
What we have done in the last few years is to move from medium term notes and bonds to rather short-term money. We have been able to ratchet that down and we are not borrowing that total $30 billion offshore. In fact, since I have been in this House, I can remember a time when the Government of Canada encouraged provinces to borrow offshore because that would put pressure on
Supply
the Canadian dollar and drive its value up. That is gone now, and we are not interested in pursuing that avenue any more.
As far as the other part of his comment goes, the debt servicing and reduction fund is not a shell game. We are in better shape than some of the provinces are, because a lot of them have issued bonds of a fairly long-term nature. They have to let those bonds mature before they can pay them off, or pay a penalty for paying them off early. Most of our dead instruments are relatively short term, many of them less than a year, many of them less than two years. As the money comes into the debt servicing and reduction fund we will be able to pay those obligations off, and therefore will not require the amount of servicing as far as the deficit is concerned. Of course, this will reduce the national debt at the same time.
You can stand in your place and say: "Well, we are going to bring the deficit down". This is my 19th year here and I have heard it so often that it is almost tattooed on my forehead. But to do something to convince people that we are going to bring it down, I think is worth while. That was the purpose, to say: "We are going to devote the revenue from the GST into the debt service and reduction fund".
I had many people say to me: "I do not mind it. If you are going to do that with the GST, I do not mind it at all. And the same with the sale of Crown corporations. Well, what do you do with that money? If you are going to dedicate that money to debt service and reduction, that is fine, that is okay with me". And so that is what we have done.
All I can say to the hon. member is that it is not a shell game. I would just suggest that he watch it closely, keep his eye on it, and I am sure he will because I know him to be a member of honesty and integrity. We will see how it goes a year from today.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am speaking to the estimates of the Conservative government. One of the reasons I wish to address this question is due to the myth this government has tried to create.

June 13, 1991
Supply
This government first came to power in 1984 on a program of fiscal management. It told the people of Canada it could manage the monetary aspects of our economy far better than the people before had done.
I must say that in 1984 I was quite naive and I thought perhaps the Conservatives might accomplish that. I must say I have been extremely disappointed, as have the rest of the people of Canada, because they continue to do and say one thing and do whatever they feel like doing behind closed doors.
One of the first things they do is they come up with stacks of estimates. These estimates are a bunch of figures and they look not bad. But the first thing you have to realize is that these are not necessarily just the moneys they are going to spend. These figures are often misleading, because it takes nothing at all for this government to bring in Supplementary Estimates. All of a sudden it is a whole new ball game, and the government has not really explained to the people of Canada what it has done.
The other thing that I wish to address is this: I first came to office in 1988 and in early 1989,1 was assigned to the public accounts committee. I was very interested in hearing many of the Auditor General's reports and they are all public. Since then I have taken on the task of going over many of the Auditor General's reports.
One of the things discovered is that if one takes the Auditor General's reports from 1985 through 1989, one finds a long chronicle of moneys mismanaged, expenditures inadequately disclosed or not disclosed at all and cost overruns. All of the items are on public record and many of them have been the subject of news coverage in the past. The cumulative effect of all these items is mind-boggling.
If one goes through and quietly adds some of these numbers up, one realizes that had these problems been addressed right from beginning, one would have saved billions of dollars. It is no laughing matter. It is certainly something that they could have done had they wanted to when they first formed the government.
The other thing that has happened is that they have used creative bookkeeping. I like to use that term because it is something that accountants can relate to. When one does not want to really disclose something one changes the format by which one presents it. That makes it very difficult for people to compare year to year.
I decided to try and review the budgets of the government from 1985 to 1989.1 picked those years because the Auditor General's reports were present for those years. I wanted to review them sequentially from 1985 to 1989 and to find out the yearly increases beyond the level of inflation in each year. Then, I wanted to break these down into spending areas: defence, health, welfare. I subtracted amounts that related to transfer payments because obviously the government has veiy little control over funding in this area unless it just decreases it. It cannot control its spending as much as it would like to I am sure.
One of the things that surprised me was that one could not do this. One could not compare year to year. Do you know why? Prior to 1987-88, government budgets were prepared according to program envelopes, nothing wrong with that, namely: economic and regional development, social development, services to government, Parliament, defence, external affairs and fiscal arrangements. This permitted expenditures within each area to be tracked from year to year.
In 1987-88, however, a brilliant move: the federal government introduced a different format, supposedly for better bookkeeping, I would think. Who knows? One never knows for sure.
Only defence spending remained in the program envelope. Other more generalized categories such as major transfers to persons and transfers to other governments replaced program envelopes, whereas earlier fiscal plans contained additional tables relating specifically to program expenditures by category. These too were removed.
In 1989-90 the budget format was again altered, this time to include three new categories: subsidies, Crown corporations and other operations. These three categories had not previously existed and accounted for approximately $32 billion in government spending.
Do you understand what I am getting at? It is very easy to generally say: "See what great guys we are", because there is a lot of room for hiding and manoeuvring and all the rest of it.
The result of these format changes, of course, is that while cumulative program expenditures can be compared from year to year, it is no longer possible to determine the increases within any given area of spending. Strange, isn't it?
June 13, 1991

It is worth while noting that program expenditures which amounted to about $87 billion in 1984-85, the year the Conservative government came to power, have increased to an annual amount of $103.5 billion. Just interesting. We are not talking about interest charges here; we are talking about program expenditures. There is a little bit of difference. Why the huge increase? It may be justified and it may not be, but at least, when you look at the auditor's report, $500 million annually could have been saved within these program expenditures if moneys had been managed with regard to economy and efficiency.
Many times when one looks at the Auditor General's reports one realizes that program objectives are not met, maybe due to political interference. The Auditor General infers that but does not necessarily say it. It is quite obvious when one considers the building of a correctional centre in an inappropriate area and it just happens to be the region of the party leader's riding.
I have got details of it here. This was reported for the year 1986, as having happened in 1986, which is before my time. I am just repeating what the Auditor General said in those years. It states:
Political objectives outweighed program objectives. Correctional Services was required to build for no program reasons and was required to build institutions at certain economically depressed areas to increase employment.
This may be a good idea, but it certainly is not good fiscal management.
This meant that Correctional Service Canada had to build at higher security levels than needed, such as protective custody, when it already had surplus capacity. That was in 1986.
Ten billion dollars was lost due to a late decision to cancel the special handling unit at the Atlantic institution, creating a contingent liability of $1 million to the contractor. One goes on and on.
One hears about additional costs of $4.6 million due to major design changes. That is not a small amount of money, think about it, $4.6 million. A drop in the bucket. We talk about deficits and how well we manage things. We have another one here that says $1.7 million went for brick cladding for concrete walls. Additional.
Supply
What I saw when I was looking at all this is that it is almost a given that when a government contract goes out, whoever gets the contract gets cost plus. One wonders. One gives out a contract and then one comes back and adds in one's extras. There are examples of that everywhere. One does not have to go very far. Every year it seems to happen.
Now what kind of controls it has over its tendering process, I do not know, but there are very good examples of it. One can go through the Auditor General's report and it is very obvious.
One of the ones that just happened, I think it was reported in 1990, was the amount of money paid by DRIE in February 1987 to a company in Alberta for the development of a turbo-charger, despite the concerns of the NRC. In January 1989, the new Department of Western Economic Diversification took over this program and made a second payment despite information not being provided in accordance with the agreement. To add insult to all of this, in March 1989, it learned that the prototype that it had been funding had been destroyed in 1987, but the final payment was made anyway. After all, it was a buddy. Who knows? What is the justification?
These are examples that are taken directly from the Auditor General's report. Each and every one of you can get the reports out yourself. Some $148,500 was approved to construct a golf course, including the retroactive reimbursement of cost despite program criteria requiring that no significant contractual commitment be made prior to a request for funds. When they went out and asked for the money the project was almost finished. Kind of a neat deal, eh? I would like to do that. I will go out and build myself a house and then I will go and ask people for money and they will give it to me. I think a lot of people in Canada would like that.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: Sure.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Those are the kinds of things that have been going on, despite all the claims of great management and great fiscal responsibility.
The first myth that this government brought forward was that the Liberals were such terrible spenders. They were such terrible spenders that they took over this terrible debt. One of the things they failed to mention was that for 1984-1985, Marc Lalonde, who was then finance minister, had projected a deficit of $29-some billion, which was very high. It was the end of a terrible recession.

June 13, 1991
Supply
What they failed to tell people was that they allowed this deficit to rise to $38 billion because it gave them a cushion, a real neat cushion. At the end of 1984-1985, rather than having a deficit of $29 billion, it was $38 billion. Let me point out that the recession was well on its way to being over. Things were coming back, things were looking very good.
Let us just set things straight here. We went from a projected deficit of $29 billion to a deficit of $38 billion, and they say: "Well, it was the Liberals that did it", except they formed the government in September 1984. The fiscal year goes for longer than that, much longer than that. They had a party and they paid off whoever they had to pay off and built whatever they had to. And I love it when I get them responding because it always tells me-

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: It means it hits home.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-that it is hitting home. This is one of the truths that has not been said.
Then this government continued to spend, continued during the best years that we have had since the Second World War, having high deficits despite increasing taxes more than 31 times, till it brings us to today. We now have these extremely high taxes, where we are asking Canadians or telling the Public Service: "Tighten your belts, you cannot have an increase, you cannot do this".
Does this government do it? Does this government lead by example? Absolutely not. Just think of it for a minute. This is a country with a population of 26 million people. We have how many ministers? Is it 40? Correct me if I am wrong. There are so many of them, it is difficult. They add them and subtract them, and there is always a new one somewhere. There are 40-some ministers. In the United States, with a population how many times larger-

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: Some 150 million.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is larger than 150 million. How many ministers do they have to run that country? Under 20. So I wonder, if the Americans can do it with under 20, why cannot we? The Conservatives like to do everything that the Americans do. As a matter of fact, if they are in power much longer, that is where we will be. We will be with the Americans, we will belong to them.
In this case, maybe they should be following a little bit in their mode. If I can tell the people of Canada what happens in ministries, each minister has to build himself a little power base. If you have a very small staff, then you have no clout. You have to build this power base and have all these big offices, and you have to have all of this staff. You have to justify your existence. Therefore, your budgets have to be larger. And the fight goes on. Then this minister writes to that minister, and that minister answers back, and then there is a lot of justification for jobs.
If you want to create employment at that level, that is fine, but you should not run on the fact that you are fiscally prudent because that is not a fiscally prudent method of behaving. I am very interested in seeing this government finally come out and do something and really show the people of Canada that they can be fiscally responsible, not just tell others to be fiscally responsible. That, to my way of thinking, would be the way to go. We create ministries so we can supposedly help areas of the country. We call it regional development and sometimes the grants are good. Often they are not worth much of anything.
In terms of some of the things I have uncovered under the Auditor General's report, bridges that lead to nowhere. We have all heard of that. Highways that are built for reasons that do not follow the criteria of the program. There was a host of them in 1989 that were reported under energy, mines and resources that were under the Canada-Nova Scotia Development Fund.
Many questions were asked in the House of Commons at that period of time. Of course there was a non-answer.
When we say that the people of Canada have absolutely no faith in this government, we know why. It tells you one thing and does exactly the opposite. It tells you that the GST will be revenue neutral. Obviously it is not.
Their own member who is the chairman of the finance committee said over and over again that it was going to be a cash cow. Everywhere else that the program was brought in, large amounts of money were brought in that were supposedly unforeseen.
June 13, 1991

I am waiting to see what the government is going to do because now it has seen the light. It now has a deficit reduction account. I just love it. I think that is a great idea. When I go home, I am going to open myself another account and I am going to start putting money in that account.
The only problem is that if I do not have more money coming in, how am I going to cover the other account? It is going to get larger. You only have so many pockets and you only have so much money. You can play around all you want. The fact of the matter is that we still have a problem.
You have to be more responsible. That is what we are saying. Whether you like it or not, you have not been responsible I ask that you go back to your ministers and tell them to get together, streamline.
I am supposed to be speaking to Madam Speaker. I am sorry, I had forgotten in the moment I have. My colleagues on the other side are so happy with my speech that I understand they are going to go right back to their ministries and ask them to streamline things, to quit pretending, and to start being honest.
Maybe the people of Canada will like this a bit better. It cannot get much worse.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have listened attentively to the hon. member for Sudbury. She has asked us to go back and streamline ministries.
Streamlining ministries in order to save money means you have to cut out public servants. Is that what the hon. member is asking us to do? Is she asking us to cut down the size of the Public Service? I suspect that this is what she is inferring today.
I think she inadvertently is making that as a suggestion. I am not sure that she predicts that.
She talks about the projections when we came to power of what the former finance minister in his budget address in the spring of 1984 had made in this House of Commons. She failed to realize the economic paper that was put out by the finance minister under the capable leadership of the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre in November of that year, how we set in train and how we
Supply
were going to try to get our arms around money that was being spent.
In today's edition of The Citizen, if she were to read it, it says that the Tories have literally reversed the country's fiscal picture by adding $30 billion annually to the credit side of the country's ledger.
In other words, there was more money going out to pay for the programs and transfer of payments to individuals than what was coming in to the tune of $16 billion. Add that to the interest charges of the $200 billion debt that was there and you have quite a difference.
That has been reversed. That has taken a lot of hard work and is taking place. If per chance there is more money that comes in through the GST than we had planned on, we are going to put that money against the deficit reduction so that it does not go into paying for more programs.
The Canadian people have been asking for this and I suspect if the hon. member were to be honest with us today, she would have to admit that her constituents are telling her that about the GST. My constituents are saying that and I suspect that her constituents are not that different. She said she has made a study of the various Auditor General's reports. I would ask her, did she not realize that the Auditor General, about three years ago said: "At long last, I can now say that the money is being spent where it was allocated to be spent". That was the first time in his tenure, and he had a contract for six years; I think it was in the fifth or sixth year of his contract-that he was able to make that statement.
Does the hon. member not admit that is a very positive remark from the Auditor General and goes a long way to signifying that at long last the government now knows where its money is being spent? True, too much is being spent. I agree with her. The hon. member will have to admit that there were already pieces of legislation that had been enacted and so we had to turn around and change the structure. That is precisely what the GST was, a structural change. That is difficult. Structural change is difficult.
I might add that the hon. member's party did not try to help us. They had a lot of criticism, but never any constructive suggestions as to how we might improve it. It was just a case of: "Do not do it. Leave things the way they are". However, things were not working.

June 13, 1991
Supply
I have to end my remarks at this point. Does she not admit that what she reads in today's The Ottawa Citizen and on page 28 of our Quorum really is quite factual? I would encourage her to possibly consider mailing it out to her constituents asking for their comments.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am going to start with the first item he addressed himself to: Did I want to lay off all of the public servants who work for all these ministers?
What I say is that it is not the public servants who are at fault in this whole thing; it is the ministers. When you have a minister of native affairs and a minister of state for native affairs who do absolutely nothing or next to nothing, I cannot figure why there has to be two of them with their chauffeurs, their cars and their big offices. That would send a big message; I like the idea of cutting back.
On the contrary, this government has tried to blame the public servants. I think it is an absolute shame they are projecting to freeze salaries of public servants, especially the very low-paid public servants.
Do you know that a large number of public servants in this country earn below the poverty line, and you are freezing their wages? Yet you come to us and tell us what a great job you are doing. If you really want to freeze wages, then do it for everyone. Do not single out one group of people who have worked very hard for you. That is another problem you are creating by being that difficult to deal with, your people cannot work properly for you.
If you are always giving your public servants a hard time, how do you think they are going to feel? Do you think they will go to work every day and be happy and super-productive? I tell you, absolutely not.
On the question of taxes and the great fiscal management, I am going to tell you what is happening in my riding and it is happening all over Ontario.
In the early years of the recession, especially in the riding of Sudbury, we were very hard hit. As a group of people, we worked together to build on our strength, our resource sector. We had an entrepreneur who did a very good job. His name is Ken Burgess. He started a business and he went into manufacturing. It was a spectacular success. He expanded and he opened six plants across Ontario.
I am going to tell you the announcement he made on Tuesday of this week. He is closing all of his manufacturing plants. He says increases in taxes, and the higher Canadian dollar are hitting that group of eight companies hard and they have decided to just plain close up shop.
One of his businesses was in Cambridge. I quote from an article in The Sudbury Star, quoting Mr. Burgess:
Every third building in Cambridge is empty right now. Hundreds of
companies a week are moving out of the Ibronto area and to the
United States-I think the manufacturing days in this country are
numbered unless our governments wake up.
Tell me, is that not an example of the kinds of things that are being said everywhere? I hear it in the House every day. I do not know what you are hearing but I heard of this man who was successful in very difficult times and now suddenly in 1991 he is closing all his manufacturing plants because he cannot compete.
When is this government going to face what they have done to the people of Canada with these taxes? It is an absolute shame that our own people cannot compete because the environment has not been created for competition. The day they start recognizing this and doing something about it we will all be a lot better off. It is not just a question of saying one thing and doing another. It is a question of all of us working together. None of us is perfect, least of all the people across the way.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member implied in her comments that we had somehow or other added another $9 billion to the deficit when we came into power. I want to tell her how that $9 billion came about and she can go back to the auditor general and get his explanation.
We came into power with a budget that was already in place, a $29.5 billion deficit-

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: I don't believe that for a minute. You would say the same thing about the NDP.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Auditor General came to us and said there are $9 billion of expenditures that have been included as capital expenditures and are no longer capital expenditures. They are straight-line expenses. Therefore you are going to have to increase the deficit by $9 billion. That is how it came about. It was nothing that we did. It was money spent by Marc Lalonde and his people. That is the first thing.
June 13, 1991

Go back to the Auditor General, check it out, and he will tell you the truth.
The member talks about reducing the number of ministers. When I came here years ago we did not have a Minister of State for Small Business. Through pressure from a variety of people we suddenly had a Minister of State for Small Businesses. He used to send questions and notes across the floor to us: "Please ask me a question. I haven't anything to do". In 1979 when we went into his office to see what we would do with his operation we found there was a Minister of State for Small Businesses, a secretary, a speech writer, a driver, and one researcher. That was the total ministry. He had no line responsibilities. He was not responsible for any legislation. He came in the House of Commons, sat in his seat and sent notes to the opposition which said: "Please ask me a question. I am lonely".
That is what your government did.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I leap humbly into the breach. I have heard some interesting things about debts and deficits today so I think I would like to start speaking today about the deficit and deficit reduction.
What I have seen since being here, and particularly since 1984, of course started long before that. I agree, with the member for Fraser Valley East that it started before that. It seems to me that what has happened over the course of time is that both of these parties, the Conservatives and the Liberals, can take a lesson from the squirrels. During the summertime when food is bountiful and the nuts are plentiful they go out and gather nuts and they save for a winter day so that they have something to eat.
It seems to me that both the Liberals and the Conservatives have forgotten that winter is just around the comer. In the good times, since 1984, the economy has been fairly buoyant and the present Conservative government has forgotten the winter-we are now in the dead of winter-and there are no nuts. They haven't collected them, they haven't saved them; they have been eating everything in sight. This party hasn't paid any attention at all to what is going to happen later. They have not paid attention to history and learned that at the end of every upswing comes a downswing. They have
Supply
continued in this way each year that I have been here. I have looked at the budgets and have seen that they are going to reduce the deficit. At the end of the year when we got the figures in, I found that no, the deficit has not been reduced. In fact, because of this or that or the other thing, whether it be the Persian Gulf war, the interest rates, or whatever, we haven't been able to reduce the deficit.
If I recall correctly, two years ago it was going to be $28.5 billion. Last year it was up to almost $31 billion again. Now this year I heard the same figures again-$28 billion-and maybe this time the government will make it. They finally listened to the opposition. They listened to the New Democratic Party and are starting to drop the interest rates.
I remember when the Minister of State for Small Businesses was before the committee on his estimates two years ago. In questioning him he threw a question back to me and asked: What is small business looking for; what do you say they are looking for? At that time I remember I told him that they were looking for lower, stable interest rates. Well, they are starting to get lower interest rates. And if the minister did it, then congratulations to him. But they have finally started listening to us, after two long, hard years. The Minister of State for Small Businesses talked to the Minister of Finance and convinced him that was what small businesses wanted. They needed it, they needed it to survive.
But before the minister gets too blown up with importance, I want to read a little quote to him from a research paper from his favourite institution, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, prepared for their offices back in January, I believe. It says: "Business conditions have undoubtedly been worsened by government policy, most notably the federal government's monetary and tax policy. The high interest rate strategy has placed a particularly heavy burden on small businesses which do not enjoy the financing flexibility open to large firms. The impact has been particularly severe in construction, manufacturing and the retail trade. In addition, the detrimental effects of the stubbornly high interest rates, coupled with a high Canadian dollar at a time of economic recession, has been exacerbated by the federal government's goods and services tax."

June 13, 1991
Supply
Madam Speaker, we now have lower interest rates and hopefully they will get lower and stabilize for the sake of the small business community. But we still have the goods and services tax. No matter where I have gone in Canada since January, since the implementation of this dastardly tax, I have heard the small business community complaining about the implementation, the administration and the cost to them of the GST. I have spoken to lawyers and small business firms, I have spoken to medium sized firms, the ones with computers, the ones that say "we can do the work, but it costs us heavily in time and money management."
The criminal lawyers tell me that they give a single quote-$1,000, $2,000, $3,000, $2,500, whatever it is-to defend a person on a criminal charge. Well, they either raise their rates by $500 to round it out, and they don't feel that they can do that in today's recessionary times, or they eat the GST. The criminal lawyers I have spoken to in the last couple of months tell me that they are, in fact, eating the GST.
I have spoken to insurance agents in small communities across Canada who tell me that as a result of the exempt provisions in the goods and services tax, they cannot write off their capital investments or they can write them off but then can't take the rebate for the GST, the input tax credit.
This causes an undue burden. What do they do? They have to pass on that cost once again to the consumer or cut back in their meagre profits.
Food retail outlets in my province and in my communities such as Super Values, IGA and Giant Foods all sell a combination of foods, prepared foods and items such as women's hygienic products, tampons and the like. These have GST attached to them. In this particular case, one of the examples I gave is unfair to women. It is as important to women as sustenance and food. This government should consider that in looking at where it is going and what it has done with this tax.
It goes on. It was interesting in going to a couple of places recently and seeing the small family shops shut down, and talking to the people about it. They were saying that they had shut down just after the Christmas trade of 1990 and prior to the GST in 1991 because they
were not willing to go through the hassle at that stage in their lives. Some of them were older and had been in business for a number years and did not want to go through the extra burden of trying to look after this tax.
Talk to the farmers who are members of the small business community. I think it was stated well by a potato farmer in Prince Edward Island when he said: "We work from dawn until dusk. We come in, we eat, we go to bed and the cycle starts again. We do not want to have to come in and have to do this extra bookwork after a full, long day's work in the fields to keep up with the GST." That is what has happened under this tax. The government has continually hurt the small business community.
It is interesting to note what has happened as a result of the fiscal and monetary policies of this government. We warned the government some two years ago that if it brought in the GST at that stage, we would be in the depths of a depression. That was two years ago. I am no economist and I knew it and this government continued to ignore it. Now what has happened is that we have the highest rate of bankruptcies, business failures and personal bankruptcies that we have ever seen in Canada. The rate is higher than it was in the depths of the 1981-82 recession.
The last figures I had show bankruptcies for 1990 total 11,642 and they have increased some 32 per cent already this year. They surpassed, for the first time, the 1982 recessionary peak of 10,765 business failures. This is an increase of 34 per cent.
This government is proud of its fiscal and monetary policies. It tells us how great it is doing and yet at the same time we are watching the business community taking a bigger beating than it has ever taken in Canada in modem history in this made-in-Canada recession. It is unbelievable.
The government continues to tell us how great things are going, how good its monetary policies are and how wonderful its fiscal policies are. I have got one word for it, hog-wash, simply hog-wash. We have got major failures.
I will refer again to this document from the Canadian Federation of Independent Business: "There is however a sharp contrast between the position of the banks today compared with the early 1980s."
June 13, 1991

Does it ring a bell? Who puts $30,000 a year into the coffers of the government? Certainly not the small business community. We see a sharp contrast in the position of the banks today as compared with small business.
I quote further. In referring back to the 1980s, they say:
At that time the banks were burdened by losses they had incurred from their massive loans to large corporations and Third World countries. Today, the banks are in a much better position, and could well afford to be more patient with firms struggling to survive in an uncertain and difficult business environment.
It appears that the friends of the government, the rich get richer and the poor get poorer. The tax policies of this government have shown that. The figures over the last few years show that the burden has shifted to middle and low income Canadians and away from the top wage earners.
If we couple the banking situation and the GST, we note that in the use of credit cards, VISA, Master Card, American Express, the merchant fee that is paid, whether it be, depending on the card, 2 per cent up to 5 or 6 per cent in some cases, is added at the end of the tally which includes both provincial sales tax and the goods and services tax. So on a large ticket item a merchant can end up paying 2-1/4 or 3 per cent of the 7 per cent that has been paid on the item.
If you look at the figures of what is charged to credit cards throughout the course of a year in Canada and look at what the GST is on those figures and then you multiply it by the percentage that they take up in a merchant fee, we know that the banks now, as a result of the goods and services tax, are getting somewhere in the area of $16 million extra as a result of the merchant fee on top of the goods and services tax. That is using 1989 figures. The figures for today, I would suggest, would be higher, given the fact that there is an increase or has been an increase in the number of credit cards outstanding in Canada and the number of transactions going on those particular credit cards.
It is interesting to see how closely aligned are the government and the big banks. In going further with that and talking about bankruptcies, the government today tabled the new Bankruptcy Act. It is interesting because they have set up another fund, which is a good idea, to ensure that wages of those working for firms, corpora-
Supply
tions or others which declare bankruptcy or go into receivership get paid something for their wages.
What the government did was interesting. It set up a fund and it is now going to cost the employers 10 cents per week per employee to be paid into this fund. As I understand it, this will also be paid by federal, provincial and municipal governments.
Once again we look at the trickle down effect because the municipal governments cannot deficit finance as can the provinces and the feds. They are going to have to come up with the money out of their budgets. Where do they get the money? They increase the property taxes to the ordinary citizen of their communities and the small business person.
I want to ask why they have not set up a priority system? The Minister at Consumer and Corporate Affairs essentially told us, "Well, it did not seem to be the route to go, that if they set up this, it was a separate system, self-administered." If you look into it deeper, what it comes down to is the banks did not want to give up their priority to a preferred creditor such as a wage holder.
Yet if we look at labour standards legislation in all of the provinces, it ensures that wages are looked after in priority to everything else that they have jurisdiction over.
Of course, the provinces do not have jurisdiction over the federal government and Revenue Canada. It was also interesting that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has looked after the revenues of the country. That is admirable, to say that the directors and executive members of a corporation will be jointly and severally responsible for the debts of that corporation.
I could not find anywhere in that legislation anything that gave the small business person the same kick at the cat as the federal government. That is something the government should look at if it really, truly believes in the small business community.
If I look further into the estimates, it reminds me in looking at cutbacks, the centralization of services and what not, that we often have a tendency both in power, I suppose, and with our bureaucrats who assist us in our legislation and in our policies to ignore the small communities and how important various services are.

June 13, 1991
Supply
In Penticton, the largest community in my own riding, there are rumours running rampant that an old age pension, guaranteed income supplement and Canada Pension Plan office will be closed and centralized to Kelowna, up in the next riding up.
You might say well, it is all in the Okanagan Valley. Fair enough. But if you look at it in people terms, it is totally different. In those areas, about 35 per cent of all citizens are over 65 years of age. They often do not care to talk on the telephone. They like to catch a ride with their neighbour or drive themselves and go see someone face to face in a small office. When you are on a limited income, and you have to drive from Osooyos to Kelowna, about 140 or 150 kilometres, it is a great imposition. It is four hours of driving time in order to see the person you want to talk to about a problem with the old age security.
My office is in the same building as that particular office, and I see the number of people who go in. I have a number of those people coming into my office when they have difficulties. It is a real convenience. It is not as if it was a small community. It services a veiy large area.
Sometimes I wonder about some of the policies of the government. It has to pay more attention to people and less attention to policy and friends. The estimates and where the government is going, both fiscally and monetarily, leaves a lot to be desired. I believe I speak for the people of my riding. I speak reasonably for the people in the small business sector as the critic for my party, the New Democratic Party, when I say that something has to be done.
We have started, as the minister has told us, in getting lower interest rates. That is a start. But if we are going to continue, if we are going to start putting people first, we have to start here in Parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I just want to pose a couple of questions to my hon. friend who made a number of philosophical statements at the beginning about the way he believes the fiscal policy of the government should be operated to help the small business community.
The hon. member mentioned deficits and expressed his concern that the federal government has been spending too much money. It is amazing to hear that from an NDP member because never, since I have sat in this House, have I ever had an idea yet from the NDP on how to cut spending. Their proposals are always to increase spending.
Anyway, he says we should have cut spending more than we did although they never helped us with any ideas on how to do it. I want to bring him back to a different province, the province of Ontario which now has an NDP government.
I have a press release here that announces that the Moody Bond Rating Service has lowered the province's credit rating by two notches. It has been followed by the Canadian Bond Rating Service, the Dominion Bond Rating Service and Standard and Poors.

Madam Speaker, perhaps our colleagues across the floor would like to take note of some of the figures and facts that I shall be giving and see how a very efficient government operates. At the same time, I would reserve a couple of my comments for the end, since I did not have the opportunity to ask a question of my colleague.
This year the main estimates totalled $158 billion. Through these estimates the government is seeking Parliament's approval for $47 billion in new spending authority. The remaining $111 billion represents statutory payments that have had previous parliamentary approval.
These main estimates demonstrate our continuing commitment to control spending and contain the cost of government, the need for significant changes in the way government operates, and our commitment to deliver services to Canadians in the most efficient manner.
Since taking office in 1984, this government has given a high priority to reducing the cost of government operations while still providing Canadians with the programs and services they need. In this regard, much has been achieved over the past six years. Annual growth in program spending has been reduced, on average, to 3.7 per cent. In this regard, we have to look at annual growth in operating and capital spending, including public service salaries which we have dropped to an average of 3.3 per cent; and the Public Service has been reduced since 1984-85 to roughly the same size it was in the 1970s.
These achievements show the government's commitment to increased efficiency through the rigorous control of expenditures as well as the implementation of
innovative management procedures. These achievements also reflect the government's commitment to good management and to the careful stewardship of the taxpayers' dollars. Our record is one of success.
The year-over-year increase in the main estimates is the outcome of a number of decisions affecting the budgets of all 142 programs delivered by 118 departments, agencies and Crown corporations appearing in the estimates. This increase can be divided into two broad categories: adjustments to statutory items, which amount to $7.2 billion, and changes to voted items, which amount to $2.7 billion. Therefore only 27 per cent of the growth in the main estimates relates to voted items.
Statutory spending is $110.6 billion, or 70 per cent of total estimates and will grow by 7 per cent. Spending in this category includes such things as major federal transfers to Canadians in respect of Old Age Security, guaranteed income supplements and family allowances, and transfers to the provinces for health, education and social assistance.
It is important to note that the major factor underlying the growth in the voted portion of the main estimates is the carry-forward items, funded initially through the 1990-91 supplementary estimates. Items previously approved through supplementary estimates account for 44 per cent of the year-over-year growth of voted main estimates. The other categories such as higher personal costs, increased workload and new program initiatives, play a relatively minor role.
On a consolidated basis, four areas account for more than 80 per cent of total allocated budgetary spending: public debt charges take up 27.4 per cent of the total; social programs 36.1 per cent; fiscal arrangements close to 11 per cent; and defence spending 8.1 per cent.
Social programs are the largest component of over-all spending. During 1991-92, the federal government will direct $57 billion, which is 36 per cent of its allocated main estimates, to improve the social conditions of Canadians. The departments of Health and Welfare Canada, Indian Affairs and Northern Development, Employment and Immigration Canada make up over 90 per cent of the spending in this sector.
June 13, 1991

Through these social programs, the government is continuing its efforts to help those in greatest need through programs of assistance to the economically disadvantaged. The government's programs and policies will continue to ensure equality of access by all Canadians to the benefits of Canadian society.

These estimates fully reflect the second year impact of the expenditure control plan announced by the Minister of Finance in the 1990 budget. In the budget the Minister of Finance announced a number of reforms intended to bring about both immediate savings and lasting efficiencies in government programs.
The key to this program of restraint is a continuation of the expenditure control program together with tight controls on the cost of government operations which are
expected to produce a savings of nearly $870 million to Canadian taxpayers in the current fiscal year.
Over the five-year planning period, 1995-96, cumulative savings to Canadians will amount to over $5.2 billion. The expenditure control plan is extended to 1995-96. The budget also contains further measures beginning in 1991-92 to restrain spending on programs and operations of federal departments and agencies.
Over-all spending on operating and capital for existing programs will be effectively frozen as of 1990-91. This will be accomplished by a 3 per cent cut in the 1991-92 budget and capital budgets of each department.
In addition, departments will be required to absorb any increased salary costs arising from new collective agreements. As a result any wage increases will be paid for by a corresponding reduction in the number of jobs. Depending on the results of collective bargaining, this could entail a reduction in employment affecting as many as
6,000	jobs in the civil service.
Together these measures have reinforced our message to Canadians that the days of easy spending by the government are long past. The reality is all the more significant as we come through a period of economic recession and downturn coupled with unforeseeable external pressures for new spending.
Our budget also contained other significant initiatives. First, the Minister of Finance on behalf of the government is bringing forward draft legislation to put statutory limits on spending. This should provide Canadians with greater assurance that program spending will be managed within the fiscal framework.
Second, the government will reduce discretionary grants and contributions by $75 million. The hon. House leader, Harvie Andre, has been discussing with colleagues how these reductions can best be achieved.
Third, the government will streamline its operations by reducing the number of its executives by 10 per cent.
These reforms are necessary to make funds available for essential programs and services. However, reducing costs is only one aspect of the reforms of this government. These measures also reflect a profound realization that the present cost and complexity of government operations can no longer be justified to Canadians. If this government is to serve Canadians well, we must do it through new forms of service delivery and through organizations that are more efficiently managed.

June 13, 1991
Supply
Therefore, to improve efficiency within the Public Service, innovative management practices will continue to remain a priority of this government.
The government has introduced a wide range of initiatives since taking office in 1984 to improve the management of the expenditure of our budgets. The actions have been taken and will continue to be taken and they will produce results for all Canadians and Canadian taxpayers.
For example, revenues from external user fees now exceed $3 billion, which is more than double the 1984-1985 levels. The government is continuing to seek out new areas where the application of user fees are appropriate.
The government, through initiatives such as this has adopted a management strategy based on a more businesslike and frugal attitude to its operations. This, I understand, goes against the policies of our counterparts, the New Democratic Party across the way.
It has implemented measures to realize cost savings and improved administrative practices to deliver programs more effectively. This has been achieved through such initiatives as contracting out, special operating agencies and privatization.
The government believes that many services and functions are best carried out by public service employees. However, to provide a full range of options for delivering services to the Canadian public, certain functions are better done through the private sector, through contracting out.
Special operating agencies continue to be a viable mechanism for improving the delivery of our very important public services to the Canadian public.
Six more agencies have been announced through these main estimates, including the Canadian General Standards Board and the Canadian Conservation Institute. More candidates will be identified over the coming year, with a strong emphasis on organizations that directly serve the public where the potential for improvement is greatest.
Privatization will remain a key priority for this government. The government's program has already devolved more than 18 Crown corporations that have other corporate holdings to the private sector and other levels
of government. The government will privatize CN Exploration, an oil and gas company, and will wind up Petro-Canada International Assistance Corporation and the Canadian Oil and Gas Lands Administration.
The initiatives reviewed have helped move the government a considerable distance in managing itself more productively. The government will maintain its twopronged approach of top-down restraint on departmental budgets and of management policies that modify the institutional and working environment of public service managers.
These measures reinforce the consistent actions the government has taken since 1984. We must control the cost of government operations. We are also expected to engender considerable change in the way departments and agencies do business, that is in the nature and type of resources used as inputs in the technology applied and in the organization and methods of program delivery.
By changing the atmosphere in which government business is transacted, it becomes easier to make the structures more business-like. In keeping with the business-like environment, the government will be eliminating person-year controls and moving toward operating budgets.
Person-year authorities are a control mechanism used to limit the average number of employees that a department or an agency can use in the delivery of its programs. A person-year represents the employment of one person full time per year or for one year the equivalent of three persons for four months.
Controls on person years are used by the Treasury Board to complement conventional budget controls. This system of controls has served over the years to limit the size and cost of the Public Service and encourage the search for labour-saving efficiency which we can also use in cost saving factors. This has been confirmed by the Public Service 2000 task force report and the seventh report of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts.
The Treasury Board has begun to withdraw its control of person-year authorities in cases where suitable budget-based controls and incentives are in place to induce cost-effective, management decisions and the most efficient use of resources.
June 13, 1991

I would close by saying that when we speak on behalf of the government in terms of Main Estimates and Supplementary Estimates, that this movement toward operating budgets is a reflection of our commitment to Canadians to promote efficient practices within the Public Service. As I mentioned, the PS2000 task force and the Standing Committee on Public Accounts agreed with this.
The government is confident that operating budgets will promote more effective use of the taxpayers' money. This change is another example of our government's commitment to reform that will perform better service to Canadians.
I have listened to the other comments that were made by my hon. colleague across the way and will not go into more details concerning the New Democratic Party government in the province of Ontario. However, one thing I have learned since 1984, being a member of Parliament and, of course, we know that sometimes if we come from Quebec it makes it a little hotter than if we happen to come from other parts of the country, one thing that my people have told me at home since 1984 is that they want to pay, they want a service. If they do not pay then they have to cut back.
There are two methods that this government or any government can use, we can tax or we can cut. Our government is, in the most humane way, trying a little of both, which we have tried to approve and apply on behalf of our government. The NDP government can only talk about corporate bums, but the corporate bums supply thousands upon thousands upon hundreds of thousands of jobs in this country. Ontario is going through the situation now where business is going against them because they do not like their budget.
We cannot insult everyone, but what we shall do as the government is be very human and very Christian, if I can speak from the Christian point of view. Being a Christian of persuasion myself, and God fearing of any religion, without insulting any religion across Canada, we will administer this government so that all Canadians can have services that they need and we will be there.

In 1987, the labour force engaged in cultural activities was estimated at 400,000 Canadians. So says Stats Canada, according to Allen Gotlieb, the present Chairman of the Canada Council.
Arts related employment was as large as the agricultural sector in terms of employment. In fact it was the fourth largest sector of employment in Canada. Cultural revenues were estimated at $13.7 billion in 1987 and have grown immeasurably, as I will point out shortly, since that point. There has been an incredible ripple effect on the over-all economy. The income in this sector, with tourism and all the other benefits-whether they are the hot dogs or the peanuts sold, or the popcorn in the theatre that we all like, or the Coke or Pepsi-is in the range of $29 billion. Those are a lot of zeros. The industry buys a lot of food, provides a lot of jobs and is on a par with the metal and mining industry, in terms of revenues.

speechtext: So whatever we are doing with culture, we are helping it.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is a very big, important and beneficial area of our society. I would like the hon. member to read the Masse-Levesque commission report on national development in the arts, letters and sciences which was tabled in the early 1950s at a time when there was very little federal involvement in the arts. That report realized that Canadians' cultural identity, if we were to survive, required an activist role-one of partnership between the federal government and the provincial government, municipal governments and the private sector. That is how we have established Canada on the world map. We have produced, and can be very proud of, artists who are the expression of who we are within Canada. I am sure you would agree with that point of view.
June 13, 1991

This is not to say, when I talk about the federal role, that the provinces must not play an important role in cultural endeavours. However, I would caution that provincial initiatives are most effective when they are complemented by a federal presence in the sector.
For example, restraining the flood of foreign cultural activities would overwhelm the capacity of any single provincial government. Our proximity to our friendly neighbour, the United States, poses very special problems that are best met collectively right across this land. The pervasiveness and the power of the American cultural machine-through its film industry, television industry, music industry, the integration of those industries, and its distribution and marketing-is such that a fragmented system of cultural support and promotion would be easily overwhelmed if we did not stand together as Canadians shoulder to shoulder, coast to coast, en anglais ou en franqais, n 'importe.
We need to be vigilant in this government. A headline in The Globe and Mail today reads: "First day of trade talks produces discord". What does that headline go on to say? It says: "Canada-U.S. disagree over cultural industries". Sure they disagree because Canada has been able to and-if it continues to stand tall-can stop the overflow of American cultural homogenization around this world by saying that every country has the right of access to a certain percentage of its own market. If America has 94 per cent of our film market, how much does it want-100 per cent, or should we be allowed to have 3 per cent, 4 per cent, 5 per cent, 6 per cent? Could we go on to 10 per cent of our own market? That is something we should be allowed to do. If the American people, the average people in the United States, understood what the Jack Valentes and Carla Hills of this world wanted to do they would say: "Quit it, stop badgering your good friends and neighbours, the Canadians".
I believe that where we have now had the Constitution of Canada dominating our agenda with the Belanger-Campeau commission, with the Allaire report, the current discussions around the devolution of culture and communication powers to the provinces are very worrisome.
The total removal of the federal government from these cultural fields would have a devastating impact on
Supply
national unity and on cultural sovereignty in Canada, leaving us with an arrangement of a purely political and economic nature.
I would like to quote the Canadian Conference on the Arts which says: "Canada would cease to be a nation and would become a corporation." This side of the House sees a public federal role as necessary and complementary to the provincial, municipal and private sector initiatives to ensure viable, cultural activities. We see the role of the CBC, the National Arts Centre, Telefilm Canada, the museums, the National Archives, the library, the National Film Board and Canada Council as well as other federal institutions and programs as important and key.
They must be kept to reflect Canadians to Canadians. Without an activist federal government in the cultural arena, Canada will be nothing more than an association of economic states. There will be little opportunity to develop in the way of foreign influences and in the way of our personality.
The federal government's recent actions in this budget of 1991 hit the arts community very hard. In total, culture has lost $169 million for 1991-92 and the carnage may not be over. The big losers will be the four large projects: the performing arts buildings for Toronto, Edmonton and Montreal as well as the cultural research institute announced by the former Minister of Communications only days before the budget.
We need that research institute. I do not care where you put it, but you need to put it in and you need to integrate it into the kind of work that we are doing so we can do our work intelligently with the proper number crunch figures and the proper goal set for the future within this country.
These four projects totalling $151 million have supposedly only been delayed, according to the government. The main concern to the arts community is the government's intention to reduce its over-all grants and contributions to all sectors by $575 million over the next five years.
This year, grants and contributions will be cut by $75 million and each year thereafter by $125 million. It is still not known how Canada Council, Telefilm Canada, the Museums Assistance Program, the Cultural Initiatives Program and the postal subsidies program will be affected.

June 13, 1991

With regard to the postal subsidies program, we heard the minister today talking about how marvellous the post office has been since it was privatized, but he forgot to mention that he saved $110 million on the backs of the Canadian cultural industries, newspapers, magazines and community newspapers of this country.
If you look at the graph which was presented to us this morning in committee, it is extremely interesting to see that the government can talk about how good it has been in terms of allocation of current dollars. That is lovely, except it forgot there is an inflationary factor. Every one of us knows that it does not cost the same amount of money to buy a bottle of milk and a loaf of bread today as it did in 1984-85.
Here we are in 1991-92. If you look at the current dollars versus the purchasing power of the constant dollar, you would see that this government's allocations have gone down significantly.
I will not give the figures now but if someone wants to ask me after, I would be happy to give a breakdown of these figures. What has gone on here is that the decisions by this government are now going to be reviewed on a behind-the-scenes basis by the hon. Harvie Andre, the government House leader.
I would like to suggest that he may not be in the best position to review a lot of the things that we have been talking about. His review would remind me and hearken back to the Nielsen review, which was rather dramatic and Draconian.
As well, I have been hearing how we have been so good to our youth. We well know that there is a Canadian Jobs Strategy allocation program and a Summer Opportunities program. They all have special fancy names, but what they mean is that students and community groups need help and extra manpower during the course of a time frame which is generally the summer time. That money has been cut in my region alone by close to 20 per cent. That is a serious concern to the arts and cultural community because that jobs strategy cut will be in the amount of about $100 million. It represents a cut of about 5.5 per cent and it occurs at a time when cultural organizations have been pushing for new training and for human resource development programs for the burgeoning youth and cultural communities, which are really vibrant, exciting and dynamic. I know if you go,
as I do, to youth theatre programs, to the amateur development programs, to the parks and the playgrounds, to the CEGEP level and see some of the productions that have come out-

And today, thank you, Degrassi Junior High is a perfect example. There is so much talent out there, but we need to find the tools to enable them to demonstrate and produce and direct at a national level.
When I look at the CBC, the government's lack of vision and commitment has produced a starveback of our national broadcaster. In fact since 1984, this government has been slashing away at the CBC. If government cuts, inflation and increased costs due to the government's GST, and lack of action in providing for ephemeral rights in copyright are all taken into account, the CBC has lost between $240 million and $400 million in only seven years. Last December, because the government throttled the CBC, the corporation was forced to take measures to address the shortfall of $108 million by closing stations in Goose Bay, Matane, Toronto, Comerbrooke, Sydney, Rimouski, Sept-iles, Windsor, Saskatoon and Calgary.

I was in Rimouski when nearly 5,000 people demonstrated against this decision. They were furious. I went to Newfoundland, in Comerbrook, and I had the same experience with hundreds of people who demonstrated their objections to cutbacks that were both inevitable and intolerable. There were petitions, and action was taken by both employees and listeners. However, this government is deaf and dumb. It doesn't understand the issues, it didn't do anything about it. Meanwhile performers were in a bad way. And they still are, with an average salaiy of about $15,000 a year.

So local productions for the most part have stopped. Radio Canada International, Radio-Canada international, has been reduced, as has the parliamentary channel. We pick this up on a temporary basis. We are still talking about privatizing the right of elected members of Parliament to speak to their constituents without worrying about whether the private sectors like how we put it on, the hours we have used, whether we have exempted their time and who shall be seen. It is ridiculous.
June 13, 1991

Supply
As a result of these cuts, 1,100 jobs have been lost, all because the government does not understand why we need a public broadcaster. They do what no one else can do. They bring us the voice of Canada from coast to coast to coast. No private broadcaster can afford to do that. The public broadcaster does it, and does it well. It is important that we keep that link and allow among the exploding spectrum of choices that we have, from America, Europe, Britain, France-all wonderful, and choice should be there-a national voice which sets standards. We cannot afford to continue decimating that service across this land.
Now we have the status of artists legislation, which is welcomed in this House and by the arts community, but I wish it was a little bit more substantive. A lot of it is smoke and mirrors because the concrete ability to realize an improvement in the effective spending power and income of the arts community is not there yet. We have forgotten about income averaging. This arts community knows very well that this year you may be well employed, this month you may have a job but next month you do not. There are good artists and those who are learning to be effective, who are painting and starting to sell. This year they sell well but next year they do not. They have to have income averaging.
This government will not hear of changes within the revenue code or the Revenue Act, which would only be sensible if you addressed the arts community and its particularity.
We did not do anything about bankruptcy protection, which is fundamental. We have done nothing about the public lending rights. We are moving to an open shop from a closed shop and you, Madam Speaker, understand l'Union des artistes et ACTRA who know about ensuring their own artists a job before foreigners come in here. The Americans have moved from an open shop to a closed shop. So thank you very much. There we go, we will not even have access to the American stage, but they can come in here and take jobs from our workers.
With Radio Canada International I guess the best argument is that the Prime Minister's own friend, the Senate chair of the Transportation and Communications Committee, Findlay MacDonald, spoke about it in the media and was quoted widely and wildly. I would read into the record some of what he had to say, but I just want to make a point of bringing to your attention as
well-I have one minute left-that we cannot forget the National Arts Centre and the museums.
We have a War Museum. We sent our troops to war. We have pride in these people who represented us and defended us. We treat them so shabbily with the way we look at our museum, but we put millions and millions and millions into bricks and mortar in Quebec. I do not care if you want to move the War Museum to Quebec, but at least let's have something that will honour our citizens and the work that they have done and the valour that they have displayed, not disgrace them. Do not hide from view the beauty and the wonders of the arts and the artefacts that we have from the efforts that they have put in.
The National Arts Centre is also of great concern. There is a $369,000 deficit and there is no accountability in the system that was set up and complete disregard on the part of that board of trustees and its directors. That is worrisome.
I would love to have read what Findlay MacDonald had to say because I think that it displays the inability of this government to have a cultural vision, to understand the importance of Canada's voice, not only provincially, not only federally, but internationally. That is what we went ahead and cut as well. We cut our own throats. We are perfectly ridiculous in the way we manage our budget and make choices.
It is not to say that I do not understand that we need deficit cutting-yes, we do, and we have to be better managers-yes, we do, but you have an opportunity and you have choices in the course of that opportunity. This government's choices have been disgraceful, particularly in the arts world where the bricks and mortar have to be held together so that this country is a country that can stand tall in the world of nations.
