I welcome the question from my colleague from Fredericton.
As the House draws to a close and we are all getting a little bit overwhelmed with the number of meetings and the hours that we are spending, I appreciate more than ever the kind of work that we have to do, although the public thinks we do not work and I have tried to calculate what our 18 hour days really add up to.
Through the ability to respond to my hon. friend who is now the chairman of this committee, and I wish him well in that task, I would like the public to know that together I think that we can look at the kinds of questions he just asked me.
He made a cute little comment. He said: "You almost sounded like a Conservative", because I talked about fiscal responsibility. I guess, my hon. friend, the difference is that I am definitely not a Conservative, nor am I an NDPer. I am not frozen in either ideology. I chose to be a Liberal because I believe in fiscal responsibility. I believe that one must support the social needs and the social values of this country while balancing them on the scale of justice with respect to economic need.
You need to have that scale go in a fair measure and in a fair balance in the course of a mandate. In the instance of the Conservative government we have had, you have been blessed with seven rich years. If you had been fiscally responsible as a government over those seven rich years, during the coming seven lean years, I hope it will not be that long, we would have had the kind of cushion that would have enabled us to live much more sensibly in the years ahead.
With respect to this scale of justice and where I would have looked to cut or to have been more fiscally responsible, I tried to indicate this morning that I thought the Department of Communications ought to look at how we use our money in the production of film, which would be video, one of the communicating tools that is most effective and has the greatest impact on our society. We know that adults watch about 24 hours a week of television. We know that children spend more time watching television than they spend in school. Therefore, the production and distribution of those communication vehicles, television and videos, are very key. If we look at it and priorize where we are going to put our moneys and use them effectively and not scatter them in a variety of programs and institutions, then I think we could be more effective.
Over all, I would suggest that my choice is no deficit, no cuts and careful scrutiny of where we spend it. The goal is the growth and development of a Canadian cultural industry which will cement this nation through knowledge, understanding of its growth, its beautiful history, its wonderful stars and the role models whom we have in every field of endeavour, just as much as in any other country. Certainly we have just as many super stars as the Americans have except we have not promoted them.
June 13, 1991

I would not cut in actual dollars anywhere. I would refocus my priorities because I think that there is something we cannot afford to do; we cannot afford to cut in our cultural properties and in our cultural agencies. We can afford to cut elsewhere. It is a matter of priority, and that is how I would look at it.
I think I pointed out in terms of the hon. member's third question on federal and provincial that it is absolutely fundamental that we maintain a national presence and national institutions which show and encourage the presence of excellence across this land. This does not remove obligations and rights from provinces and municipalities to foster the kernels of greatness, the folklore and the general culture within their own area of expertise.
I think that where you can run complementary programs such as Quebec does in film development you also see the potential. Money is put in through the potential of capital cost allowances and tax write-offs. They know. If anyone knows, it is Quebecers who know, and I include myself in that Quebecer scene.
We know that it is those instruments of song, dance, film and video that absolutely protect and enable the growth of the culture expressed through those artistic endeavours. They have used fiscal policy to enable the growth and development of those instruments. That is what I would do in terms of federal-provincial relations.
I certainly would not remove the federal presence or the national institutions. I would support a shared jurisdiction along with the private sector.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate today. The motion before the House fails to take into consideration all the positive aspects of our economic and fiscal policies. To start with, I would like to say that it takes a lot of patience and willpower to listen to speeches like the ones we heard from members of the Liberal Party of Canada and from the hon. member from Mount Royal in particular, about the cuts made by our government in areas as important as, among others, equalization payments. This afternoon, I checked with the Department of Finance about transfer payments to the provinces. They are in three parts, and I think there is a lot of confusion amongst Liberal and NDP members. The first part is the Established Program Financing, the second equalization and the third the Canadian Assistance Plan.
I listened to what the hon. member for Mount Royal was saying about equalization. I wish that, in the next few days, she would check the actual figures because, in Quebec in particular, they increased from 3 billion dollars in 1984 to 3.8 billion dollars in 1991-92, and now 4 billion dollars. That means, for Quebec, an increase of 100 per cent , in equalization payments over just eight years.
In politics, it is very hard to avoid being overly partisan and saying just about anything, but I urge the Liberal Party of Canada to analyze the figures concerning transfer payments to the provinces. Since 1984, there has been an increase of up to 6 per cent per year. It is an area where our government has been most generous. I have all the figures here and I might come back to them later on, Madam Speaker. Still, I believe that when you say something in the House, you should have the correct information.
Regarding Quebec in particular, the transfer payments were 8.153 billion dollars in 1984, Madam Speaker, and they will reach close to $11 billion in 1992-93, an increase of almost 35 per cent. I do not see any reduction there, it is a rather substantial increase.
In a speech putting into question the financial management ability of our government, there should not be any question regarding the significance of our economic development program, as outlined in the February 26 budget. The objective of the Budget is crucial: to get Canada out of the present recession and put it back on the road to growth and job creation.
We must emphasize that our government is trying to completely change all the political culture that had been built and nurtured by the former Liberal government. This policy recognizes that the key to economic recovery and durable prosperity during the next few years is the development of a climate which would help bring down inflation and interest rates and keep them down.
All Canadians gave us a clear and strong message during the consultation period that was conducted by the former minister of Finance, and the future will tell how effective his actions and his management are. The clearest message was the need to reduce the interest rates while, of course, taking the free market into account, so that all Canadian businesses could be able to compete internationally.
In order to reach this objective, the plan sets out specific goals whereby inflation would be gradually brought down to 2 per cent by 1995.
Our main actions deal with three particular areas, Madam Speaker. The first one relates to federal spending control. We should emphasize that it is the federal government which, in the last six years, has shown the most restraint in its spending, as opposed to the municipal and provincial governments. Government spending growth has been kept below a 3 per cent. No other government, Madam Speaker, has maintained that rate. This performance has been recognized by all world organizations and by OECD, among others.
There is also the second aspect, the deficit and debt reduction. It takes a lot of gall, Madam Speaker, for a Liberal member to say that the government should have acted more responsibly. They went as far as mentioning the name of Marc Lalonde who pushed the debt from 18 billion dollars to 200 billion dollars and who doubled the deficit in one year, from 14 to 28 billion dollars. They dare to tell us that we have no sense of responsibility! I find it unacceptable for a member to stand up in this House and say such exaggerations and inaccuracies. As to our strategy of drastically cutting the costs of government operations, especially salaries, Madam Speaker, of course, we hear attacks mostly by Liberal and NDP members. It is normal coming from opposition parties because for 20 years, we saw a management philosophy that could be called "put it on my account". We kept spending without ever paying. It is unbelievable! We have even been held responsible for the 1984 deficit of $40 billion, a few minutes ago. And it is when our government came to power that the deficit started to
June 13, 1991

decrease. It went down 25 per cent since we came to power.
It is the reason why, Madam Speaker, our plan for economic recovery and our budget rejected specifically this approach of irresponsably increasing public expenditures and the deficit. Such spending would inevitably bring back higher deficits and a galloping debt that would in turn lead to another period of economic slowdown. The budget rather reaffirms the fact that a better control on public finance is an essential element of the balanced economic framework that we must put in place to insure a permanent recovery and prosperity.
The public will be confident that our progress in reducing inflation and interest rates, and in increasing productivity and personal prosperity, will not be engulfed in the quicksand of deficits ans public debt, with the resulting tax increases necessary to face the situation left behind by irresponsible people.
To develop our plan for economic recovery, we turned to the future, but we also drew lessons from our past economic development. It required a lot of courage, Madam Speaker, to redress the situation left by Marc Lalonde and associates. During nearly 25 years, from 1950 to 1973 inclusively, Canadians saw their national economy and personal prosperity improve considerably. Canada's standard of living nearly doubled within one generation. The growth did not happen by chance, it was not accidental, it resulted from sound economic policies. Inflation rate was then less than 3 per cent, which helped maintain interest rates low. Federal government annual deficits were low or non-existent. I recall that unrestrained and uncontrolled deficits appeared in 1974, particularly under Messrs MacEachen and Marc Lalonde.
As I said, federal govemement annual deficits were low or non-existent. Companies increased their investments considerably. We became more productive and more prosperous, and employment progressed markedly. Unfortunatly, these lessons were forgotten from 1974 to 1984. Governments had let inflation go sky high before trying to control it with restrictive monetary policies. However, those policies were always relaxed before
Supply
prices had really stabilized. So the net effect of each series of policies was to have them firmly ingrained in the public inflationist wishes and bad habits, and the govemement only compounded the problem by spending more than he received in taxes.
The philosophy of the day was to live beyond one's means. That is why, Madam Speaker, it was so difficult for us in 1984 to be a responsible government and to commit ourselves to controlling the deficit. That is why the deficit escalated to 38 billion dollars, almost 40 billion dollars, Madam Speaker, with a budget of about $100 billion or 105 billion dollars while the national debt shot up from 27 billion to over 200 billion dollars. It is no wonder then that economic growth and production went down between 1974 and 1984. Businesses had to fight on two fronts: on the one hand, stronger government interventions, tax collections and the national debt- clearly, the government had no choice-and, on the other, growing competition world-wide. Heaven knows that factor is not decreasing.
The weakening of the Canadian dollar was not sufficient to stop those trends. We are still paying today for that incredible period. If it was not for the service of the debt that we inherited in 1984, Madam Speaker, there would be no deficit and our debt would not have reached the $400 billion mark it will cross this year.
Since 1984, the government has been busy rebuilding the foundations necessary to support a sustainable economic prosperity. Our record shows the very real progress we have achieved. I take this opportunity to mention to you again, Madam Speaker, that international organizations, have acknowledged that Canada has now a policy and a plan for economic recovery which is the envy of many other countries, particularly if we consider the initial situation which we had inherited.
The debt growth has been considerably reduced from a 22 per cent annual rate to about 8 per cent, Madam Speaker. The deficit, though still too high, has been reduced by half in relation to the national revenue. Inflation has been brought down to a level equivalent to about half of the average rate in the 1974-1984 period.

June 13, 1991
Supply
However, to help our country overcome its current problems and achieve a long-lasting prosperity, we must work harder to put our public finance on a sound basis. The economic recovery plan suggests basic and decisive measures to that end-and, Madam Speaker, I am pleased to mention them: the capping of wage increases for members of Parliament and federal civil servants over the next four years; the extension until 1994-1995 of the expenditures control plan established last year with a view to bringing the deficit down to $6 billion from a level of $40 billion it reached when we came into office, Madam Speaker; the adoption of legislative measures setting absolute caps to the federal government programs expenditures over the next five years.
Unbelievably, Madam Speaker, this is the only government in the world to legislate in order to push its economic renewal plan through.
We will use the GST surplus, among other things, to better control the federal debt. That is unprecedented in this country. Under this legislation, GST revenues will be allocated only to reduce the runaway debt, and not for new expenditures as the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party ask us to do repeatedly.
With these measures, Madam Speaker, we will achieve real progress. For 1990-1991 and the next fiscal year, our deficit will stay at $30.5 billion, despite recession-related problems. We could well have had a $35 billion deficit because of this recession, but thanks to the government expenditure control program, the deficit stayed at $30 billion.
Then, in 1992-1993, the deficit should fall considerably and drop to $24 billion, and then fall, three years later in 1995-1996, to its lowest level in 20 years, $6.5 billion. For the first time in 25 years, the federal government will have no new loan to incur at that time.
What we have to deal seriously with is the credibility of our goals for deficit reduction and debt control. From 1985 to 1990, Madam Speaker, our annual projections for the Gross Domestic Product growth, the inflation, the unemployment rate and the interest rate have always been quite accurate, compared to forecasts made by 14 private organizations.
In fact, a recent study published in the Quarterly Economic Review, from the Department of Finance,
shows that over the entire 1985 to 1990 period, our global forecasts have been the most accurate. So, we should really look forward to 1995 with confidence.
At the same time, we consider ourselves realistic when we say that the deficit will drop to $24 billion by 1992-93. It is easy to understand, Madam Speaker. We will no longer have to support the transitional costs for the GST, which will represent a $2 billion savings. Obviously, there will not be another war in the Persian Gulf. The expenditure control plan will help with further savings since we are keeping increases in expenditures by departments to a bare minimum. The increase is not to exceed 3 per cent.
There have been years, particularly under Marc La-londe as Minister of Finance, when expenditures increased at a rate of between 15 and 19 per cent a year. That was quite an achievement. The decrease in interest rates will also reduce debt charges. It has already started to do so. The economic recovery will help reduce unemployment payments and increase government revenues.
In turn, this large reduction of the deficit, combined with the recovery of the national economy, will favour a reduction of the debt in proportion to our economy for the first time since 1974-1975, when the disaster started under the government of Mr. Pierre Elliott Trudeau.
This major reorganization will mean that government revenues, combined with the sustained benefits accruing from lower interest rates and expenditure restraints legislation, will be sufficient to eliminate the need to borrow by 1994-1995, not 2020, Madam Speaker, but 1994-1995. That is in line with the goal set in the 1989 Budget in spite of all the problems encountered since. Because of higher interest rates and the recession, we did not change the date; instead, we took appropriate financial means to put our economy back on track.
I would like to point out, Madam Speaker, that all the salary restrictions we are imposing on parliamentarians as well as on the entire public service tell the Canadian people, both in the private and the public sector, what the markers should be in Canada in terms of salary increases if we are to succeed in bringing down inflation and the interest rates. We simply cannot afford to grant raises that promote inflation.
June 13, 1991

This leads me directly to the other part of our plan for economic recovery. As I said at the beginning of my speech, the result of lower interest rates translates into a reduction in inflation expectations and a change in our habits as a society. It is no wonder that, for the past decade, the countries with the lowest inflation, namely Germany and Japan, have enjoyed the lowest interest rates. The lesson is good and we should persist, Madam Speaker.
Federal expenditure control and salary restrictions are important steps in alleviating inflationary pressures. But the economic recovery plan goes even further. It sets out specific targets to bring inflation down to 2 percent by the end of 1995.
These targets will add a public dimension to reinforce and support our government's financial and monetary policies, Madam Speaker. Setting out clear and realistic targets will encourage Canadians to lower their inflation expectations and help us stabilize prices more quickly and with much less disruption.
We will make it, because these targets reaffirm and make clearer than ever before this government's commitment to price stability. With the full support of government, the Bank of Canada will make sure that these targets are achieved and the copying of expenditure will only reinforce this commitment. These measures will revive the confidence of Canadians and encourage them to change their behaviour, whether we are talking about prices set by companies, long-term contracts, negotiated wage settlements or the inflation risk premium demanded by investors. They will be less demanding when they realize that the value of their income, their investments and their savings will be maintained. That will ease the transition towards lower interest rates and strengthen the competitive position of companies and workers vis-a-vis the international competition that is invading our homes, Madam Speaker.
The economic recovery plan is more than just a commitment to economic progress and sound financial management. It is a concrete and durable strategy aimed at creating confidence in the economy and economic growth, and in the long-term prosperity and security of Canadians, on a sound foundation, a strategy initiated in 1984.
The plan for economic recovery is based on the fundamental realities of today's world. To remain competitive in the global context, countries and companies must put this at the top of their list of priorities in their
Supply
policy planning process. This conviction was the driving force of the agenda for economic renewal we tabled in 1984 and the structural reforms we implemented to get rid of obstacles to industrial efficiency and to stimulate our economy and our ability to compete.
These structural reforms include deregulation in the energy and transportation sectors. All Canadians are aware of the consequences of those measures, Madam Speaker. As for measures to help the unemployed acquire new skills and obtain the training they need to find jobs and keep them in a rapidly evolving global economy, we have changed the old Liberal approach that allowed people to work a few weeks and then live off the government for the rest of the year. That is not what Canadians want. That is why we put the emphasis on training.
We have invested several billion dollars in training, because people change jobs more frequently than they used to, an average of every five years, so we had to make funding available to retrain Canadian workers, and we did that, Madam Speaker.
I would have liked to expand on certain statements made by the Liberals this afternoon about the financial situation of this country, which is steadily improving. The deficit was about $40 billion when we came to power, and a few years from now, it is expected to be about $25 billion. I would have liked to talk about transfers to the provinces, which have increased steadily since 1984. There is a lot of rhetoric about this particular issue, but I can say that in Quebec transfers have increased 35 per cent since 1984, and I am very proud of that.

Madam Speaker, my colleague mentioned the national deficit, indicating that it was high when the Liberals were in power.

But that it not what a sensitive government, a people-oriented government truly concerned with the social welfare, the well-being of the population, would do.

June 13, 1991

As one of my colleagues pointed out, we should not have to sell the furniture in order to pay the rent. But that is precisely what has been going on since 1984. Just think of the cuts in health care and education, of the expenditure freeze imposed upon these two areas over the next five years. That is incredible, at a time when we should be investing even more in these areas.

speechtext:

Funding for specific programs has been frozen, Mr. Speaker, espe-
June 13, 1991

daily in my region, but with the co-operation of the Government of Quebec we are able to deliver the goods.
Mr. Speaker, I would have liked to continue in this vein, but we will have a chance to get back to this.

I would like to comment and ask a question about the Liberals who were talking about the financial situation. He said that this innovative measure to encourage private research would cost the government about $100 million a year. It ended up costing $200 million! They passed the $100 million mark on the very first day. It was a mad rush, because this turned out to be a stupendous tax loophole. Companies, big brokerage firms and big law firms went on a roll, at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer. They made millions risk free, even before the actual scientific research started, and then there were the others, the people who committed fraud.
Mr. Speaker, an item in L'Actualite said it was the robbery of the century, perpetrated by the Liberal government. In fact, Conservative minister Michael Wilson had to put on the brakes in a hurry. It was his first official act, but it was already too late. In nine months the bill went up to nearly $3 billion, one-tenth of the national deficit. This is enough to build 50 hospitals in Canada.
My question is this: Could the hon. member for Chicoutimi tell us this evening whether this disastrous Liberal program, implemented in 1983-84, contributed to the federal deficit?

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are
here tonight to talk about the government's estimates. Having listened to my colleague across the way on the debt, I am still waiting-and have been since February- for the bill that would ensure that all those extra GST revenues would go to pay off the debt. That is what I call irresponsibility on the part of the government. It is allowing those funds to go into general revenues instead of paying off the debt. We will get the bill in September and let's see if it is retroactive to January.
This government does not know what responsibility is all about. We have had to listen to aspersions on the civil service, we have the GST against the people's will. This government does not know what responsibility is, either to the civil service or to the Canadian people.
I want to talk about two areas of irresponsibility here tonight, relating to defence and to the fisheries in an area that should not have the problems that this government has created.
We know that this government is supposedly doing a review of our defence policy, the second in four years. It cannot even plan long term. It is doing the review to determine what the goals should be for our defence policy and how the department spends its almost $12.6 billion budget in the 1991-92 Estimates that we have before us.
We have heard all sorts of rumours in the media and leaks from the Department of National Defence as to what this review will mean. It might mean base relocations, it might mean base closures, it might mean withdrawing from NATO, it might mean anything. However, it is all speculation. This government loves to play with people's speculation.
However, the government has not involved the Canadian people in deciding what the role of the Department of National Defence should be. We do not know whether it is a cost-effective review. We do not know if it is just a trial balloon to see how the Canadian people will react.

June 13, 1991
Supply
Canadians want a review, they want to know how this government plans to spend the almost $12.6 billion budget. They want to know where our defence policy is going to be in the next 20 years and what purpose Canadians think the military should serve for Canada. In other words, they want a review process that is going to be open, fair and responsible.
To date they have not seen this. They want to see that they are getting the best bang for their dollars, and to date they have not seen that.
In the United States, where a similar process appears to be going on, the elected people are going to the people to see what the effects are and what the defence policies should be. Not here in Canada. We do it by speculation in the press.
There are a number of areas where money could be saved or reallocated without cutting our militaiy muscle. Indeed, I think we could save enough to reverse the trend and actually start building up our military again.
Let us look at these figures. A March 1988 survey in Armed Forces International ranked Canada highest among all western nations with a ratio of 16.2 generals for every
10.000	active duty personnel. At that time, I think the active duty personnel in Canada was roughly about
80.000	to 85,000 people.
That ratio of 16.2 generals for every 10,000 active personnel is higher than the United States. It is higher than the United Kingdom and it is even higher than the Philippines. Donald Grant, in The Globe and Mail on May 27, had an excellent review of this point. He said: "In 1990-91 we had 122 people with a rank"-in Canada, not somewhere else-"of Brigadier General or higher. They had average salaries ranging from $94,000 to $131,000 per year".
He said that we have more generals than we have tanks, 122 generals to 113 tanks. That is okay, it is important to have a back-up general in case one of the tanks breaks down.
We have more officers than we have privates, 16,096 privates to 18,861 officers. To top it off, Donald Grant- and I thank him for his analysis because he writes on
military affairs and he is in The Globe and Mail and if he is in The Globe and Mail it has to be real-writes that the almost $12.6 billion budget for defence supports only
10,000	service people who are combat ready or who support combat ready troops.
Mr. Grant has described our Armed Forces system as a triumph of bureaucracy over common sense. I agree that this government is allowing this to continue. As long as we do not have a public and fair debate across Canada on what our military should be we will continue to have a top heavy military, a top heaviness that is unmatched anywhere in the world.
I ask the minister of defence whether he is looking into this factor. Will he give us a cost effective military that is oriented toward active duty soldiers and training. Let us look at the figures in the estimates again to see where else we can find questionable spending.
In the 1990-91 estimates we find that $90.4 million was spent on other professional and special services. This is a military that is top heavy with generals already. There is no specific accounting for these services, just a figure in the column.
We also find that $21.8 million was spent on consulting services, whatever that means. It should have been defined.
Another $30.4 million was spent on contract administration. These figures alone total $182 million and none of it goes directly to putting sailors on boats, soldiers in the field or pilots in planes. In short, none of it goes to defending our country.
The Department of National Defence does not need to spend millions on consulting. Just go and ask the Canadian public what its priorities should be. Ask the generals to go to the public with their defence policy to determine whether it matches what Canadians want.
I could bring a panel of housewives from South West Nova who know how to spend their budgets better than the Department of National Defence does. I guess the minister does not see the relevance of a real public debate on national defence. I do not claim to have all the answers but I think I know what some of the right questions about our defence policy should be.
June 13, 1991

I hope the minister will look first at improving efficiencies within the existing budget before he cuts further into our military muscle.
I hope he will also look at the purposes of our national defence policy.
Canada is the second largest country in the world by land mass. We have a huge coastline which needs defending against commercial and military threats, to defend our jurisdiction within the 200-mile limit. We have a claim to Arctic sovereignty which is not accepted by our closest and strongest neighbour and yet we cannot control it. We did away with the Polar-8.
We have an enormous air space. We have national emergencies in which the military is needed to give a hand. We have an expertise in international peacekeeping which could soon be in great demand given the end of the cold war. However, when it came time to sending combat troops over to the Middle East we did not have enough.
These are the proper ends of a Canadian defence policy. These are the proper ends which I think all Canadians want to have a public and open discussion about.
How to put a priority on these things is what we should be debating here publicly and across Canada, but if we are to meet these needs we will have to increase what we spend directly on recruiting and training service personnel, not decrease. We will have to greatly increase the size of our active duty service component.
The 1989 figures show that Canada ranked second to last among NATO countries, with 1 per cent of the labour force being defence personnel. This puts us behind Greece, Belgium, Ibrkey and even Portugal.
Looking at NATO, Greece's defence personnel as a percentage of its labour force is 5.6 per cent. Canada's is 1 per cent. It is at the bottom, except for Luxemburg which is pretty close to Canada with 0.9 per cent. We have the biggest country in that group of NATO countries and we cannot come up: Greece, Turkey, Belgium, France, the United States, Portugal, The Netherlands, Italy, Norway, Germany, Spain, the United Kingdom, Denmark and then Canada and Luxemburg. The average for those NATO countries is 2.5 per cent.
Supply
It means that we need to have more people in our Armed Forces, not cut back as seems to be the remedy of the top-heavy generals as they are looking at it, rather than looking at a realistic approach of a $12.6 billion budget.
We have to protect our sovereignty. We do not need to disgrace the role of our trained seamen and our other forces with not having the ability to have backup. When it came to sending the three ships over to the Middle East, they had to be trained on the way over. Fortunately, the equipment had been sitting around waiting for a contract, which is still not complete, to put that equipment on and they had to be trained on the way over. That does not seem to be very logical training.
Before I move to fisheries, I just want to say on that subject that I think it is most unfair of this government to allow speculation to be part of its review process in the department of defence polity'. It is unfair to Canadians who want a full and public debate about the objectives of our defence policy. It is unfair to the military personnel who have served Canada so well and it is unfair to the many Canadians who directly and indirectly depend on the military.
I think Canada wants a military it can be proud of, one which can answer the needs as I have already said.
Now I want to move to another area, the fisheries. I want to talk about it because the question the fishing industry is asking is: what is the fairness of asking an industry which is only getting by to pay for a monitoring system of which it is not able to offset the cost? The market will not return the cost that it has to pay per pound for the monitoring system.
The boat quotas are one third of what it caught in the past. The one or two cents a pound it has to pay for the monitoring in the future are the profits it would have made.
I would hope that this minister of fisheries will last longer than his two predecessors. In two and half years we have had three ministers of fisheries. It shows how bad the fisheries policy is. I would hope that this minister, who has been asked to meet with all parties involved in the industry, big and small, large companies, small companies, big fishermen, small fishermen, inshore and offshore, will discuss the stupidity of this policy. He has not met yet. It is a most important issue. We saw what happened in Newfoundland.

June 13, 1991
Supply
Right now, in the Scotia Fundy, he has not even appointed someone in his office to whom they can talk. He has no assistant responsible for the Scotia Fundy. How is he going to deal with a problem when there is not even somebody within his office for the people to talk to, to ask him to come and deal with it, let alone for me, as a member of Parliament, who asked him since the beginning if we could have a meeting? I have given up asking for that meeting.
I want to explain the system of dockside monitoring which I have been talking about. This system is being implemented in Scotia Fundy by an employment program from manpower. It is now training 133 new people, but not for the Department of Fisheries. These fishermen and these companies will have to pay in the future to have somebody come down and monitor and weigh their catches.
I will get to where it is coming from. The industry did not ask for this. I want to explain what happened just this Sunday in one small harbour. A boat was coming from George's Bank. Think of a 65-foot dragger coming from George's Bank with only the 30,000 pounds of ground-fish it could have because of regulations. It had probably travelled 12 hours to get there and it phones in. This is what the dockside monitoring does. You have to hail. Hail is picking up a phone which some of the small boats never had to have before. They need to have a phone system so they can phone onshore. It has to be six hours before you can land your fish. Six hours before, regardless of a storm or whatever, and you have to wait outside that dock for three hours after you get there if it is not within the full six hours.
This boat was on time. It had said it would be there at 8.30 in the morning to be weighed. Now, this is Sunday. The boats cannot tell when they are going to go fishing. The weather has a lot to do with whether they can go fishing in the course of a week. It had gone. It was quite warm in Nova Scotia last week. Most people would say it was one of those beautiful times when you would not want to have fish waiting in any hold because of the heat. It would start hurting the price of the fish on the market.
That does not matter to the Department of Fisheries. That is inconsequential. The boat came in with 30,000 pounds, arrived, as it had hailed and told it would be, at
8.30. Nobody was there except the company, the loaders and the unloaders for the company who were getting paid double time because it was Sunday. No one came. Finally, the owner had to get in his truck and go down the road quite a distance to get a fishery officer to come back and make sure he had the same amount in his log that he hailed six hours before. There was nobody there to check it.
I know you are giving me a signal, Mr. Speaker, but this is quite important. I want you to get the right picture. It is that additional insult to people that this minister has got to come down and take a look at.
There are two things that have to be remembered. This is a program imposed by the department to help it monitor the fish.
It is a program that no one goes out to fish. It does not look at it that no one would go out to fish unless there were fish to catch. I do not know any fisherman who would go out to fish if there were not fish to catch.
I do not know any fisherman who would not have abided hailing his load in, by a log book and a random inspection of his load. That department does not look at that. It has to have people go down there, look at it and weigh it.
I have one more minute, but I hope somebody in here will ask me a question on this because I could go on for quite a time on this.
On top of all that the minister has got to come down. He has got to walk around these streets. He has got to go into the restaurants and see the insult to the communities.
One of the municipalities wrote to the minister a while back:
The Municipal Council for the District of Digby wish to object to
the Fishery officers wearing sidearms, especially in public places
such as banks, post offices, stores-
This minister of fisheries has a lot to learn and a short time to learn it in. The first thing he could do is start consulting with the people who want to consult with him, the people in the industry, and he is not going down there, to talk about this dockside monitoring and the threat of somebody with a gun to an innocent fisherman.
June 13, 1991

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. member a question.
I would like to first point out to her that I received today a copy of the number of licences issued in 1990 by the Scotia Fundy Region for foreign vessels associated with the fishery in Nova Scotia. There were 80 factory freezer trawlers from foreign nations fishing national allocations. There were 36 large vessel licences for what it calls supporting fishing fleets. There were 18 foreign vessels fishing and doing research work with no observers aboard. There were 48 special fishing factory freezer trawler licences to foreign vessels, a total of 249.
I also received, and the hon. member would be interested, what they call a herring by-catch licence amendment which says: "While conducting the silver hake mackerel fishery, the vessel", in this case foreign vessel, "is permitted to take an incidental catch of herring that may not exceed 30 per cent of the total weight of mackerel".
It appears to me, and the hon. member can correct me if I am wrong, that shows an incredible favouritism toward these large foreign vessels which have Canadian licences fishing on the hon. member's coast in Nova Scotia.
I wonder if she could comment on the favouritism shown to the foreigners and the discrimination against Canadian fishermen.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I appreciate my colleague's question. I know that I share his concern as to the numbers. Just looking at that, once it got beyond 106 to the foreigners, I thought of the letter which came in today from one of my constituents. I will get back to the mackerel. In other words, they could catch all the mackerel and still catch 30 per cent more herring. I would think that every person in my riding who relies on the herring industry should be very upset and, as the hon. member knows, we have quite a good herring fishery.
I want to just say something about those. After I did 80 factory fishery ships and 36 large vessels, I gave up counting because in this letter I received dated June 10, it talked about boat quotas. In 1990, the same year the hon. member is talking about for all these foreign ships, of the 105 C-l specialists, and I am sure that my colleagues know what a C-l specialist is, it is a 45 foot boat, around 50 per cent of the 105 were independent.
Supply
Now six months into boat quotas for 1991, there is only 10 per cent left.
You tell me how you can explain to somebody that you can have only 10 per cent of C-l specialists left when there used to be 105. You are telling me that there are about 165 foreign licences fishing where these boats used to fish. What is the sense of the policy?
I do not want to go into that. The reason for this is that these licence holders received very low boat quotas. The quota was less than 150,000 pounds per licence. It is sad to think that we have come to this point, that we give to foreigners and do not allow the people in our area to fish within our own waters. It is sad to think that we cannot have a policy from the Minister of Fisheries that would answer the people, and a minister who would look at the policy and say: "This is crazy."
I am hoping that the Minister of Fisheries, who comes from Newfoundland, is going to be able to say it. Certainly, the other two could not, and they got kicked out of that position.
When you have a policy that gives more off-shore quota in a by-catch-we do not have a marketing policy to market the fish-to those foreigners who come over here, there is something wrong with Canada.
It goes back to the responsibleness of this government, a government that will not listen to our own Canadians. It will listen to the Americans.
I kind of laughed this afternoon when the Minister Responsible for Constitutional Affairs quoted an American in answer to my leader. The Americans are the only people this government listens to. Maybe he would listen to an American in the quote. The government does not want to listen to Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for South West Nova on such a fine presentation.
I would like to take note of the comments that she made at the beginning of her speech with respect to the defence policy, the military budget and the importance of the Canadian Forces Base Cornwallis which happens to be in her riding.

June 13, 1991
Supply
Mr. Speaker, if you will give me a couple of minutes, I will use that base and relate it to defence policy in such a manner as to let you and the House know why we do have concerns about the policies and where they are going.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to speak in today's debate.
The motion before us offers the opportunity to review the trust of the economic policies followed by our government over a number of years and extended in the budget measures of February 1991.
It is important in approaching this debate to be very clear as to just what the subject is. It is certainly not the details of the program spending of certain departments and in the case of Motion No. 2, specifically, the program spending of the Department of Finance.
The items in the estimates to which objection has been taken are those which concern primarily the development of economic policy, not specific areas such as taxation or federal-provincial transfers, but economic policy generally and as a whole.
It is therefore a real pleasure to participate in the debate because I can take some time to reflect on our government's approach to the economy in the broadest sense possible. To do this I want to start at the beginning. For the government, that was the state of the economy
June 13, 1991

Supply
and the government's finances when we took office in late 1984.
We all remember the recession of the early 1980s with the extremely high interest rates and inflation, the loss of jobs, and the unwillingness or the inability of the government of the day to take effective action to deal with the underlying problems of the economy.
The government came to office determined to deal with those problems, to make our business more competitive and our economy more efficient. I remember well the extremely difficult state of the government's own finances. Program spending by the government had risen to 19.6 per cent of the GDP in 1984-85, compared with an average of 17.7 per cent in the 1970s. Of course that does not take into account the money which had to be spent on servicing the growing public debt.
Our revenues and expenditures were so out of balance that the revenues did not even pay for the program spending, much less meet the requirement to pay interest on the public debt.
The deficit for the 1984-85 fiscal year turned out to be $38.5 billion or 8.7 per cent of the GDP. This was an enormous amount of money and evidence of a profound malaise in the nation's finances.
In 1984 the debt was growing at an annual rate of about 25 per cent. In approaching the situation the government did not allow itself to be panicked into hasty, piecemeal action. We did not start throwing money at every problem, hoping that somehow it would go away. We recognized that there had to be order and clear guidelines.
Having taken the necessary time, the then Minister of Finance came to this House and the people of Canada with an agenda for economic renewal. This was in November 1984. In it he set out the principles which underline the actions taken ever since that time and which still form the basis of our policies today.
That agenda clearly pointed to the need to restore competitiveness in our economy and order to the government's finances. In formulating policy and developing measures, those two imperatives have been constantly in the government's mind. They have shaped the way we have approached problems and have enabled us to make difficult and unpopular decisions, knowing at all times that they were part of an over-all plan to do what had to be done for Canada.
Now I want to go over, very briefly, the key measures and the policy which have marked the years since 1984,
years in which there has been great economic progress made by individuals, the government and the country as a whole.
Our policies have dramatically expanded the economy's potential to grow and create wealth. This is the result of consistent, comprehensive action by this government to bring our national deficit under control and to free the private sector from structural barriers and burdens that impeded its efficiency and its ability to compete.
One important goal is to preserve and create jobs. To do this we must be competitive. One of the prerequisites to ensuring our competitiveness is a stable and healthy economic environment that encourages productive business investment. That is why the overriding agenda of this government since 1984 has been to create a more favourable economic environment for business by taking action in the two areas where we have a direct impact on the economy and where we can achieve the greatest long-term benefit.
The first of these areas has been to take action to reduce the deficit. Fiscal soundness is a key to our competitiveness because it will free up domestic savings needed to finance the deficit. These savings can then be channelled into more productive investments creating a more efficient and more vibrant economy.
We have made significant progress in this regard. We have cut waste and inefficiency in the operations of government. We have been successful in forcing the federal government to live within its means, especially on the operating side. A full 70 per cent of this progress results from expenditure restraint and not from revenue increases.
Success in restraining spending will help to make the economy more competitive and create a climate appropriate to economic growth. It will provide more savings for productive investment and create wealth and jobs for Canadians. It will, in short, make the economy more competitive.
Along with our work to control government spending we have also moved to strengthen the ability of the private sector to compete and create a bigger economic pie for all Canadians. We began by transforming a chilly investment barrier into a positive screening and review mechanism, Investment Canada. Investment Canada is now fostering a friendly, receptive and helpful investment climate.

June 13, 1991
Supply
We have also moved to strengthen and improve the climate for free enterprise through new business framework legislation that safeguards fair competition. The new Competition Act is providing long overdue stability to the competitive environment. Similarly, amendments to the Patent Act strengthen intellectual property rights, which for a long time had been asked for.
To encourage a more dynamic and active private sector, we have been overhauling and reforming much of Canada's regulatory framework. Wherever possible we are eliminating unnecessary restrictions and discouraging new regulations that are not necessary.
Perhaps most dramatic has been our deregulation of the energy and the transportation sectors which permitted a more market-oriented and market-driven approach.
Measures of reform of the financial sector have also been presented to this House. Our policies to reform this sector will ensure that it remains healthy and competitive. In doing so we are building on one of the most sound and reliable financial systems in the world.
We have a strong deposit-taking system, we have a strong capital market, we have world-scale life insurance companies. We possess the ability to finance our capital requirements in a very effective and efficient way.
Another important way in which we are reducing the government's role in the economy is by selling government-owned corporations to private interests.
Since 1984 we have privatized more than 20 Crown corporations. We will continue to privatize Crown corporations and we will sell investments where government ownership is no longer needed to meet the public policy objectives.
At the same time, we have promoted economic growth through a variety of means to encourage business. We have also taken steps to stimulate greater private sector research and development. Next to Australia, Canada provides for the most favourable tax treatment for research and development expenditures in the industrialized world.
To be competitive in today's information intensive economy requires a skilled and a flexible workforce. That is why we have put forward a proposed labour force development strategy. This strategy, which has been
before the Senate for almost a year, places a strong new emphasis on worker retraining and upgrading of skills. The strategy provides for increased federal funding for labour force upgrading and seeks ways to encourage the private sector to double its training effort.
Central to our government's efforts to build a stronger more competitive economy, with greater potential for economic growth, is the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. As Canada depends on trade for 30 per cent of our Gross Domestic Product it is vital that we secure access to our largest and most important trading partner. Gaining broad secure access to a large American market means additional sales and more jobs.
It means greater productivity. It encourages investment in world-scale plants and state of the art technology to meet the international competitive challenge. It allows greater economies of scale and specialization. That means increased economic growth.
Together with the U.S. and Mexico we are now looking forward to a North American free trade agreement. A trilateral accord would transform a free trade area of nearly 275 million people into one of almost 360 million, larger than the 12 countries of the European Community-
Trade liberalization has been a key element of our economic success. That is why we will continue to take an aggressive approach in pursuing opportunities to secure and expand access to our most important markets.
If we are to have a healthy growing economy, we cannot have a tax system that distorts economic decisions and penalizes economic initiatives. Again, this is why we are committed to continuing the process of tax reform. Under our corporate and personal income tax reforms implemented in 1987 we created a tax system that is fairer, simpler and more effective. It is a system that has helped strengthen the economy and improve the quality of Canadian society. A system that is internationally competitive.
We have also moved forward on the major challenge of sales tax reform when we implemented the goods and services tax. In today's fiercely competitive global environment the GST is a vital tool for economic advance. Fifty years of studies and reports called for an end to the existing federal sales tax.
June 13, 1991

The former federal sales tax was antiquated and unfair, nothing less than a job killer and a growth destroyer. There is not a single industrialized country in the world today that still maintains a tax like ours at the manufacturing level.
In its place we have developed the GST, a modern efficient tax of a kind that has been adopted by 48 other countries. It eliminates completely the hidden burden of tax that previously applied to so many goods and service businesses. It ensures that imported goods no longer receive an unfair advantage over those we produce at home. It will strengthen the ability of our exporters to profitably pursue international markets. At the same time, because of the refundable GST credit, it will also be a fairer tax for lower and modest income Canadians. In fact, three-quarters of families headed by seniors or single parents will have more after-tax income under the GST than under the old system.
The February budget marked a further stage in the development of economic policy. In his budget speech, the Minister of Finance produced evidence that, despite a recession-and we must always remember that we are in a partial recession at this time-the policies of the government have indeed been working. He has also presented measures to strengthen and expand the effectiveness of that policy.
The plan for economic recovery has three main elements: one, clear, achievable inflation targets; two, putting the government finances firmly on a course to a balanced budget; and three, severely restraining the operations of government.

I would like to try to frame my comments about the government spending priorities, which of course is the issue that we are discussing. I would like to try to frame those comments in the concept of community values.
I hope to be able to demonstrate that when you look at the spending priorities as determined by the estimates of this government, you can demonstrate that this government really does not understand nor does it really care about community and about community values.
What does it mean, first of all, to care about community? What does community really mean? First of all, it means supporting the comer store in your neighbourhood where your children might go in the morning in the summer to buy a popsicle. It means hoping to make the kinds of policies and programs at the federal level that will ensure that that comer store can remain viable. That it does not go out of business because you are choking it with red tape and extra taxes and taking any of the ability away from that individual entrepreneur to make a living in that community.
What does community mean? It means supporting your local RCMP services. It means ensuring that the funding for adequate policing is there in all our communities so that the officers have the budget and the manpower or the person power, if you like, the staffing, to ensure that they can get out into the community. That they have enough officers available to respond to the emergency needs that arise, but also to be out in the community, walking the streets, talking to the people, to have a demonstrated presence, a physical presence of local policing services. I will get back to the RCMP a little bit later. They are a very visible aspect of our Canadian identity, right there at the local community level, whether you are talking about a small community in the Maritimes or a small community in my riding of Okanagan-Shuswap. The presence of the RCMP is a visible aspect of our sense of Canadianism.
Community means supporting our local community newspapers, through the provision of the kinds of subsidy programs that have been made available to them so that they can ensure the mailing costs are not so staggeringly high that it puts them out of business. Until recently we had a reasonable program, I think, of helping those community newspapers, and the government is wont to eliminate those subsidies. Thankfully it has now backed off on that for the next little while, so that many of the

newspapers that were looking at a very, very bleak future indeed, have at least got some breathing space. Community values also means supporting your rural post offices, making sure that they remain a part of the community. In many small areas throughout British Columbia, and I am sure many other provinces, people in the small rural communities meet on a regular basis at the local post office. That is almost the hub, the social centre if you like, of the day-to-day business of the community. People meet there, pick up their mail, pick up their parcels, they chat about what the weather is today, they might talk about what is happening around them. It is a social centre for the community. And that centre, the heartbeat of the community, will be taken away from those people, and the service will be contracted out to various retail operations.
That demonstrates to me, and it certainly demonstrates to my friends and colleagues in Enderby and Sicamous and Salmon Arm and up in Celista in the north Shuswap, and Sorrento, in areas like Lumby, like Falkland, those small communities, that this government simply doesn't understand the sense of community.
Supporting community and community values also means programs for regional job creation, retraining of people who have been put out of work by the fiscal and monetary mistakes that this government has made over the past years. It means getting those people back into the workforce, back into the employment stream, to give them a sense of pride and meaning. That is what community is-regional job creation programs for the forestry workers and the mill workers who have been put out of work in my community, up in the area of Canoe and Sicamous and Salmon Arm. Unemployment levels in some of those small communities unbelievably reach upward to 40 per cent. I am speaking in particular of the community of Sicamous and Malakwa. Those people have been out of work since before Christmas.

Why? Well, it is because of some of the fiscal priorities that this government has set. I will talk about those in a little while and get back to them.
But supporting community and community values means finding a way of getting those people back to work, and it is something that this government, for whatever reason, simply does not understand. Community means making sure that our young people in the interior of British Columbia do not have to leave the towns in which they grew up in order to find a job. It means they can obtain the training in job training programs and post-secondary education programs that should be available to them so they do not have to leave and go to the larger urban centres such as Vancouver or Edmonton, or wherever, so there is not this migration of young talent out of our rural communities into our urban centres.
That is what supporting community means, allowing our young people to stay in the communities that they grew up in so they can take pride in that community, feel a part of that community, and work for their own future within that community.
A Mulroney vision, this government's vision, is not one which reflects community values. It is not one which, I might hasten to say, Canadians share. This government's vision of Canada and the future of this country enshrines what you could only describe as being the corporate agenda where success is measured in monetary terms rather than in social and socio-economic terms.
Canada is much more than the bottom line on a corporate balance sheet and what is good for Bay Street and what is good for the fat cats here in Ottawa is not necessarily what is good for the rest of Canada and the people out there in the regions of Canada understand when I speak those words because they know it right in their guts that the people, the system, here in Ottawa does not reflect their aspirations. It does not reflect their priorities. It does not reflect their sense of community and what this country means to them. That is why this government is headed hell-bent to defeat in the next election.
The policies dreamed up by this administration in the smoky back rooms of the Langevin Block across the
street, the policies dreamed up by the backroom boys of this government do not reflect the goals, they do not reflect the aspirations, they do not reflect the concerns of average Canadian people, whether you are talking about a small community in British Columbia or a small community in Labrador.
It has been more than 50 years, almost 60 years now, since the social democratic movement in Canada was bom. It was bom out of the politics of that kind of alienation. There was a fundamental dislike and distrust back then in the early 1930s of the elitist powers of Ottawa and the Bay Street fat cats. That movement way back in the 1930s formed in the tough times of the 1930s by a coalition of western farmers, western workers, Canadians from virtually all walks of life because they cared about their community, the future of their community, the future of their province, the future of the regions. They recognized that this country was being ran by an elitist group for its own self-aggrandizement. They said back then that it had to stop.
Fifty years later we are still fighting that battle. We are still fighting the tendency toward a central Canada fixation where the people who are making the decisions in this country do so on the basis of what is best for central Canada rather than what is best for Canada as a whole.
The social democratic movement way back then had a simple principle upon which it was established. That principle was that this country should be ran for the benefit of everyone, not just the benefit of an elite few.
The social democratic movement, under the old CCF, now under the New Democratic Party, never had the opportunity to form a national government in Canada but I want to say also that throughout the years, this traditional reform movement, if you want to put it that way, has played a pivotal and crucial role in enhancing community values. I want to say that the New Democratic movement, the old CCF and now the New Democratic movement in Canada has been the real movement of social reform in Canada. We have been the pioneers in advocating progressive programs like public health care-
