subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with pleasure today to participate in this particular debate on the spending estimates. It was just some months ago that I had another opportunity to rise on this debate and at that point I was fortunately able to save the taxpayers a couple of million dollars.
I do not have any immediate suggestions which will do that at this particular point in the debate, but I do want to start off with a couple of very direct comments which I think are very relevant to the debate we are facing today.
Recently, Mr. McKenna, the premier of the province of New Brunswick, made some very appropriate comments which were quoted in The Globe and Mail on February 28, which was about the time that the budget discussions were going on. He said: "Governments must conduct themselves like private citizens: borrow if necessary for capital assets such as a new home, but pay as you go for current expenditures like the groceries".
I thought that was a really appropriate statement by Mr. McKenna and I thought I would follow that along just to see what happened in the spending estimates which we are dealing with today and the spending estimates which we have had in the past. It is coincidental that today in The Ottawa Citizen there was another article which I would also like to quote. It also has very direct relevance to the debate we are involved in right now. It is an article written by Marjorie Nichols, a staff reporter for The Ottawa Citizen and I would like to quote from it very briefly. In the article she said: "The budgetary deficit numbers actually distort the fiscal truth. In fiscal year 1984-85, the Liberal budget deficit was $38.3 billion of which $16 billion went to pay for groceries, federal programs and salaries. In fiscal year 1991-92, by contrast, the Conservative deficit will be $30.5 billion, all of which is interest charges on the national debt."
I find it interesting that Mr. McKenna said that governments should not borrow to buy groceries-which is obviously what previous governments had been doing-and now Marjorie Nichols in response says "Isn't it great, the government isn't borrowing money to buy groceries, it is borrowing simply to pay the interest on debt"; debt going back to the early seventies and going on from there.
I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this debate, and I guess there is another series of reasons. First I want to thank the hon. parliamentary secretary for inviting me to participate in this debate with such extensive notice. It certainly gives me an opportunity to pass my notes on to you.
But what we are dealing with is, in fact, estimates that deal with about $158 billion in spending. As is typical across the way, there has just been a family squabble between the two parties and now another of the family says "peanuts" to $158 billion. Well, that is what they thought when they were spending $100 billion and now they think it is $158 billion and it is still peanuts.
Within that there are two aspects, and $111 billion of that money is in fact money that is very directly targeted for items that have been approved in previous budgets, and are ongoing expenditures year after year; the other $47 billion is in other spending programs.
June 13, 1991

Really it is these spending programs and controls that bring government expenditures totally in line. One of the things I find interesting is that last year the government tabled a document called Where Your Tax Dollars Go in conjunction with the budget. There is an interesting chart in this that I am sure you have had an opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to peruse. It shows the various program areas of government spending and how the government has, in fact, spent the money.
The interesting part of the chart is that section dealing with the cost of operation of government. It deals with the cost of the civil service, government travel, government advertising, the office buildings, the telephones, the paper and the cost of the operation of this place.
It shows that the government is in fact spending less in 1990-91 than it did in 1984, and that is after absorbing some 35 per cent inflationary increases. So, when you talk about spending controls of those very things that Canadians expect us to control, those things dealing with simple operation of government, I think we have done a remarkable job. I am talking about 1990-91 in this particular book, but what is more interesting is that dealing in the 1991-92 estimates we basically have frozen that cost of government. Here after six years we haven't increased the cost and in the seventh year we are not going to allow it to increase any further.
That is unfortunate in one sense, because I do have some very direct concern and sympathy for many civil servants who are affected by that particular freeze. It is unfortunate that we have to say to the employees of the Canadian government that we are sorry but we don't have 3 per cent, 6 per cent or 9 per cent salary increases to give you. This year we have no more money available than last year. That is not an easy thing to say to them. But we have to restrain expenditures and so we are doing that. Yes, it is unfortunate that they are affected, but I guess you would agree, Mr. Speaker, they are affected and we here in this House will be affected in exactly the same way. So what we are asking our employees to do, we the management-if you want to call us that-are also doing.
So I think the restraint that we are preaching is, in fact, the restraint that we can be very proud of because we are doing it right here in our own operations.
Supply
But it goes further than that. When we talk about spending estimates, we have to talk about a whole series of other things. I find it interesting having just listened to my colleagues opposite. They are talking about how we, the terrible Tories are doing terrible things to all of these social programs in Canada.
Of course, our contribution to many of the social programs is through transfers to provinces. I would like to talk particularly about one province, and it happens to be the province that I live in. I would like to relate it to my riding, and to the Treasurer of the province of Ontario who, of course, is a member for another riding in Ontario.
In their budget presentation, a great portion of it was a huge deficit. That deficit, I can tell you, is unacceptable to the constituents of Ontario riding as I am sure it is unacceptable to the constituents of all of the province of Ontario. What did they say in their budget presentation? They said that the Government of Canada was reducing its transfers to the province of Ontario and it was because of those reductions, to the tune of $3.4 billion, that they had a deficit as large as it was. Now, that is what they said.
I happened to have an opportunity to check this out. I noticed that in 1984-85 when we were first elected and 1990-91, the Government of Canada increased its transfers to the province of Ontario by $3.2 billion which, at an average rate, was 7.3 per cent a year. Imagine that in an inflationary time of 4 per cent to 5 per cent, the Government of Canada was increasing its transfers to the province of Ontario by 7.3 per cent. I would be hard pressed to say that the Government of Canada was dishonest or unfair to the province of Ontario by transferring it that much money.
The leader of the NDP in this House said: If we were the Government of Canada, we would spend the money just like they are doing in Ontario. That means that she would give them that $3.4 billion. I guess they feel they are short. What does that mean? It means that this year, in this year's budget, the Government of Canada would have had to increase its transfers to the province of Ontario by 42 per cent. Can you imagine that, 42 per cent. And they have the gall over there to say that is the kind of increases we should have. Yes, 42 per cent in a 5 per cent inflationary environment.

June 13, 1991
Supply
Maybe that is not what they mean. Maybe what they mean is if the government had not cut back a little bit every year for the last seven years, we would not have to give them 42 per cent in one year. Well, what does that mean? I can tell you what that means. What it means is that instead of in the last seven years increasing the transfers to the province at a rate of 7.3 per cent a year, we would have had to increase them at a rate of 14.6 per cent a year.
Now, is that not a tremendous number, 14.6 per cent a year rate of increase to the province of Ontario? I do not know where they think the money comes from, but I know my constituents are complaining about where it comes from: that trucker's strike that you all saw a few weeks back. It started at the comer of Wesley Road and Highway 401 which is right in the heart of my riding. I can tell you there are an awful lot of my constituents who are rather upset about the spending that exists at all levels of government, including this one right here, but also including the one in the province of Ontario.
When you listen to members opposite carp and cry about the rate of spending, I can tell you that the Government of Canada has nothing to be bashful about in our transfers to the province of Ontario. This year, in fact, our transfers to the province of Ontario will go up by some $220 million. Not down, but up $220 million. So when they talk about programs being devastated, it is certainly not being devastated by things that the federal government is in fact doing in the province of Ontario. It is coincidental that I have these numbers for everywhere else in Canada .1 note, for example in British Columbia, that we increased transfers there at a rate of 5.6 per cent a year for the last six years. Again, this is a number that is rather substantial.
In Newfoundland, I am happy to tell you, we increased it at a rate of 7 per cent a year. Again, it is not a bad number considering a 5 per cent inflationary environment.
Having said that, we are aware that there are sacrifices that we are asking Canadians to make in this particular
concept of getting our financial house in order. We just cannot ignore it any longer.
Financial management, responsible financial management, was our commitment in 1984.1 was not here in the first four years so I am not going to really comment about whether it was good, bad or indifferent. What I will say is that in 1988 I stood for office and was subsequently elected in November of that year. So I am here and I can say, "all right, I might have had some input". I did have some input in the '89 budget, the '90 budget and the '91 budget. I had opportunities to do so.
I do not have a problem standing here in the House saying "I was involved in that budget. Here is the money we are spending. Here is how we are spending it." Is it perfect? Of course not. We all would like to say, "Well, we could do a little more here; we could do a little less there", but we are Conservatives. We only get 98 per cent. That is the best mark we could get.
I compare that 98 per cent to the mark I would give the NDP in Ontario and although I might be biased, I would suggest that they certainly would not get a passing mark. Maybe the hon. member from the NDP might want to get up and give a comment.
What did we do from there? In 1989 we brought in our budget which set out some medium term fiscal plans to reduce our deficit and bring an end to government borrowing in markets by 1994-95. The budget reaffirmed this plan in 1990, as it said it would in 1989, and of course, here we are in the 1991 spending estimates and we are doing that.
In 1984 the federal government was handing out $1.33 in programs and services for every dollar it collected in taxes. Can you imagine that, $1.33 for every dollar it collected. That was a real bargain for Canadians. They did not realize what kind of a bargain it was. Unfortunately, they should have all been standing up yelling and screaming in 1980, '81, '82, '83, '84, "enough of these bargains. Cut it out because we know it is not going to be a bargain in the future." Unfortunately, that is where we are now. It is no longer a bargain. No wonder Canadians are dissatisfied when for every dollar of taxes they pay, they now only get 66 cents of service.
June 13, 1991

I would be dissatisfied. If I walked into the local convenience store, the local grocery store, the local men's wear store to buy something and you put something in your hands and the guy says, "well, that will be $10." You give him $10 and he takes the scissors, cuts away $3.40 worth of it and gives it back to you and says "here is $6.60 worth of the $10 item."
That is what we are doing now with the taxes we have and that is why I am pleased that in this debate, we are talking about expenditure. That is the subject we are dealing with here and I think the government is being very responsible in controlling that expenditure so that at some point in the future when Canadians in fact walk out to spend that dollar of taxes, they will ultimately achieve a dollar of service.
That is a challenge. It is a very serious challenge, but without addressing it today and tomorrow as we did in '89, '90 and '91, it just would not work. But we are not without heart. We are not without conscience. I notice that the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds is here in the House. He has comments and concerns and you know, it would be really easy for me as someone from southern Ontario to simply say, "why did we have an extra $3 billion in the spending to help the farmers of Canada in their time of need?"
I know that members opposite do not want to talk about the fact that we do have concerns. We could have come in with a $27.5 billion budget deficit, but we said, no, that is an expenditure to help the farmers of Canada. I do not have a problem supporting that.
That is one area. The other area was referred to previously when we were talking about some of the areas where government spends money. There was a comment about the fact that the Government of Canada does not do its share on research and development, and we are compared to the OECD countries.
The member was right when he talked about whether Canada contributes as much in research and development as other countries. In total on a per capita basis, no, we do not, but if you take it back a little further and look at the taxpayer contribution per capita, the Government of Canada does very well, thank you very much. What is missing is the business community, the business environment. What they need, some way or another, is encouragement to do their share in research and development
Supply
to make sure that the whole Canadian level of research and development is done appropriately. It is certainly not a problem of federal taxpayer dollars. The federal government is very clearly contributing in a very appropriate fashion.
So, where are we? Well, today with this budget, some time in mid-year, our total debt will reach $400 billion, which is about $15,000 for every man, woman and child in Canada. The interest alone on that debt will be about $43 billion.
It happens that last Monday or Tuesday I had a school group here from Bayview Public School from the town of Pickering, in my riding. There were about 40 of them from grade 8. I asked them: "Are you kids aware that each one of you has a debt of about $15,000"? They kind of looked at me and said: "No. Why do I have a debt? I do not have a debt". I said to them: "Well, you do have a debt, because we, your parents, are spending money on things, some of which you take advantage of, but we are spending money faster than we are willing to pay for the services we are providing". The kids kind of looked at me and said: "Well, is that not your role then, Mr. Soetens. Is it not your role to make sure that we do not spend money faster than we should so the debt does not go up"? I said to these students, "Yes, certainly, partially, it is my role". That is why, in 1988 when I was elected, the major item in my campaign was my comment that if I was elected I would do my utmost to make sure that the Government of Canada restricted its spending, held its spending in line so that we reduced the deficit.
I stand here ready to conclude that this Canadian government has the best record of all government levels, provincial or federal. Certainly, over the last seven years we have controlled our spending and kept it substantially lower than the rate of inflation. Although we have not solved the ills of of the country when it deals with fiscal or debt problems, I am comfortable to say that we are certainly going in the right direction.

$1 billion and $5 million. Or, if you want to take the total of cash and tax, it is $1,461,000,000. If you take the next chart, using the cash and tax combination, it says $1,454,000,000 which is a reduction of about $7 million.

That is the largest transfer from this chart which I got from the finance department. I will share this chart with you. I appreciate that the member may say that a $50 increase is not enough and I wish I could stand here and say we have sent you $500 per person more, but we just do not have the money. I hope that has clarified that position, but I have some other lovely charts here as well.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member to whom I listened with great interest gave himself a grade of 98 which he admitted was only a subjective guess. We can lend some objectivity to this estimate. The real grade is 14 per cent. That is the grade given to his party by the people of Canada right now and I suspect that that means that he will not have to worry about the next four years.
June 13, 1991

The hon. member has been at great pains to suggest, and causing all of us pain I must say, that those of us who argue, not that the deficit should be increased but rather that priority should be changed, are in some fashion arguing for an increase in the deficit.
Let us dismiss this out of hand. He was saying that he was asked by some children what he was doing about that $15,000 debt. What he did not address is that it is going to be very difficult 20 years from now for those kids to be earning enough to pay $15,000, even for a Honda, so long as the present government's policies with respect to science and technology continue.
Now, he does not seem too concerned about our relative position with the OECD. Everybody in the OECD is interested. Almost everyone who has looked at our economy is interested. I would dare say that those kids are interested in the fact that if things keep on going as they are there will be no jobs.
I want to understand what priorities justify spending in the order of $1.7 billion on a space program that the Americans are not even convinced should be set up. I want to understand what priorities have us move a science establishment 100 miles at a cost of almost $500 million. I want to know what priorities have the government investing $2.7 billion in an oil field that is going to mean more technological development in the United States than in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for his kind comments.
I had prepared some notes, but in view of the high level of discussion and the intellect that has been passing me by this evening, I have decided that I am going to take a slightly different tack from what I was planning. I am going to have to resort to a few statistics-

speechtext: Get the RCMP to look for your notes.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, no, I do not need that, I can find them myself. I will be forced to use a few statistics because, like my hon. colleague from Gander-Grand Falls, we always use statistics that matter. The statistics that I will use, for all those who are interested, come from the budget books that were prepared by the Minister of Finance.
Before I talk about them-and I am going to watch the time very carefully, Mr. Speaker, because I do not want you to have to cut me off one more time-I want to talk about predictions. For the viewers in Newfoundland, sometimes we get confused when we hear about GDPs, EEC, OECD. Some of that stuff is gobbledegargon to me sometimes, and I am sure to a lot of other people.

Supply
I want to talk about something that takes me back to my Newfoundland background, the background of a simple sailor.
I try to look at things in the smallest and most simple terms. I am looking at predictions. In the business of being at sea-most Newfoundlanders by definition know all about the sea-if you make wrong predictions, you are going to have to suffer dire consequences.
Let me give some examples. If your prediction on the tide is wrong-and the tide has a big range-you can end up by going aground, high and dry. That has happened to a lot of people.
If you predict that the weather is not going to come on and you have your ships, or boats in the case of fishing boats, alongside you will be blown adrift because a storm will come up overnight and your lines will break.
If you are at sea and your prediction about where the eye of the storm is going to be is really wrong, you are going to end up in the eye of the storm and not know it. You might sink or lose a lot of equipment and perhaps a few people.
If you make a wrong guesstimate on all of these various factors that influence mariners, you are going to arrive at your destination at the wrong time. Give or take a couple of minutes, that is okay, but we like to have arrival times within about five minutes. Even that is considered on the border of being professional.
Mr. Speaker, can you imagine somebody with a nautical background who is used to making predictions and has seen predictions pretty well on tab coming to the House of Commons and hearing predictions? You listen to them with great intensity. You take notes, go back and look for trends and projections, and then you hear another prediction. You say: "Good Lord, this cannot be the prediction that was made before."
I will be honest with you, Mr. Speaker. I have been very confused in the relatively short time that I have been in this House. Let me explain why. I think it is only fair that I go back to 1983-84, and I do not want to repeat what I said here earlier this evening.
In summary, the last Liberal government projected a deficit of $31.3 billion, and the deficit rounded out to $32.4 billion. That was not right on, but it was not too bad when I look at some of the other predictions.
I want to look at the 1984 budget. I do not want to go into the details, but I will say-the hon. minister was commenting on how close or how far off we were-that the projected deficit in 1984, the first budget of this government, was $34.5 billion. What did it turn out to be? It turned out to be $38.3 billion.
As a matter of fact, this government now uses $38.3 billion as a benchmark, as opposed to the previous figure. That is a prediction. Some predictions do not go right. I do not want to go through the succeeding budgets. However, I want to start when I really got into business in the election year 1988.1 arrived in the House of Commons in 1988. That was my year.
During the campaign, there was some confusion as to what was happening in the budget. In February 1988 the Minister of Finance predicted that there would be a 2.8 per cent growth rate that year. In fact, the actual growth was 5 per cent. That is an indicator to me, with my simple sailor background, that there were forces of inflation that should have been and could have been recognized at that particular point in time.
Were they recognized? I remember very definitely promises being made of a prison in my riding in the town of Harbour Grace. There had not been so much excitement in the town since the town was set afire in the 1900s.
The prison was promised and there were other promises made. I think they worked out to around $13 billion at the time. Somebody estimated them at that.
During the 1988 election I tried to stay on top of all the issues, but I never once heard the terms "the problem we have with our deficit, with our budget, the problems we have with the national debt". They never arose once, they were never in an election campaign.
I arrived in this House shortly after the 1988 budget, and what did I see? I saw a budget introduced called Canadian Economic Prospects in the Nineties. Then, all of a sudden, we heard all kinds of new terms which I had not heard during the election campaign. There were a number of problems identified. There were inflation increases, the interest rates were rising and then the word "deficit" came out, the big deficit that we had, the weakness in the domestic saving and the growing foreign indebtedness that we had. These were all new things to me.
June 13, 1991

I listened with great interest as the emphases on the 1989 budget, not surprisingly, were the following: the need for this and the need for that but still encouraged were the high interest rates, the high exchange rates, taxes were to be increased and expenditures restrained. The Minister of Finance thought that growth and demand would be moderate, growth in consumer spending would be moderate but resilient, I think was the term used, and labour market pressure would ease as would the cost pressures.
What happened? This is not conjecture, and this is not partisan politics, these are facts: By the end of 1989 the deficit remained the same as it was in 1984; the exchange rate moved up from 75.4 cents to 84.5 cents on the American dollar, and growth was reduced from 5 per cent in 1988 to 3 per cent.
We had the warning signs that economic times were going to be tough. The Minister of Finance really did have a chance to correct this, because the warnings were unmistakable. What did he do? He pursued the same policies, and if you look at the 1990 budget, it would appear to be a continuation of the chapter of the 1989 budget without any notice of a time warp. If you put the two budgets together, you would think that the 1990 budget was a continuation of the 1989 budget, despite all these warnings that were afloat, if I could use that term.
In the 1990 budget, the Minister of Finance exuded confidence, confidence that "after a short term of economic slowdown in the first half of the year, the imbalances would be corrected by the natural forces in the economy," and I am never sure what that means, and "sound growth would be resumed by 1991".
Inflation was projected to decline from 5.5 per cent in 1989 to 4.5 per cent by the end of 1990, and to 3.5 per cent by the end of 1991. The decline in interest rates was predicted and growth of 1.3 per cent was projected. The unemployment rate was then 7.5 per cent. It was projected to be 8.5 per cent, and then declined to 7.6 per cent. Why 7.6 and not 7.5 or 7.7 or 7.8? I do not know. 7.6 per cent in 1992-1995.
Even the most benevolent of the economic observers regarded these predictions as totally out of whack. Had these predictions worked, and at the time I hoped they would, we would not be in the state we are in today. I
Supply
would also remind the House that the prediction for the deficit at that time was that in 1990 it would be $28.5 billion and by 1993 it would be down to $14 billion.
We now know that the recession really started in about the second quarter of 1990. It may not have technically started, but the beginning was back there. As much as a year ago the economy was sliding downhill veiy fast.
I remember being here at Question Period for so long and the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister would not even use the word "recession". They did not identify it. They talked about all kinds of euphemisms and this, that and the other thing.
The expression that I remember so well was "a period of adjustment." What in the name of heaven that means is beyond me. You have to die to go to heaven.
Let me give the backdrop for the 1991 budget. It is not pleasant, but I have to remind us all. Unemployment is rising. The tax burden is so high that people are starting to do strange things. Inflation is rising. Bankruptcies have reached a record level.
We are presently in the middle of not a minor recession but a major recession, made in Canada and not world-wide like it was back in 1981-82. Public finances are running out of control and the country is in serious trouble.
This is the background for the 1991 budget. This is the background which the government admits it created. It even boasts about creating it. This is the sad tapestry against which the mosaic of the 1991 budget was created.
I am not going to go through the budget of this year because there have been many speeches made on it. I think really on all sides of the House, depending on your view, members have quoted things and taken different viewpoints and I am sure it has been very instructive to the Canadian people. I am not going to engage in partisan debate about who did what, why it was done and so on.
I am going to stick to the projections and the predictions. In going back to 1984-85 I am amazed, I am aghast at the predictions that were made and how far off the mark they were. By golly, if a mariner made the kind of predictions that were made over the last six or seven years, we would be aground. We would not be afloat. We would be cut adrift. We might even be sinking.

June 13, 1991

I hope that this is not the condition we find ourselves in today. I am more optimistic than that. I believe strongly in this country. I believe we are going to be able to pull ourselves out of this mess, but we are going to need something better to do it.
Whatever has been tried in the last six or seven years has not worked. I am not being partisan now. Going back to being a mariner, when you take over the watch from the officer of the watch or when you take over a ship from a captain, for a couple of weeks you can blame it on the guy who was there before you. You try not to do that, but there are certain things. If the drogues are missing you have to say "well, they were not there when I took over".
After six months in command you cannot turn around any more and say it is the skipper's fault, the one who left. You cannot do it. If you did, you would not be credible.
I wish, of all the things that I wish from the other side of the House, that it would stop blaming any government after a certain period of time. It is just not credible to the Canadian people, so it is not helping itself in doing that. I wish it would not do it because it is absolute and utter nonsense.
I want to remind the Chair before I get into my concluding remarks here that in the 1985 budget the Minister of Finance predicted that he would reduce the annual deficit to $20 billion by 1990. It is now 1991 and the deficit stands at $30.5 billion, the same as it was the second year that this crowd was in power.
If you want to make predictions, you could make all kinds of predictions. If I had more time I would answer some of these intellectual and perceptive questions which have been put in front of me, but I know that we are all interested in time and I may even quit a few minutes ahead of my time.
I engage in music from time to time, as we do in Newfoundland. I am a Newfoundlander. I love the sea. I make predictions about the sea. I like to play music. I like to sing. If you ask a Newfoundlander what he thought of the budgets we have had-if you pay attention, I want to
say something to you over there-what would they say about these budgets?
They would say that the tune of the budgets for the last six years has been "Happy Days Are Here Again", budget number one, number two, number three, number four, number five, number six, "Happy Days Are Here Again". What are they saying to this budget? They are saying: "It ain't necessarily so".

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my hon. colleague for making that point clear. Governments are very clever at doing things. If the proper action had been taken at that particular point in time we would not have found ourselves in the position that we found ourselves in 1989, 1990, and 1991.
One has to understand the motives of the government and-without trying to make accusations one way or another-one has to say: "Well, this is what has happened in the past". I am not going to predict the future but I get worried when I see $400 million extra being collected. Now that $400 million does not mean anything unless it is put against the base. That is against a base of $1.8 billion, $400 million more than was projected on a base of $1.8 billion. That is 22 per cent more.
We have a lot of experts in the Department of Finance and I am not attributing any partisan politics to them. I am saying that they are experts, probably as good as we have in the world, and the best they can do is predict and be off by 22 per cent in three months, revenue neutral. If that is a prediction and if that is how close they are to

These changes will-"

The employer's contribution rose from $2.73 to $3.92, another 45 per cent. I am going to make a prediction. I do not think it is over yet. I think there is more on the way whether it is called inflation or not. I will just finish off with that particular point.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak in support of the main estimates and for supplementary estimates for the fiscal year 1991-92.
What I would like to do is take a little time. Unlike the last speaker, I prepared some notes and I am going to stick with them.
What I would like to do now is quote a Labour Prime Minister from Britain in 1976 at a Labour Party conference. This is what he said: "We used to think you could spend your way out of a recession and increase employment by cutting taxes and boosting government spending. I tell you in all candour that option no longer exists, and insofar as it ever did exist, it worked by injecting inflation into the economy. Each time that happened, the average level of unemployment has risen. Higher inflation followed by higher unemployment. That is the history of the past 20 years."
That is James Callahan, the British Prime Minister speaking to a Labour Party conference in September 1976.
A finance minister in a budget speech said the following. You will also enjoy this. The finance minister said: "We intend to continue severe restraint. Our experiences this past year and our prospects next year force us all to recognize the central problems of control of public expenditures."
Many of you might think that sounds like the current finance minister, but it was Edgar Benson in October 1968.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: Wasn't he a Liberal?

He was a Liberal finance minister, speaking 22 years ago, saying: "Hold the line".
This is from another budget. The hon. member does not want to listen to this one. I have another article here that is by Mike Duffy. We all know Mike Duffy, the twin brother of the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext:
In this article, he said: "For a nation that has been truly blessed, Canadians are in a terribly foul mood. Over and over, Canadians keep being told there is an easy way out, but those Mulroney Tories are too stubborn to try it." Duffy says: "Give me a break. I do not know of a single politician who would rather make a tough decision if there were easier, simpler answers to the problem. The fact is that in our current economic situation, there is no easy answer."

The hon. member is having difficulty believing a journalist said this. Ten years ago, when John Crosbie was the finance minister, he said it best when he brought in a budget in 1979 that has been referred to, the first time we heard it: "Short term pain for long term gain". That was the budget of 18 cents a gallon.
What happened in that election? Canadians said: "I am sorry. We do not want to pay". And what did they do? They re-elected the Liberals. After the Liberals were re-elected they continued to spend money they did not have. They took out the little credit card and kept moving it through.
In 1980 the deficit of Canada was $11.5 billion. Canadians said: "No 18 cents a gallon. We do not want to face up to that". So, they re-elected the Liberals and the deficit went from $11.5 up to $38.3. We might even discount it back with the comments from the member for Ottawa, but the annual deficit tripled in those four years.
Those are comments from British Prime Ministers, finance ministers, but I have some comments from some Canadian constituents. Last November, I asked my constituents to give me input that I could pass along to the finance minister when he was preparing his budget. These are comments that came in to me three or four months before the budget came out. These are comments from Canadians. I do not know which party they support, but they probably support Canada. These are ordinary Canadians.
Here is one quote: "When my budget is tight, I have to cut charity donations and cut out non-essentials. Charity
Supply
begins at home. The government must as well. Keep all program spending to pre-1989-90 levels". That was one constituent.
Another one said: "A further general tightening up is necessary to bring spending under control". There is a constituent with common sense: "Tighten your belt".
Another one said, and this is a good one: "There is no easy way to cut costs when your spending has already outstripped your revenues. When it comes down to the nitty-gritty, then all Canadians must bite the bullet".
Another constituent wrote in saying: "I am getting sick and tired of carrying the bulk of taxes and wish the government would practise what they preach and start cutting back".
Finally, another constituent wrote in and said: "It takes courage to tell the nation that we must live within our means and act accordingly or face the devaluation of our currency to dissolve the national debt, but in doing that you would ruin people like myself who have saved responsibly".
This person recognized that if you do not get the debt under control, if you allow inflation to grow and inflation grows to 20 per cent, those Canadians who have saved responsibly are seeing their savings eroded away because of inflation.
Canadians might look at the projection of the $30.5 billion budget deficit for the fiscal year 1990-91 and 1991-92, and wonder how the government earned the reputation as a resolute fighter against excessive spending.
The amounts are the same so how can the government say it is fighting the deficit? Well the yardstick by which progress must be measured is the level the deficit could have risen to had we followed the free spending ways of previous governments.
In the current fiscal year, Ottawa must turn to the public financial markets for only 15.7 per cent of its cash needs, compared to 27.3 per cent in 1984-85.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1991-92-CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 1, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext: Remarkable progress, excellent.

speechtext:
To put that in terms to understand, what we are saying is that in 1984-85, when the government was spending money they had to go out and borrow 27 per cent of that in the public market. Today, in this budget here, we are out borrowing 15 per cent, because the government revenues have also grown.

June 13, 1991
Supply
I think if Canadians look at it in those particular terms, they can understand that if you have to borrow less money, you must be controlling your deficit.
When we took over, Ottawa was forced to borrow enough money to cover all its debt servicing costs and the $16.1 billion in program savings on top of that. In 1984-85 the government was bringing in revenues of approximately $70 billion. Government spending, not including interest on the debt, was some $87 billion. Here we are as a government, as a nation, bringing in $70 billion and spending $87 billion on programs which Canadians at the time had voted their governments to provide.
There is a shortfall in those programs of some $17 billion. What has happened over the past seven years is that government revenues have increased. Why have they increased? Because more Canadians are working since 1984 and the government has increased taxes. No one is denying that. What has happened is that instead of running a deficit of $17 billion on programs, we now have a surplus of some $12 billion. So we have seen on program spending, improvement. Because of that improvement we are able to take that excess $12 billion, and are we spending it on new programs? No, we are trying to control our expenses and what we are doing is using that money to pay on the interest which has accumulated over the years.
We have also seen many different ways of looking at the debt. Some people have suggested that the debt in 1984 was some $200 billion and they say the debt has doubled in the last seven years. That is true, the debt has doubled. Why has it doubled? Partly because there is $200 billion sitting there and whoever the government was it would have to pay the interest on that $200 billion.
For those Canadians familiar with a simple thing called compound interest, they would know that you have to carry that burden and that accounts for a large portion of the debt we have today.
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce has called on Canadians to go on what it calls a deficit diet reduction plan. Being on the deficit diet simply means that we have to curb our appetite for government programs.
The Chamber of Commerce said that we can no longer assume that we need something, a new community program, for example, for which we can automatically turn to any level of government for the cost. The Canadian Chamber of Commerce said that all Canadians must reduce their expectations of government. The business community is first in line to cut back on its consumption from the public purse. It says we need broad public support if governments are going to bring all government spending and consequently the deficits and the debts under control.
As major transfers to other levels of government represent almost 25 per cent of all federal program spending, these programs definitely have to come under review from the finance minister. Under the Established Programs Financing, the federal government provides equal per capita financial assistance to all provinces to carry out responsibilities for health care and post-secondary education.
Since 1984-85, the amount spent on established programs financing has increased by $5.4 billion to almost $20 billion. There is another transfer payment called "equalization" which provides substantial additional assistance to lower income provinces through the equalization program. Its purpose is to enable all provinces, rich and poor, to provide reasonably comparable public services, including health and post-secondary education at reasonably comparable tax levels.
Equalization payments, which have increased to about $8.2 billion, represent an average increase over the past six years of 7.1 per cent.
Under the Canada Assistance Plan, the federal government reimburses provinces for 50 per cent of the eligible expenses for social assistance payments and services to persons in need.
The Canada Assistance Plan programs have increased from $4 billion to just under $6 billion in six years.
As my time is concluding, I would like to talk about the cost of financing the debt. Again, we talk in terms of billions of dollars. It is difficult for anyone to understand exactly what a billion dollars is. The cost of financing the debt back in 1968 was about 12 cents on every tax dollar. I have no idea, if nobody in Halifax is listening to the CBC, why everybody talks about what they heard on the CBC wherever Haligonians meet.
I suggest that the current member for Saint-Maurice, if he perhaps ever came to Halifax, would know a little bit more about the situation. But in the meantime, he should perhaps leave the representation of Halifax to me.
Oh, wait, sorry, one further comment. I want to say that I did not-and I apologize-make a single comment about what this group has done to the health care system in Canada. I certainly could have. I will be happy to, because it is a disgrace and a disaster. But the member was clearly either not listening or listening to someone else.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to tell you a little story. I hope I have enough time to get to the happy ending, which is when the Conservative government took over the reins of this country.
Let me go back just a little bit in time and talk about a regime that saw itself slipping from power. It said: how do we keep hold of the reins of power?
I hate to attribute motives that may have been less than honourable to past members of this House, but I think evidence shows that there was a very deliberate plan in place by previous governments of this country to keep the reins of power. They used the opiate of the people, their own money, and the federal government's spending power, to keep them sedated, to keep them feeling that somehow everything was rosy, that all things were wonderful and that the time to pay the piper would never come.

June 13, 1991
Supply
I lived in those times. I was a young girl, in fact, when those times occurred. I remember the days in 1967, for example, when we were right at the peak of our international power when we actually had a surplus in this government.
The dream merchant came along who had wonderful things to peddle but did not have anything very solidly founded in reality. He convinced Canadians that if they would just follow his plan for this just society, this new Canada, that somehow all their dreams would come true.
Mr. Speaker, I would remind you that there was something else happening in the world in those days. It was the time of flower power. It was the time when everybody was on something a little strange, smoking weird weeds and things like that. Canadians and the rest of the world had lost touch a little bit with reality.
Canadians can be forgiven for following the song of the pied piper, for getting carried away on these Utopian dreams that said: "We can have it all right now. Everything we want will come to us and it will be ours. Nobody ever has to pay."
Nice story, but like all fairy stories this one had to come to an end. In fact, the pied piper of Hamelin did not have a dream to lead us to. The money he was spending on us kept us sedated, that opiate of the people, our own tax dollars that we use to feed people, to keep them quiet and make them feel secure that everything is all right.
All of that bubble burst, and we came in touch with reality. In 1983-84, I remember as a member of the Chamber of Commerce in Winnipeg and as a member of the community, the absolute desolation that people felt. There were no jobs out there. There was no hope for our youth. We did not think that Canada had a future. We were mired in debt, and worse, we had no leadership. There was no plan. There was no vision. There was no future for Canada.
That changed in 1984. The current Prime Minister came around. This government was elected. It had a plan. It had a sense of the future. It had a sense of direction. We are taking the country toward a goal that has promise, vision and reward. This is not just an illusion. These visions and these promises are based in firm, solid reality.
I am proud to be part of that reality and very proud to be part of that government. I hope that I did not bore you with my speech. The hon. member opposite obviously enjoyed it very much. I saw her applauding. She agreed with every word I said as she so frequently does.
I think that if Canadians at large would really listen to what we are saying and see what we are doing, they would understand that we are building a very firm foundation for the future. There is a Canada out there that we can all feel proud of and one that will give everybody, all of our children, some kind of hope for the future.
Canadians are proud. In two weeks, we will be celebrating Canada Day, and Canadians will have an opportunity to think about what it is that gives us this sense of pride, vision, the future and nation. Part of that will be their own sense of having a firm economic foundation and a government with a sense of leadership, direction and vision. They will be glad that the fairy tale was over in 1984.
